en: K.P. Jayaswal Commemoration Volume, Patna 1981, pp. 242–276. Revised by Michael Hahn based on the 1981 publication. 1. Ajātaśatru.
Since Ajātaśatru became virtuous after overcoming great evils by approaching and associating with the righteous, one should therefore cultivate only those who possess good qualities.

Oh, the power of the expansion of virtues! For by associating with those who are oceans of virtue, even one devoid of merit comes to attain the renown of virtue through unreal qualities among those adorned with virtue.
Yet, although that king was slain by time through that false attribution of greatness,
he attains a brilliance shining with virtues in the spring, like a tree consumed by frost.
For this is the natural perfection of a person whose conduct is consistently virtuous:
that even when they encounter adverse circumstances, they truly become a cause for the manifestation of their virtues.
Therefore I say: even dwelling in hell, terrifying with its flickering crests of fire, is better than the abundant pleasures of the lords of gods for one who has been rejected by a true friend.
Thus it is heard: King Ajātaśatru, having departed from his own city for the purpose of capturing a preeminent wild elephant, beheld a great and noble tusker charging toward the forest.
Upon seeing him, he pursued that very elephant; and that tusker—
Remembering the lakes adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, where droplets were tossed up by the wind from the wings of *kādaṃba* geese, and which possessed groves of young,
tender *kaseru* creepers, he proceeded with speed toward the forested mountains.
Longing for the trees resplendent with new shoots and the emerald-green meadows rising up like sapphire-blue,
the elephant, with its trunk spraying droplets of water, sped swiftly through the forests like a cloud filled with rain driven by the wind.
Then that lord of the earth, mounted upon an excellent horse possessing a swiftness of speed exceeding even the wind, and having left his supporting forces far behind, before long reached a forest.

It was a wilderness dense with thickets of thorny trees such as *khadira*, *badara*, *bilva*, and *iṅguda*; its regions were difficult to traverse, being matted with groves of reeds, *kāśa*, *kuśa* grass, and bamboo thickets;

its ground was whitened by fragments of skeletons and bones, worn out, decayed, and scattered about; and it was filled with terrifying and deep chasms, precipices, stumps, and ant-hills, making it difficult to enter or exit.
And that lord of elephants vanished from the sight of the king;
the king, his opportunity for valor frustrated, his efforts slackened and disordered by the exhaustion of summer heat,
and the hair on the crown of his head greyed by contact with the dust of the earth, fell into a state of confusion through sheer terror.
In that forest, strewn with rhinoceroses, tigers, boars, buffaloes, and serpents, which was as dark as the tip of a sword-blade...
Wandering alone, afflicted by the heat of the sun’s rays and tormented by thirst, that king suddenly beheld a path leading to the lord of mountains.
Following her for a moment, he saw from afar a region on the mountain ridge, dense with excellent trees whose branches were thick with dark, broad, and glossy leaves;
having seen it, he spoke with great joy.
In this region, there must surely be a lake whose waters are covered by a forest of fresh lotuses,
or else a stream of water falls from the interior of a mountain, possessing the clear beauty of a jewel-disk;
for the trees nearby have their abundant, dark branches and twigs nourished by its proximity.
By means of which these virtuous ones adorn this mountain, just as they adorn the entire world.
Due to their distance,
these [clouds], heavy with their burden like masses of clouds,
have indeed reached a state of supreme growth after encountering a reservoir of water.
Having approached a true friend, just as virtuous people [approach one], their enemies are utterly destroyed.

Thinking, "Therefore, I shall go from here," he approached that place and, looking all around, beheld in a certain thicket of excellent trees [a being] who had finished his meal, seated upon the expanse of a broad stone slab; whose physical form was gentle, with the movements of his senses stilled by tranquility, and who was visible amidst the offerings of flowers.

Upon seeing the Śākya monk, he felt comforted, as if gladdened and as if at rest; having tethered his horse to one side, the noble and steadfast man, with great humility and as if filled with devotion, addressed that monk with a breeze that was cool, fragrant, and golden-hued from the pollen of a forest of blooming lotuses.
"Venerable sir, you ought to point out a place containing water.
He then pointed it out.
Thereupon, the king, having approached that body of water as indicated, was freed from thirst and the exhaustion of fatigue... [and so forth].
With the surface of his forehead moistened by droplets of perspiration from the rays [of the sun],
though he drank water cooled by lotus and lily stalks, his mind, afflicted by intense exhaustion, found no peace.
Then that monk, having gazed upon the king with eyes moistened and cooled by the nectar-like essence of profound compassion, said:

"The popular saying—that those accustomed to comfort do not know the sufferings of others—is observed even in those whose power transcends the ways of the world; for it is as if [the king] were a person of weak character."
Is it not so, venerable sir?
Though already scorched by the sun’s rays of piercing brilliance, the earth is further consumed by the pitiless forest fire;
like a woman tormented by the sorrows of separation from her husband during his journey abroad,
she is now intensely heated by the most fierce solar beams.
But those who lack spiritual friends and are devoid of discernment are like men whose nature is dominated by passion, captivated by the amorous charms of women.
Afflicted by heat and unable to foresee the danger that has arrived, the frog takes refuge in the hood of a serpent for shade;
[it seeks] that which offers pleasure only at first sight— just like royal fortune (*rājalakṣmī*).
Perched within the hollow of a withered śāla tree, the pigeon cries out in vain, its throat parched;
likewise, the fool who professes a self, his mind swooning from the poison of thirst for rebirth, is like one trapped in the abyss of ignorance.
These elephants, scorched by the mass of the sun’s rays, find no composure either on the dry land or in the waters,
just like ascetics of fickle and limited intellect who wander through villages and forests in full bloom.

Just as the water of a pond comes to an end, leaving behind only a residue of mud reddened by the dust of withered moss, so too does the eloquence of one who speaks slowly in an assembly vanish when his own intellectual power has been refuted. (GoAś 18)
These birds avoid the forest trees whose masses of leaves have fallen away and whose branches are withered at the top;
like ignoble courtesans who have forgotten the pleasures of former enjoyments, they shun those who have lost their wealth and essence and possess little strength of character.
This circle of tree leaves, tossed upward by winds harsh with the ashes of forest fires, whirls without ceasing,
like the wheel of saṃsāra being incessantly pressed upward by the wind of karma that knows no restraint.
At its edges, it is rough with contact from fragments of cracked shards;
near the water’s edge, it is neither liquid due to the trickling of water nor excessively dry;
and in its middle portion, it is drenched by turbid water that remains only slightly.
The mud, containing within it a shimmering school of small fish, goes to dryness.
With its variegated leaves slightly withered and discolored at the base, possessing a mass of dull dark-green foliage that is hard and reddish at the root, having a moist luster in the middle,
and with its sprouts and petals drooping and darkened by the heat at the tip— the creeper is like a dancing girl.
In this age, the nature of true manliness and righteousness withers away incessantly, like the waning moon in its final phase.
Because the rays of this sun were so frequently scattered by my parasols— white as the orb of the cloudless moon and radiant with the luster of jewels— at the time of my departure,
this sun surely carries within his heart the resentment I have accumulated.
For whom the fire seems to burn with the sharp rays and sprouts of the words of wicked people.

Then that monk, wishing to speak on another matter, manifested a smile. The king, looking all around and seeing no one else, concluded that the renunciant had shown a smile specifically with reference to him; his mind overcome by curiosity, he said to him:
O Venerable One, this body of yours, steadfast in discipline, and this smile of yours are maintained with such composure;
yet this mind of mine wavers like a forest creeper struck by the wind—what indeed is the cause of this?

Then that king, his mind even more bewildered by the arising of doubt and agitation, again questioned the monk regarding the purpose of his smile. And that monk, out of a desire to be of service to the king, spoke to him.

The sun’s heat burns your body, my child; therefore, this [body], though accustomed to comfort, is a nest of disease. For those who are tormented by suffering, [even] pleasure becomes a source of pain.
O Lord of Men, garments, parasols, trees, mansions, sandalwood water, garlands, and so forth are merely the causes for the destruction of that [merit];
by what means, then, will the future suffering arising in the Avīci hell be brought to an end? GoAś 26.
O ungrateful one, when you inevitably encounter manifold suffering at the very moment your life-breath is obstructed, then—
[when] that [suffering] is upon you— your fear of elephants will be of no avail.
—in an instant. // GoAś_27 //
There, the fire fueled by karma perpetually blazes, intoxicated by the drinking of the blood, fat, and wine of the wicked;
it embraces its own offenders with dense, arm-like flames as if they were kinsmen. (GoAś 28)
They call it *avīci* because there is no interval (*vīci*)—not even a single gap of suffering—whether sideways, above, or below;
for that reason it is well-known as "Avīci. Therein, the shattered mass of existence spreads throughout the other hells.

There, you who are accustomed to the embrace of hundreds of flames and ought to cultivate the affection of guests, have fallen into distress when scorched by the sun’s rays; yet you fear a pearl necklace more than a serpent with terrible venom.

It is a marvel that you have not collapsed at that very moment after killing him— the one upon whose lap you sat, grey with the dust of the earth, and who, though his heart was pitiless, raised and protected you with love. GoAś_31 //
By him who, in childhood, wiped his lotus-face— soiled with saliva— with a hand as copper-red in its palm as a blooming lotus petal;
now that you have placed him on your lap, O wretched one, his side-locks of hair are curled.
Those who— [verse fragment] — // GoAś_32 //
Having slain even your own father, that righteous King of Dharma,
your mind distracted by the intoxication of the addiction to the taste of sensual pleasures,
you wander about in a state of apparent health, having entered the hall at the gateway to hell.
For they wish to touch you with the flaming hands of the fire of hell.

Driven by the fierce winds of your own karma, you will go on foot to that miserable hell—its interior made tawny by rows of blazing flames, surrounded on all sides by a mass of high, impassable, and unbreachable iron mountains; it is terrifying, crowded with throngs of living beings whose refuge has been snatched away, who are cut, split, agitated, shrieking, dragged out, crushed, squeezed, tossed up, scattered, plundered, and stripped bare;

there, with your arms raised and your voice wretched, you will dwell against your will, drenched in blood vomited from wounds inflicted by the blows of flaming spears, discuses, swords, and lances, and tormented by the extreme heat of manifold, fierce sufferings.

With eyes fixed upon the hollows of flaming circles of fire, with lips bitten by throbbing rage, and with upraised weapons, you will be threatened by the executors of Yama’s command crying "Stay! Stay! Terrified, looking toward the quarters of the sky, and with great difficulty uttering the words "I stand here," what state will you reach when held fast by your own evil deeds?

If you were to reflect upon this, O Lord of the Earth, it would surely be as follows: "In the intense heat of summer, these [sufferings] are like the sun's rays; yet ordinary people, for the most part, do not experience agitation unless they are struck by them. But those situated within the machinery of suffering, overwhelmed by futile lamentation, pain, and grief, grieve excessively."
Moreover, O dear son!
Having drunk honey held in the fingertips of your beloved, its moonlight-like luster gathered within the petals of her sighs,
tell me, how will you drink the copper-colored fire, its mouth forced open by the mechanism of a pair of tongs?
Having bathed in the water of the house pond, which is adorned with laughing lotuses and lilies,
embraced by the shade of trees and creepers bending over its banks with flowers,
and filled with the oozing fat from the carcasses of damp and perspiring human skeletons—
Having fallen into the heated waters of the Vaitaraṇī river, when will you be liberated from this suffering?
Having attained wonderful pleasure in a palace whose peaks are as white as autumn clouds, adorned with rows of flowers, and made sweet by the music of lutes, flutes, drums, and song;
[yet it is] constantly filled with a mass of spreading flames from clearly blazing fires.
Having reached the Avīci hell, struck by manifold sufferings, what indeed will you do?
Seeing his beloved— adorned with nothing but modesty, full of courtesy, and graceful in her conduct— with eyes expanding in joy at the sight of her unrestrained confidence,
[he beheld instead] those whose faces were made terrible by the knitting of uneven brows and the sockets of their eyes blazing with anger.
Upon seeing the servants of Death approaching you face-to-face, you will fall into utter delusion.
With glorious men holding beautiful chowries, with various kinds of horses, and with Kalinga elephants adorned with variegated northern blankets and used for scenting,
whose poison-like fierce anger was [fully unleashed]— [the army marched forth].
With feet shattered, you shall carry blazing chariots.
By you, the crest-jewel— fragrant with the scent of *bakula* flowers— is borne upon the head, as is a crown bristling with radiant gems;
and the inauspicious discus, tawny with its circling garland of flickering flames.
Carrying it upon your head, you shall experience the fruit of your own fickleness.
And furthermore:
A transgression of the command of Kali occurs only after a very long time for that sage at whose birth he was present— a sage who knew how to bring about the welfare and peace of living beings—
when that Blessed Lord, the Master of the World and remover of the afflictions of existence, was there.
What other destiny could there possibly be for those who are utterly corrupt than this?
When that ascetic, by whose radiant rays of fame the ten directions— once shrouded by thick veils of darkness— were as if opened wide, was approaching his end, [the world fell into darkness].
Struck down by his own very deeds, he is one whose self is wounded.

He who, like a mother, a father, or a kinsman, feels compassion for all living beings; who, with a mind turned away from self-attachment, remains unshaken by the afflictions within the dense forest of the wilderness of birth, aided by the companions of wisdom, heroism, compassion, and skillful means.
That Blessed One has attained unsurpassed awakening; what honor does he not deserve?
The Teacher bore the initiation for the performance of establishing the welfare of the world, which is exceedingly difficult to carry;
how then can they corrupt their minds even toward him, who is the very abode of mental serenity?
O Lord of Men, the bitter fruit of association with the wicked has now arrived for you, leading to an unfortunate state;
reflecting upon this, you should cultivate the company of virtuous people.
Then there will be for you an exit from the cage of calamities.

Even though things have come to this pass, O protector of the world of men, you must still exert effort toward the abandonment of evil and the arising of virtue; perhaps thus there may be an end for you to the ocean of calamity.
Having embraced royal fortune— which is beset by manifold calamities and whose nature is as fickle as the waters of the ocean tide— you have committed evil that ends in hundreds of sufferings.

Having fixed your mind upon sensual pleasures— which are terrible with many kinds of calamities and which, when examined, yield only a meager arising of happiness— you have yourself made your own self a witness to the sufferings of miserable rebirths.
The wise do not declare that an action performed with intentional motivation ever perishes;
even after ten million billion eons, it inevitably arises to bear its fruit.

For this very reason, the Blessed One—the best in the world, the light of the world, composed of compassion, and free from desire for worldly enjoyments—proclaimed that embodied beings possess their own karma. (GoAś 50)
In this very world, the wealth of men is plundered by water, fire, kings, and thieves;
yet they prevail through their own past actions. Therefore, it is one's own karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—that governs men.
When a man turns away with a steady gaze, his life bound for but a single moment and facing death,
then surely karma alone is his refuge.
One's own kin behave like strangers at the time of departure; one is deprived of house, wealth, and other possessions by others.
However, for embodied beings who proceed in accordance with the transition to a new existence, it is their own past actions that follow them.
Moreover, O Great King!

For a living being fallen under the power of death, whose lips and throat are parched by increasingly violent gasps for breath, whose chest is heaving due to the onset of hiccups, whose speech consists of indistinct and broken syllables, whose eyes are rolling in agitation, and while his vital organs are being severed—

As if departing in anger without taking leave of the vital points (*marmans*), the winds have caused the great machinery of the collection of joints to fall into a state of looseness; while life makes every effort to go elsewhere, amidst the intervals between the piercing falls of sharp needles of pain.
For one traversing a desolate path, perilous with dense darkness, there is no friend other than merit; therefore, exert yourself toward what is beneficial.
Moreover, O Great King:
One must inevitably abandon even one's most beloved kinsmen;
one must enter the terrifying and perilous wilderness all alone;
and one must dwell for a very long time in exile among people who are strangers.
Therefore, one should repeatedly prepare this abundant provision of wholesome merit for the journey.
Then that king, so deeply moved by that monk that in an instant he both desired to accumulate roots of merit and felt his mind agitated by intense fear and despair, spoke:
Therefore, O Venerable One, tell me now what I should do, if you have compassion for me;
O ascetic, lift me up with mercy, for I am a wretched man fallen into a great ocean of calamity.
Though we have been addressed by your words, which are as cool as clouds, breezes, and sandalwood, we remain tormented;
our minds, defeated by the greed for sense-objects, are pierced by hundreds of thorns of our own past misdeeds.
In the past, I—whose self was not disciplined—embraced the pleasures of attachment to sense objects, which are bitter in their transformation;
I committed many evil deeds that now burn my mind.
Fie upon this inferior, uneven pleasure based on the sense objects, practiced by the ignoble and unstable!
For by resorting to it, men here become constant objects of pity for those who loathe the sense objects.
Discipline was disregarded, fame was crushed, and lineage and future prospects were abandoned;
through the greed for sensual objects, one acted turbidly and openly displayed improper conduct by means of sacrifice.
Through the fault of habitually associating with unsuitable people, the destruction of my natural virtues has occurred solely because of my own misfortune;
I have been deceived by the words of ignoble men of treacherous intellect.
That I have been born here as one who must be pitied by those whose wealth consists of virtue.
Virtuous people, whose conduct is naturally beautiful, do not follow after the honeyed words of the wicked for the sake of honor.
I have become the target for hundreds of arrows of calamity from those dwelling within this dense thicket of misfortune.
Having bound the snare of hope for a mere fragment of sensual pleasure within the mind, and having cast it away like withered blades of grass,
he who possesses virtuous conduct has himself accumulated heaps of actions that are bitter in their ripening— like lofty peaks of a mountain—
so that they will consume me once again.
How could that hellish fire, with its fiercely stirred, disordered, and flickering tawny flames, not be [terrible]?
For even one who is sinful by nature dies indeed, but would any other person like me— who am constantly dying—
ever attempt to make the pitiless Death-goddess my slayer?
I have now fallen into utter confusion regarding the directions; toward which quarter shall I go?
O Venerable One, I seem to be sinking in a lake of grief, overwhelmed by my own evil conduct. This mountain seems to be splitting asunder today while supporting me.
But by taking refuge at your feet, it certainly does not split into a hundred pieces. (GoAś 65)
Then that Great Being, perceiving that the king’s mind was filled with agitation and determining that he was a vessel for the highest good,

said: "Therefore, O Great King, [seek refuge] in that very Blessed One— who is compassionate toward those falling into misfortune, who is the support for all people, who has abandoned the entire realm of sentient beings, whose application toward the welfare of the whole world never falters, and who is the abode of an immeasurable collection of pure, noble, and supreme jewel-like qualities."
Go for refuge to Śākyamuni, the Great Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, and the All-Seeing.
From him alone shall there be an end to the succession of your sufferings...
[as a seed sown in a fertile field becomes abundant fruit, bitter yet pleasing to the palate].
Or rather, it is the very nature of that field to produce all crops with equal quality;

likewise, even slight acts of benefit or harm directed toward the Blessed One do not reach their limit during this age of evil, for it is a time when the entire stream of afflictions has been brought to rest.

Then that king, his heart softened by the desire to accumulate a burgeoning store of roots of merit, having conceived love, reverence, serene faith, and great respect for the Blessed Buddha, gazed upon the monk with a face and pair of eyes— soft, half-closed like buds, dejected, and clouded by the moisture of tears born of conviction; his throat choked with a flood of tears and his knees resting upon the surface of the earth.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke as follows.
I go for refuge to that seer, the sole kinsman of living beings even at the cost of their lives, the one true friend, the one supreme teacher,
the protector of those beings who turn away from the deep ravines and caves of suffering in the three worlds.
The Teacher, the all-pervading Lord, who is the reality of the ultimate truth and the master of the true meaning.
Again and again, I go for refuge to the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the most worthy of refuge— even now,
I take refuge in that very Blessed One of inconceivable conduct.
The unsurpassed resolute intention that purifies the seed of the poison of conceptual proliferation.
I take refuge in that very Buddha, who possesses the nature of being solely intent upon performing benefit for the world,
and who [manifests] in a hundred ways and a thousand ways— [even though he is] devoid of the notion of abiding.
The helmsman for the ocean abode of sea-monsters.
I believe my very being has now been purified by the waters of merit arising from prostrations to the Teacher— waters as stainless as the mass of moonlight from the unbroken orb of the moon.
For who, indeed, having prostrated before him whose inner resolve is gladdened by intense compassion, [would not be purified]?
Having crossed over the river that possesses fierce precipices and crocodiles of despair, he has reached the shore where suffering has ceased.
Where even a single instance of mental malice in one of unrefined intellect spreads out the entirety of cyclic existence with hundreds of calamities,
how could a single moment of clarity of mind not sever that web of threads consisting of thousands of calamities?

I pay homage to that Lamp of the World, who has taken refuge in whom I have entered the noble path of Samantabhadra— which opposes all unwholesome conduct— and who feels compassion for those who are most wretched.
Having spoken thus, that king, turning away from his addiction and possessing unwavering faith in the Blessed One, the Fully Awakened One,
bowed with his head touching the ground to that monk and departed toward his excellent city.
Having attained such faith in the Perfectly Awakened One, that lord of men reduced the mountain range of his karmic obstructions until only a small remnant remained;
for whatever evil is committed against a Jina comes to destruction through those noble deeds.
For indeed, this [reality] which has the nature of a vajra can be inscribed by means of a single [method] alone.
Even if one must have the body of the Teacher cut with saws whose jagged teeth are sharpened by biting, it is indeed his command that must be carried out;
for those who turn away from it fall into hells dreadful with rows of flames.
By being devoted to his commands,
one attains the eternal bliss of prostration.
Therefore, I declare my own intention: I would endure to dwell even in the entirety of cyclic existence, even in a hell world terrifying with horrors, if it were adorned by the Victors;
but I would not remain for even a single moment in a city of gods, nor in a world empty of the Perfectly Awakened One.
In which the festivals of merit were plundered by hosts of Rākṣasas whose conduct was characterized by upraised violence.

Therefore, as long as the entire world has not yet fallen into the vast pit of negligence— the pit spread by false views and dogmatic opinions— and as long as the sun of the teachings of the Omniscient One has not set, one should for that long partake of this elixir of his words.
Having fixed one's devotion upon the Omniscient One, the Supreme Teacher, one should listen to the speech of the Sage, which is beautiful in every respect;
casting aside thoughts of evil deeds consisting of worldly afflictions, there is no task more supreme or greater than this.
What is the use of hearing for those who listen to what is untrue? [The rest of the verse is omitted.

2. One who craves existence [is attached] to the miserable states, to the paths of saṃsāra which for the most part are uninterrupted.
The activities consisting of suffering are necessarily under the power of karma and the afflictions.
It is thus heard:
there were two monks who had both attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). One of them, through the total exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*), realized arhatship;
the second, however, remained satisfied with that much alone.
He was addressed by that Arhat:

"O gentle-faced one, exert yourself to pacify the poison of the remaining afflictions. Existence has the single flavor of suffering; the means for achieving wicked and sinful success are [merely] 'blessings' that change in a mere moment and are not to be trusted."
Life is of an unperfected nature; sensual desires are like illusions, contrary to reality, fraught with fear, enmity, and calamity.
Having undertaken nothing but evil deeds, they are a source of contempt for those of unrefined intellect and bring even the wise into ridicule.
Even when pursued by them to a slight degree, they bring about great suffering;
no one who falls under their sway remains unscarred or uninjured.
Even those possessed of a sense of shame, when overcome by these, adopt the behavior of cattle.
These do not take into account the transformation brought about by the decline of age;
these arrogant ones utterly delude even the ascetics.
These destroyers of the highest good and adversaries of virtue, having transgressed the noble boundary that bears the splendor of the discipline of modesty, manifest nothing but ignobility.

In an instant, they defile a person’s excellence of virtue (*śīla*), even though it possesses the splendor of combined radiance. When virtue is destroyed—which serves as the gateway to all [spiritual] domains—then concentration (*samādhi*) is deprived of its secret essence and is no longer capable of bringing about the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Indeed, the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) has passed away through the pursuit of these obstacles that are difficult to overcome.
And as for those cravings for sexual pleasure that are common even to dogs, pigs, and the like—who among virtuous people would even mentally desire them?
He said to that Arhat:
"O gentle-faced one,"
Existences are of the nature of suffering, and the highest good is difficult to attain;
life is exceedingly unstable, and sensual desires are the source of hundreds of faults.
My states of woe have been exhausted; only a small remnant of the ocean of existence remains.
Having experienced divine bliss, I shall certainly attain nirvana.
Moreover, for those who have not performed meritorious deeds, fear arises from states of existence;
for those endowed with the equipment of merit, existence is a supreme festival.

Having quickly gathered together those who are like the blind upon a path that has been blocked—amidst the dense thickets of various calamities and precipices of misconduct—even the noble ones are led along a terrifying path; thus, the impure sense objects proclaim their own power.
Then that Arhat, perceiving that this venerable one had fallen into a state of mild spiritual urgency, said to him: "Venerable sir,
the states of existence are full of opposition, defiled by meager enjoyment,
and as terrible as the falling of the edge of a sharpened sword."
O dear one, these states of existence are not capable of being grasped, like enraged serpents;
they possess the power of mouths made terrifying by the sight of gulping down poison and fire.
By those whose minds are purified of the stains of the latent impressions of active engagement,
all activities whatsoever have been abandoned by the Lords of the World.
Seekers of their own welfare avoid from afar those who conceal their true nature,
like deep pits whose edges are hidden and which inspire fear with the danger of falling into them.
He revolves at the mouth of pleasures accompanied by suffering—
he, you, who delight in states that are momentary and unworthy of being accepted.
The Tathāgatas have declared that the reconnection of the stream of all conditioned formations once severed is the root of suffering and exhaustion.
These destinies are indeed deceptive even for the great;
they are truly the practice grounds for the falling of various iron arrows of misfortune.
This entire poisonous tree of saṃsāra is ablaze with masses of flame-like garlands from the fire of suffering that spreads in every direction.
Lusting after the enjoyment of existence, they enter of their own accord into the stormy days of the darkness of delusion;
with perverted intellects, they wander like the intoxicated, their vision impaired in thick gloom.

When men scatter their speech— which is harsh at first impact yet sweet in its ultimate effect— upon those intent on their welfare, they become submerged in a flood of the mire of misfortune and remain devoted only to sighing.
Those who attend upon the eloquence of the virtuous— which smiles like a flower— as bees do upon a flowering creeper,
cast off the abandonment of improper deeds and shall never again behold the terrifying face of the Kali age.
He said to that Arhat:
"These flowers of your words are unsurpassed;
however, there are the calamities leading to the miserable realms which I have experienced, and they were exceedingly terrible."
Venerable sir, I am experiencing for now that pleasure which serves as the cause for their remedy.
Then that Great Being, his agitation further intensified by those words of his, said:
"The Lords, whose speech is never in vain, do not describe even a momentary arising of existence.
For indeed, this emergence of the aggregate of aggregates is the source of manifold evils."
For the wise person who is devoted to establishing the welfare of the world, the undertaking of the continuity of existence is appropriate;
for those whose minds are fixed upon unsurpassed knowledge, the arising of existence is even dearer than the happiness of worldly existence.
But he whose mind is agitated by a mere fragment of the taste for rebirth seeks further existence out of delusion;
in vain he seeks a calamity that afflicts all sense-bases and faces every direction.

Existences are accompanied by sorrow, fear, and conflict; they are avoided by the virtuous of noble mind, like poisonous trees whose crests are stirred by the wind and whose hollows are inhabited by serpents.

It is said that seven more births remain for you; yet there is no fear for you of a further basis for rebirth. Even the attachment to existence, which is as impure as ornaments and ointments worn by the ignorant, is cast off by men.
You have already transcended the suffering of the miserable realms, yet you seek the course of rebirth;
for what man who wishes to live would consume even exquisite food that has been defiled by potent poison?
Moreover, O you who delight in existence:
for a man who, like a worm wallowing in the filth of a refuse heap, dwells somehow or other within the womb of his mother—is that not a great calamity? (GoBhl 24)
Is the suffering of a man being born— not by a stream of refuse that is his body, but by a foul, rainy gloom of blood and impurities— not equal even to the sufferings of the miserable realms?
Carrying a skeletal machine worn out by old age, as coarse as palāśa leaves scorched by a forest fire,
and with his joy somehow drained away by exhaustion— is not such a human being equal to hundreds of calamities?
With his own physical being pierced by diseases that burn, are incurable, and are as terrible as the falling arrows of Death,
he experiences the states of woe even here in this very life.

When, with his white eye-sockets rolling back and his face distorted like that of a tiger, terrifying and as if his very organs were being torn apart by a weapon-like wind that pierces the vital points,
he was seized and struck down before his kinsmen by the crocodile of Death; then—
What suffering indeed could be greater than that which is spread abroad by one who is enraged?
Moreover, Venerable One,
even the terrible Avīci hell— tawny with rows of blazing flames violently stirred by the propulsion of karma— does not cause you pain.

Those familiarities which produce weakness of intellect, which are devoid of meditative concentration, which breach the shore of virtuous conduct, and which are defilements characterized by swelling pride— these cause mental fever.
Then, as if manifesting the inherent wretchedness of sense objects, he said to that great seer:
"The mind attached to sense objects is turned back with difficulty,
like the Ganges, whose trees on the banks are overturned by the waves of water and current."
Many other learners as well, longing for the enjoyment of existence,
satisfy their collection of sense-faculties with sense-objects without falling into despondency.
And that Arhat, his mind even more agitated and fearful by those words of theirs, said to that trainee:
"For those of great discernment, the restraint of the mind is not difficult;
nor should one follow those who have been conquered by sense objects. (GoBhl 32)
Indeed, it was by me alone that the mind, which was unrestrained by sense objects, was restrained;
and by other heroic practitioners as well. Why then do you not follow their example?
If you should fall into negligence regarding sense objects that lead to ignoble conduct, alas, you are lost!
But if your mind does not become dispassionate toward them, tell me, what purpose is there in those things which have become a source of harm?
For those whose senses are overwhelmed by sense objects— which appear auspicious only through the delusions of their own minds—
all sufferings dwell nearby, terrible with their falling upon them yet unrecognized.

Deceived by the faults of attachment, a man does not perceive that the pleasures of sense objects— which follow upon their diminution and bestow the undiminished nectar of bliss— are devoid of true essence.
For those men whose minds are attached to the enjoyments of existence, there is contempt in their vicinity;
their hearts are distorted by sense objects, and the gateways to the lower realms are obstructed.

In the forests of asceticism, the wise take delight by disregarding the pleasures of desire— which are subject to change, inherently restless, and charming only through a perverse attachment to meager happiness— and instead they find joy in that which is not of such a nature.
Having restrained the mind that wavers on the swing of negligence by taking refuge in delight in the inner self,
the practitioners of yoga who do not abandon their practice rejoice in manifold superhuman modes of conduct.
Desires approach a person as if they were delightful merely through false attachment;
indeed, it is the ignoble objects of the senses alone that prescribe for men the vow of wandering through the cycle of rebirths.

In this world, which is like a tree marked for destruction by the onset of calamities and is overwhelmed by the demoness of the afflictions, the Tathāgatas—who bring about natural well-being—do not always appear. // GoBhl_41 //
Thus, this opportunity, suitable for the application of wholesome practice, has somehow been obtained;
in the matter of its execution, you are the authority, for a forest of birds is merely a place of clamor.
He said to that Arhat:
"O best of speakers, even if I were able to disregard my longing for enjoyments in a happy rebirth,
you should not speak to me thus again and again."
But because this night-stalking woman of sensual thirst carries me away,
O Lord, you reproach me out of excessive compassion.
That Great Being, once again stirring him with words tender with compassion, said:
"O child, we are weary from gathering drops of blood within these afflictive and perilous existences;
increasing our painful boundary and rendered helpless by manifold obstacles, we work only to our own and others' ruin."

O Great-souled One, tens of thousands of aeons have passed for us, whose bodies are being tormented by cruel, mutually antagonistic, and unappeased elements— like black serpents provoked to fury— and who are left without refuge.
We have been struck down by the aggregates, which harbor causeless enmity like enemies with raised daggers;
we have been tormented by sense objects that are like jars of poison. Therefore, let this attachment to the calamity of worldly pleasure be severed.
He said to that Arhat:
"If I do not sever the continuity of the aggregates in this very life,
I shall deliver myself after rebirth by means of your word, O Conqueror."
He replied to him:
"Even if this is so, nevertheless,
since you must die but once, you are seeking death yet again."
Having clearly seen that light, you plunge once more into vast darkness;
having found the auspicious path, you resort to a perilous wrong track— you who, though desiring the city of immortality, abandon it for something easily obtained.
Having crossed over the unfathomable mire, turbid with swarms of wriggling worms, why do you, O wise one, wish to fall back into it? Having been freed from diseases, you strive once more for disease.
Yet you, being pitiless, still long for further existences and sufferings.

O long-lived one, having abandoned those devoid of hope, lacking a final end, terrifying due to the ease with which they fall into ruin, full of enmity, filled with agitation, rendered tasteless by the heat of humiliation and contempt, and struck down by the falling arrows of calamity;
May you always cultivate the perfect path that removes the fear of cyclic existence.
Although he had already perceived the suffering of saṃsāra, through the force of his habitual passion,
he spoke to that Great Being as if piercing him with arrows of speech.
Those Bodhisattvas wander for many eons on the path of existence;
yet they are well-disciplined even after wandering through seven births—what kind of suffering can there be for those who wander thus?
Pierced by those words as if by a goad, that monk spoke to him whose mind was afflicted by the wretchedness of craving for worldly existence: GoBhl_54
O monk, you have not yet realized the suffering that awaits those wandering in existence;
having disregarded our words, you shall realize it once again.

And again I say to you: those pure beings who are resolutely intent upon birth itself, [seeking] the great bliss of tranquility and the extinction of nirvana— those for whom even the remainder of afflictions has its power pacified, and even their very appropriation [is stilled].

Those whose minds are overcome by compassion and who have accepted this entire world as their own self— their activity within the realms of existence is praiseworthy, but not so that of one whose intellect is perverted by the relish for worldly becoming.
Those beings who possess inner strength are not touched by the dust of sensory objects because their intentions are secluded;
those who, like the great mountains, act for the sake of others, are never distressed by sufferings.
Such Bodhisattvas, assuming rebirths, serve as embankments against the moats of others' cities.
They may appear splendid, yet it is not fitting for those who seek only their own sustenance to remain in the realms of rebirth for even a single moment.
For those whose every application is like the digits of the moon— sustaining all living beings and protecting the entire world as fathers protect their children sunk in the abyss of suffering—
the teaching of their birth is a festival for the great who have practiced virtuous conduct, a preeminent glory.
Due to your passion for striving after your own self-interest, you fall solely into the power of death.

At the time of their birth, the darkness that had completely enveloped the mind— though it was vast and familiar within the hollows of its own limbs— is wiped away by the rays of their virtuous conduct;
and the worlds seem to emerge from the midst of the terrifying, great flood of the mire of suffering.
For those who are skilled in benefiting others, their play consists precisely in such a continuity of births.
What need is there for more?
All these preeminent teachers uphold the weight of their observances and precepts; they possess the steadfastness of those at the forefront of the vehicle of Dharma;
their vigor is elevated by compassion; and they resemble the moon in gentleness yet shine with the brilliance of the sun.

The Bodhisattvas are always the escorts through the wilderness of birth, the destroyers of Namuci, the showers of sparks from the lamp of wisdom, the consecrations of omniscience, and the pairs of supreme persons.

Even when addressed in this way, he continued to remain devoid of any effort toward accomplishing wholesome qualities: "For those whose minds are parched and withered by a deficiency in realization, what can external favorable conditions do for embodied beings? (GoBhl 61)
Sages do not wash away evil with water, nor do they remove the suffering of people with their hands;
they do not transfer their own realization to others, but rather they teach the dharmas that are to be accomplished through easy practice.
Then, having passed away in due course, he took birth in the womb of a woman whose husband was away in Bharukaccha. After some time, he emerged from the womb;
and when his mother beheld him, disregarding her maternal affection and fearing public scandal, that poor woman lamented in various ways.

And though being entreated by her friends who shared her joys and sorrows, she, unable to endure the calamity of separation from her son, took that most charming child upon her lap and, with words faltering due to the force of her sobbing, surely spoke something to this effect:
When a son is born, mothers in this world of living beings become joyful at heart, seeing the fortune of their lineage awakening on all sides with uninterrupted vigor;
for those relatives swaying with joy, that day does not seem long.
But how is it, my son, that you were born for the sorrow of me, whose fortune has risen so poorly?
Now, impelled by my own past actions, you must experience the unbearable calamity that is the fruit of my own wicked conduct;
these and other multitudes of misfortunes are flashing down upon their heads.
Those who, having abandoned shame—which is cherished by the virtuous—resort to heedlessness.
O son, today you shall eat the fruits of your misconduct, as your mother’s soft skin is being devoured by birds with sharp beaks and claws, while you yourself become a mere morsel for them.
Fie, fie upon the attachment of the worldly, which flows with unprecedented force and is terrible in its consequences—
that by which a person, their intellect overwhelmed, acts with such shamelessness even toward things like these!
Alas! My mind reels in this perilous crisis, terrifying with its far-reaching despair, wherein, out of fear for public rumor, I am casting you, my dear son, into the wilderness.
Alas, how cruel is the working of fate; indeed, what I have undertaken is difficult to accomplish.
What shall I do? To whom shall I go for refuge? My heart is struck by the arrows of grief for my son. (GoBhl 68)
Alas, I am destroyed by a pitiless mind that follows the path of the fire of desire;
for this most difficult slaughter shall indeed be committed by me, devoid of shame.
Why does this earth not split open? Where indeed is that hellish fire, the carrier of oblations, who would not consume me—shameless as I am—as one might burn a handful of dry grass?
The net of light blazing from the mass of its extended crest is now falling upon my head;
yet, with a heart devoid of compassion, I am casting away my son, whose lotus-face is rendered impotent by the consumption of the flavor of my breast-milk.
While she was thus lamenting in various ways, the night became one with but a small portion remaining.
She said to her attendant:
"My dear lady, let it be known first what remains of the night."
She replied:
"O Mistress, for now the sky has its borders rosy with the garland of the sun's rays, its stars have become sparse, and the moon has turned away."
Like a sandbank of the ocean, it was coppery with the powder of coral and featured swans resting comfortably amidst half-blossomed palāśa flowers.
She said:
"This heartache of mine, which has persisted for a long time and arisen from my own misfortune— go, abandon this child."
Having spoken thus, her heart choked by the force of her tears, she suddenly fell to the ground and fell into a deep swoon;
having promised "so be it," she took that ascetic with her.
He scattered it upon the great highway like an unprecedented offering.
The cruelty toward my son has been laid bare, inauspicious and tormented by the suffering of birth;

yet, because of long-standing familiarity, my love for my husband remains deeply rooted and has not been seen [as such]. By the rains of embers of my own misconduct, I have consumed both lineages as well.
Alas! The nature of sensual desires is unreal and the source of all suffering.
Because his mindfulness was lost, he did not cry out; and because he was a seer of reality, he did not become angry with his mother.
But seeing that state within himself, the fool censured his own mind.
This was not my mother’s doing, nor is this calamity of mine without cause;
these misfortunes were created by yourself. O mind, abandon your despondency! GoBhl 77.

O ignoble one, having deceived that fragment of a mind, why now, through delusion, do you despair over the enjoyments of existence— which are terrible, giving rise to intense suffering— acting thus without reflection?
O ignorant one, having disregarded the words of that well-wisher who has himself been consumed by rebirth, why do you now fear suffering? This [suffering] is the very creation of your own karma.
Those who do not honor with their practice the words of compassionate teachers will encounter these and hundreds of other such distressing calamities.

The more he experienced the sufferings born from the onset of intense dualities, the more profound was the spiritual urgency that arose within him; with a throat choked with tears, the wretched man, his soul distraught, lamented:
"My teacher has departed, leaving behind these terrifying abysses and precipices covered with sparse grass—the miserable existences within the ocean of saṃsāra."
But we, whose souls are afflicted by a mere fragment of physical pleasure and who have lost all sense of shame, have met our end once again even after seeing the very shore of the ocean of existence.
Having burned the poisonous tree of the activity of the aggregates with the fire of wisdom,
and having attained mastery over all states of existence, the Sugatas— festivals of radiant glory— have brought about the welfare of the entire world and departed into peace.
Alas, we who are greedy for sense objects and covetous of existence have been ruined.

O you who are skilled in the yoga of discerning what is possible and what is impossible, it was rightly described by you with unsurpassed speech that the momentary arising of the aggregates is fraught with suffering;
therefore, like birds abandoning trees ablaze, you have abandoned these fragile states of existence.
The masters of mind, the yogins, are extinguished like fires struck by water.

Even after applying themselves to the dense thickets of scripture and allowing their minds free range therein, men are reckoned in this world as "of little learning"; for the noble ones say that the fruit of learning is the restraint of the mind.
Being pricked as if by the points of needles by ants with curved and formidable fangs,
his tender limbs greyed by the dust of the earth, he rolled over again and again.
Surrounded by millions of flies, his limbs soft and his hands and feet agitated by his efforts,
he writhed piteously and, filled with remorse in his mind, reproached himself in some way.
With his face turned away by the circles of cruel-sounding crows swooping down, he, rendered powerless,
met with an inauspicious calamity amidst the discordant cries of jackals, which were as terrifying as garlands of fire.
Even the mind of the Noble One, though naturally gentle, trembled.

Surrounded by throngs of flesh-eaters bold in their passion for killing others, he appeared almost devoid of life; yet he proclaimed the sufferings arising from the desire for even a fragment of worldly enjoyment, and his words were free from any taint of craving.

As he was thus wandering at the city gate in a state of great distress, a bull leading a herd of cows that were coming out saw the Venerable One; by the power of the workings of destiny, it stood near him like a father until the entire herd of cows had passed by.

With his body afflicted by extremely intense pain, his life-breath having reached his throat due to a lack of strength, let even this despair—"I must experience further calamity after death"—serve as a remedy for the suffering of that moment, for death itself. With his body covered in the dust of the earth stirred up by the flapping wings of forest birds, without a cry, with his lotus-like hands, feet, and face moving only feebly, let him now realize: "I shall no longer exist."
He began to pay homage to the Blessed One.
Then, as if drawn by the remnants of his own merit, lay followers arrived at that place, engaged in conversations based on the recitation of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Seeing them, he felt as if he had been restored to life; with soft and clear words, he extended his hand—tender as a lotus petal—and spoke.
"O noble sirs, please remain for a moment out of compassion for us!

Then, suddenly startled by hearing that voice and filled with the inquiry, "What is this? How is this?", they stood there, O gentle-faced one, and comforted that Great Being; yet, agitated by curiosity and eager to approach, they spoke again as follows:
Considering your state, your age, and this excellence of your speech,
our minds— agitated by curiosity— do not remain still.
Therefore, gentle sir, tell me: who indeed are you—a god or perhaps a dānava—and how have you come to this state that causes distress to virtuous people?
He said to them:
"I am a human being, O Great Beings; I am neither a god nor a Dānava.
It is through the thirst for the enjoyments of existence that I have reached this state."
Then, having heard those words, their minds agitated and uplifted with agitation,
they replied to him once more, moistened by the nectar of compassion:
"O virtuous one, we are lay followers who always seek what is wholesome;
we wish to hear it in detail, provided that you do not consider it a burden."
He spoke thus to them: "You are indeed my dharma-brothers;
let our sufferings first be warded off, and afterwards I shall speak in detail."
Having promised "So be it," and having taken them gently by their hands,
they wiped them and spread out their own garments, and seated them upon them.
With his body healthy and his mind composed, that virtuous man, examining the four truths as they had been perceived, soon cast off his gross impurities like dross from gold.
Like the sun dispelling the darkness of night with its rays, he [the Buddha] stripped away the specific latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation; thus,
his body— lightened by the removal of the heavy burden of effort and filled within with the expansion of immeasurable merit— shone forth.

Then that Great Being, having accomplished his purpose, abandoned that state for even a moment; out of great respect and solely to preserve his gratitude toward those lay followers, he assumed the cross-legged posture in the sky and, while being gazed upon by them with great reverence, related to them in detail everything as it had occurred, and spoke to them once more.
He who delights in birth delights in suffering;
one who delights in suffering is never liberated from sufferings.
The arising of this body, which resembles a festering boil,
is the very birthplace of calamities, distresses, and the burning pains of suffering.
All the pleasure belonging to the realm of saṃsāra, even when condensed into a single mass,
is overwhelmed by the momentary suffering of birth for human beings.
Like sharp iron spikes smeared with poison, like the crests of fire fanned by a powerful wind,
or like showers of stones accompanied by terrifying roars— such are the onsets of worldly existence, difficult for embodied beings to endure.
The intellect, which clings to the miseries of the continuous chain of existence and is shrouded by the darkness of perversion,
casts even a superior being down into the bottomless depths of calamity, from which it is difficult to escape.
For a person who takes up this [body], which resembles the bursting of streaks of lightning, which is bound to various forms of calamity,
and which is crowded with the transformations of conditioned phenomena, there is never any well-being.
Having themselves ignited the fires of existence— the habitual tendencies of conceptualization fanned by the wind—
these people, experts in misfortune, burn their own collection of sense faculties as if they were filled with rage.

O Lord, embodied beings— deceived by their conceit of happiness— are deluded regarding these enemies born of themselves, which are by nature suffering, inherently fragile, and as devoid of essence as a fragment of foam upon the water.
Having heard this mockery of mine, which torments the ears, what man indeed—
whose senses are not overwhelmed— would take pleasure in existence, which arises from manifold afflictions?

Being thus established, those whose minds follow no attachment to worldly existence or its enjoyments, and whose actions are completely purified, abide in that eternal, peaceful, and superhuman bliss.

Those virtuous ones whose pride has been destroyed and whose conduct is completely pure stand at the pinnacle of all prosperity— those who do not slacken their cultivation for the sake of pacifying the poison of worldly activity and grasping.
Having proclaimed the minute fragments of faults and the splendors of existences arising from various kinds of calamities and perils,
that seer, having stirred the assembly, immediately attained tranquility like a fire doused by water for the sake of the lay followers.
Thus ends the *Bhavalubdhakāvadāna*.

4. *Kapīśvarajātaka* = *GoKī*
The sons of the Tathāgata practice renunciation in such a way that,

out of compassion, they relinquish even their own lives for the sake of living beings, as if discarding diseases with ease; whereas the base, devoid of all fear, bind themselves to a delight in the commission of evil.
Having become single-mindedly intent on misconduct, they go downward, as it were.

Thus it is heard: once, it is said, the Bodhisattva was in a certain place where the uneven ground was covered with carpets of emerald-green grass, its luster like that of emerald gems; its borders were adorned with fragrant flowering creepers, and it was shrouded by trees bent low under the weight of fruits endowed with various colors, scents, and flavors.
In a vast forest encompassing lakes of pure water, where lotuses and blue water-lilies were in full bloom, there lived a lord of monkeys.
Although he had brought his merits to the highest excellence by dedicating his mind through great compassion,
that virtuous one nevertheless entered the lowest state of existence as an animal for some particular reason.
Performing noble deeds through both auspicious and inauspicious actions, as if playing upon the stage of existence,
he demonstrated the illusory nature of rebirth in its various forms, preceded by skillful means.
Although he had brought about the cessation of miserable rebirths by long remaining absent from the causes of ruin, he—
overcome with compassion— entered the animal state of woe, which consists of the darkness of delusion.
This world, lacking any support, revolves within the cycle of rebirths by the power of karma;
yet for him, whose intellect was faultless, there was freedom of will regarding both auspicious and inauspicious actions.
Although that Great-souled One had fallen into a state of ruin by means of his body alone,
he shone forth with a noble intention made tender by his unimpaired practice of virtuous qualities.
Having avoided from afar the conduct of the ignoble as soon as he heard of it,
he illuminated the noble path that leads to the arising of auspiciousness.
Precisely by abandoning the perversion of the notion of a self, he relinquished his own conduct,
which was attached to personal pleasure and followed the ways of ignoble people.
Beholding his beauty of conduct, which was contrary to his birth,
even the sages became slackened in their self-contempt.
There, attending upon his blind and aged mother, and desiring solitude, he abandoned his own troop and wandered through various forest regions abounding in flowers and fruits with an untroubled mind;
carrying her on his shoulder over uneven terrain, like a lord of monkeys bearing a garland that never wilts.
He attained incomparable freedom from debt toward his mother, who had been exhausted by the labor of bearing him in her womb and thereafter.

That being of pure essence attended upon his mother with various kinds of fruits whose flavors were brought to perfection by ripening, with honeyed flowers infused with fragrance, and with waters made delightful by blossoming lotuses and water-lilies.
Bound by that compassion, the lord of monkeys dwelt in secluded mountains and forests.

Then once, a certain hunter, armed with a bow, carrying a quiver on his back, with his girdle tightly fastened, and radiant with a mass of hair bound and hanging down like a creeping vine, came to that place while pursuing wild beasts;
his eyes were bloodshot with rage, and the expanse of his chest was dark as a mountain rock.
Then, seeing that inauspicious being with tawny, disheveled hair bound in clusters like creepers and earrings— like Death itself descending— the living creatures within his range fled elsewhere,
leaping over even precipices entangled with thorny vines.
Then that evil-minded one, his mind inflamed even more by the fire of anger due to the fruitlessness of his efforts, shook his head and sighed;
and wiping the sweat from his forehead with the hem of his garment, he beheld that lord of monkeys standing at the side of the tree, looking upon him with compassion.
And having seen him, he blazed up even more intensely with the fire of wrath.

Unable to harm the powerful one, the wicked—whose eyes were parched by their own malice—became inauspicious, like poison-spitting female jackals provoked by causeless anger, cruel in their intent to do harm to the virtuous. (GoKī 14)

Then that evil-minded one, having fixed a sharp arrow upon his bow, rushed with speed toward the Bodhisattva. But that Great-souled One, perceiving that his body was exceedingly attractive and thinking, "He has no such intent toward me,"— though capable of resisting him— passed beyond the path of that arrow with great velocity, his mind free from agitation, like a bird.
Although that Great-souled One was capable of pulverizing a mountain peak with a blow of his fist,
out of compassion for that wretch, he moved beyond the path of the falling arrow.

And that lowest of men, his heart agitated by the force of an even more intense fury and resentment, rushed toward the mother of the Bodhisattva like one who has drawn back a sharp arrow or a thunderbolt. Minds hardened by the practice of habit through engagement in ignoble conduct roam unrestrained among the people, acting without reflection upon evil deeds. (GoKī 16)

Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "Before he destroys my mother," disregarding even the loss of his own life, approached with a hurried and agitated gait and spoke to that hunter with words that were conciliatory, calming, and sweet:
"Wait, wait, O Great Being! Do not kill my mother!"
What merit do you see in killing this aged woman, whose eyes are fixed on her departed husband?
Surely, O long-lived one, your own mother is dear to your heart;
by analogy with your love for yourself, do not cause my mother distress.
It is not fitting for you, a virtuous man, to kill my mother, who dwells in the lonely forest subsisting on fruits, roots, and water. (GoKī 19)
Even when their conduct has been insulted, men of lofty spirit do not strike back out of pride against one whose mind is overcome by wretchedness.
How is it that compassion does not arise in you as you strike this innocent woman, who has already been slain by her own harsh deeds from the past?
Moreover, how indeed are you not ashamed to discharge this arrow, stained with the blood of the king of beasts, against the body of a female monkey?
These two arms of yours, swelling with pride, with elephant-heads upon them and forearms hardened by the bowstring—
when employed for the sake of the wretched, they clearly manifest your misfortune.
This arrow of yours, with its heron-feathered shaft, has never before missed its mark even among the wives of the lions;
yet now, like a bee directed toward a rival elephant, it is being employed against the fortress of the monkey.
Even when entreated by an enemy whose eyes overflow with tears,
the steadfast become more beautiful through the excellence of their anger being subdued at that moment.
Therefore, look toward the higher world and toward this aged mother of yours who has no other refuge;
do not fall under the power of the night-stalker of wrath, which brings hundreds of misfortunes in both worlds.
Even though he was addressed in this way, that man—whose heart was as hard as stone due to the habitual practice of cruelty—disregarded those words of the Bodhisattva upon merely hearing them.
Words spoken by virtuous people become useless for those whose minds have been made harsh by addiction to evil;
they are like torrents of water falling from clouds onto trees whose crests have been scorched by the fire of a thunderbolt.
Then the Lord of Monkeys, perceiving that the man of ignoble deeds was devoid of conciliation, fell into reflection:
"If this ignoble wretch strikes my mother while I look on, that alone would be my total destruction.
Therefore, sacrificing my own life, I shall protect her and this fame of mine, white as the night-lotus."
Granted, when I am dead, this distressed woman will die,
wailing piteously and lamenting, "Alas, my son!
Nevertheless, it is more fitting that my destruction occur first.
I have no power to witness the calamity that has befallen my guru.

To think that one who has been born will not perish is unreasonable; for birth itself is, by necessity, the cause of downfall. And when the calamity and torment of death are equal for all, death is better for one whose intention is dedicated to the welfare of others.

This festival, which marks the culmination of the period for repaying the labor she has undertaken— labor sustained by the carrying of her womb and bound by affection— has now, in due course, arrived for me with its extraordinary intensity.
But my singular, irresistible resolve drives away my grief, for it considers that if my mother learns I am dead, she will abandon this world of the living out of sorrow. (GoKī 32)
For his sake, however, this calamity has befallen my eyes; he shall not see me being slain by that sharp, cruel arrow discharged by the hunter.
And that this ascetic, having committed a sin, shall undergo terrible sufferings—
this thought burns my mind as if it were consuming me, regardless of his own loss of life.

Fie upon this state of being an ordinary person, a slaughter wrought by the demon of affliction; fie upon this "wise" man who brings only misfortune, for he pointlessly casts this world into the bottomless depths of calamity from which it is so difficult to escape.
Then that being of naturally pure nature, even in that state, his mind free from the agitation of unfamiliar grief or dejection, spoke to the hunter:
"Since this arrow raised by you, dear father, is not in vain, strike me without hesitation; do not commit the slaughter of one already dead."

Then that old female monkey, perceiving the Bodhisattva’s resolve—which was exceedingly difficult to perform and heart-rending—beating her breast with both hands, spoke to the Bodhisattva with a throat choked with tears and a faltering voice:
"Son, do not act rashly! Let this [lion] strike me instead."
What would be gained by my being dead, or even by my being worn out and drained of essence through old age?
"Father, that I live with a troubled mind, sharing in sorrow—
that is surely not better than the supreme essence of the bliss of being accustomed to union with you."
While you live, many who subsist on righteousness live;
when you have closed your eyes, it is evident that all the quarters of the world are closed.
Filled with agitation born of old age, my eyesight departed;
longing only for death, I am devoted solely to sighing.
"You are the very essence of my heart, my little son; through you I draw breath.
Know that while you live, I am truly alive, even though I am as good as dead."
As you approached, having entered the vast wilderness of old age, death came to me by fate alone, like a place of refuge. (GoKī 42)
Then the Bodhisattva, having bowed down and wishing to persuade her, spoke to his mother with words that were cool with compassion yet seemed as if they were burning her:
"For the sake of even a tiny creature, I would sacrifice even hundreds of bodies;
for the sake of my mother, even another person would abandon their body without any distress."
O Mother, I shall attend to this wound of your body myself, for it is terrified by the prospect of falling into intense calamity.
And bodily suffering does not produce such pain for me as I am tormented by this burning mental anguish.
Having disregarded even your own execution for the sake of protecting my body,
how shall I be able to endure this unbearable mental suffering?
Moreover, Mother:
all heights end in a fall, all unions with beloved ones end in separation,
and all accumulations end in the bitterness of depletion, like lamps at the break of dawn.
Living beings are like play-deer for Death, whose power is great and irresistible;
for embodied beings wandering on the path of saṃsāra, the imitation of dharma is the highest [virtue].

Then the Bodhisattva’s mother, her heart deeply moistened by those words— which were cool, unlike anything from other beings, the very outflow of compassion, overflowing with supreme affection, indifferent to her own life, and tender with unfading gravity and faith—
filled that forest with a pervasive voice and cried out piteously.
These words of yours, though cool, burn me like the falling of snow upon a creeper whose leaves have turned pale from ripening.
Alas, you who are devoted to your mother, whose mind is friendly even toward enemies, who are naturally noble and gentle in disposition—
having abandoned your son, where indeed will you go, O pitiable one?
Today, you have made me a target for the arrows of a hundred sorrows.
Alas, alas! I am ruined, wretched and fallen from fortune, by fate whose cruelty toward virtuous people is as ruthless as man’s own.
Protect me! Why do you abandon me this very instant? O son, am I not indeed your mother?
Where have those sages of blazing power gone today?
And where have those forest deities, your friends, departed? It is said that one who lives by the Dharma protects the world for the sake of Dharma.
Why does the world appear empty of my son as it closes its eyes?
The mountains, their heat blocked by rows of *kadamba* and *kubja* trees, possess waterfalls;
and the rivers bear garlands of waves, green and slender with the pollen of blooming lotuses;
and the forest ranges are stilled, while the moonbeams are brilliantly illuminated by peacocks.
And may the days, made radiant by the rays of the sun, protect my little son.
Even the insentient trees trembled at that weeping;
yet the heart of him whose desires were cruel was not softened in the slightest degree.

Then that evil-minded man, his heart inflamed by the fire of anger ignited upon hearing those words, disregarded the conclusion of the story and struck the Bodhisattva in a vital spot with a sharp arrow,
depriving him of his life.
At that moment, the quarters of the sky became shattered by the howling of jackals.
A dense darkness spread over the world, dark as a herd of elephants;
the mountains, their stones dislodged, trembled as if out of fear, and dust, tawny like a circle of swarms of locusts, fell from the sky.
At that moment, as the second sun rose, the rivers— with their terrifying dried-up waters, chasms, and caverns— became like a second sun;
blood fell from the sky, poured out as if from the mouths of jars.
When the lord of the monkey hosts, that sole jewel-mine of virtuous conduct, was slain.
Then that bandit, having committed that most cruel deed, immediately set out for his own dwelling, his heart agitated by the signs of its retribution.
And there, due to the transgression of that act, a great fire blazed forth—terrible, filled with a mass of irresistible and impetuous flames.
Even from afar, he saw it approaching, flickering with the tossing of the wind.
Immediately, fire embraces [the body] with its long, flame-arms as if with a beloved; for living beings,
an action whose fruit is magnified by the excellence of the field of its performance, which is unimpeded by other actions,
and which is as fickle as a physical transformation, does not wait to be deposited within the body.
Embraced by the flames of the fire, driven by the wind and spreading through the parched undergrowth, that man of cruel heart fainted and cried out, "Alas! Alas! in distress.
Tossed by the wind, licked by a row of flames, and with his throat and palate choked by a mass of pungent smoke,
that wretched man fell down and leapt up again and again like a distressed fish.
Even after burning the mere skeletal remains of that base man, the fire did not quickly subside as if out of wrath,
desiring to consume even the earth defiled by him.
It blazed forth, with flames turned tawny by smoke,
within [the heart].
The continuous streams of flames hanging down from the expanse of the sky, white as blossoming *karṇikāra* flowers,
shone like the flowing exudations of the Golden Mountain whose peaks were melting away at the time of universal dissolution.
Burnt already by the fires of his own evil conduct, that evil-minded one— along with his wife, sons, and wealth— is burnt again by the fierce flames like a withered tree;
yet the hellish fire, fueled by his karma, burns him even more intensely.
The fire, for a long time, possessed a mass of flames whose mouths were stained by the darkening of smoke.
Having understood this catastrophic ripening of the fruits of evil deeds,
one should avoid improper conduct as one would a female serpent;
and one should gladden the mind in actions that inspire confidence.
In the sons of the Jina, who are devoted to the welfare of beings without any ulterior motive.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth [tale], the *Śrīkapīśvarajātaka*.
