5. Since living beings who act harmfully toward their mother fall here in this very world into the abyss of calamity, virtuous persons—whose minds are constantly filled with love, faith, and great respect—[should protect] their mothers.
They are to be served.

As it is heard: he was adorned with a multitude of virtues like a garland of blossoming white water-lilies, moons, and *kunda* flowers; he had acquired in previous births an immeasurable, faultless, and vast collection of all the necessary provisions.

There was a caravan leader named Mitra, who was a repository of jewels equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) and whose vast accumulation of the finest riches was enjoyed by his own kin, the poor, and beggars;
his prosperities were exceedingly abundant and delightful, being solely devoted to the singular essence of helping others.
The rays of that noble being, white as water-lilies, were like the hands of the moon in a cloudless sky.
The minds of those possessed by hope, which had been scorched in many ways by the fires of craving fierce with the flames of grief,
were brought to tranquility by the sprinkling of the water of generosity, made delightful through affectionate solicitation.
Seeing this world— its festive joy of giving abandoned out of fear for the loss of wealth, its noble intentions corrupted by being under the sway of the demoness of greed and affliction—
he, out of compassion, bestowed wealth upon the helpless, the wretched, the weak, and the sick.
Having repeatedly considered one's own life to be as fickle as the waves of an ocean driven by the wind.
Upon which, having fixed their minds, the greedy plunge into the pit of sin— whose interior cavities are terrifying with the flames of manifest fire,
and whose edges are as flickering as the lashes on the eyes of exquisite women dancing to the force of the wind.
He bestowed those objects through gifts that were capable of pacifying the suffering of those who sought them.
Since he was childless and possessed of wealth, when the glories of sons— repeatedly brought forth by hundreds of his desires—

were forcibly made to have the house of Death as their sole refuge, their power being terrible and beyond all remedy like a fire fueled by the intense wood of enmity, then he, even though following only the path of common worldly rumor, descended [into the world].
He began to petition specific deities— Dhanada, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śaṅkara, Janārdana, Pitāmaha, and others— for the sake of a son; in whichever lake of a son, filled with the clear waters of merit,
he chose for his growth, there arose the lotus of the glory of a great and flourishing lineage.

Each of those [limbs] of his, rendered sapless by the sprouts [of his youth], was dried up by the clusters of the sun's rays, just as the sun dries up water; his body was like the orb of the sun at the end of an aeon.
He beheld Rudra, who bears a crown of many skulls, the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the creator, the one whose banner is the sea-monster, the son of the Mountain’s Daughter,
and the one seated upon a peacock; he also saw the Gaṅgā, with its waters as white as a conch shell, and those various gods.
Desiring a son, he went for refuge and gave many gifts again to the twice-born.
Whatever various [remedies] people perform through auspicious recitations, and through the hardships endured by vows and fasts—
with their minds immersed in the pursuit of success regarding sons and wealth— he cast aside those various [efforts] and dispelled his weariness.

When, despite various kinds of vows, fasts, and auspicious rites that cause exhaustion to both body and mind, his sons never at any time came back to life, then a certain virtuous man spoke to him as he was sinking into the waters of a vast and deep river of grief: "Even though you have performed many kinds of vows, fasts, and auspicious ceremonies that cause weariness to both body and mind, your sons have never at any time returned to life.
At this very moment, as you are sinking into the waters of this exceedingly vast and intense river of sorrow, a certain good man has said this to you."
The actions of embodied beings alone support all their prosperity;
for living creatures, falling from a lofty peak does not lead to well-being.
Many have fallen into affliction because their minds were tormented by craving for a son;
yet they do not live even now—why, then, do you distress yourself over this?
How could the inhabitants of heaven, having been liberated from their karmas, go to other states of existence by the power of their satisfaction?
For how could those who cannot attain a self-existence without certain [causes] undergo birth without them?
Those who are embraced by the creeping vines of the flames of the many sufferings of saṃsāra generally seek the happiness of humans, gods, and nāgas through giving and other virtues;
but you, dull-witted as you are, are being mocked by some, being mad with the hope for a son.
You, who desire to reach the heavens by relying on a flight of stairs consisting of great [virtues].
I shall explain another rite to you for the sake of success;
you too should perform it at some time for the sake of complete accomplishment,
should a son be born to you named Kanyakā.
Proclaim this throughout this entire land for the sake of its renown.
Then, after some time, she gave birth to a son who, like the sun-girt with its mass of rays, illuminated the vault of the sky; he was the glory of his own lineage,
possessing a brilliance as white as a freshly severed peak of a mountain of pure,
refined gold, and a broad, radiant head resembling the full, stainless orb of the moon.
His two arms hang down like the beautiful trunks of a rutting Airāvaṇa elephant, and his eyes have dark, reddish corners like a mass of blooming petals from a split blue lotus.

His form shone like gold fallen from the peak of Mount Meru, endowed with the delightful major marks that were radiant like clearly shimmering rainbows, produced by the power of great merit accumulated over many thousands of eons.
It was encircled by sprouts of jewels, matted together by the mass of its own rays that had been cast forth.
With a mind uplifted, he beheld his son named Maitrakanya, who was beautiful with hair as dark as a row of bees or yak-tail fans, possessing a broad and even forehead and a glorious, prominent nose.
After ten days had passed, he made it known throughout the world.
With various foods and drinks that were abundant, nourishing for embodied beings, and endowed with special qualities,
and with moonbeams as bright as nectar, it attained prosperity like the tide of the ocean.
Reared by nurses with milk and the scum of clarified butter,
he caused his beautiful body to grow like a lotus situated in a lake.
Then his father, the caravan leader Mitra,
having loaded the ship with goods along with the merchants, entered the ocean with joy.

In the great ocean where waves were increased by the agitation of *timiṅgila* fish, and where the vessel of living beings was destroyed by sea-monsters, when his father had passed away, he said to his mother: "What deed did my father perform? (GoMk 20)
Then his mother, her heart withered by the grief of separation from her husband,
fell into deep reflection: "Drawn by hundreds of snares of hope, a person does not perceive death, just as an elephant, miserable in its craving for sensory pleasures, does not perceive its bonds."
Even if I were to tell my father that he is on a small boat,
he too will meet his destruction in the ocean because of my sluggishness.
As long as this entire world does not ask him about the true livelihood of this country, nor tell it to him,
so long is it fitting for me to keep this son within the jaws of death.
To restrain [the world], which is dense with various sufferings and calamities and beset by disease.
Even a stranger who abandons the path frequented by the virtuous and resorts to a wrong path should be restrained with effort by wise people; how much more so, then, one's own son?
Then she spoke to the people:
"My sons, your father supported me by working as a sweeper;
if I am to be made happy, let him establish a sweeper’s shop."
Then, on another day, the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having honored his mother’s words with his head as if they were a garland of flowers,
entered the butcher’s shop.
For that being who was great in the accumulation of merit and possessed compassion for all creatures, [the following occurred].
On the first day, the wealth acquired amounted to four kārṣāpaṇas.
Delighted, he gave that wealth to his mother, who was suffering from the burden of carrying him in her womb,
so as to cut through the misery and calamity of poverty and to produce the fruit of great enjoyment.

Now, those long-established merchants in that excellent city, observing that the Great Being— who had won over the people of the market through his principles of impartial conduct and his natural kindness— was coming to them for the purpose of trade, spoke to him in order to turn him away from that business.
In former times, your father was a merchant-guild leader and a perfumer in this city;
with what intention do you abandon that livelihood and resort to another?
Then the Bodhisattva, having abandoned even that livelihood, established a perfume shop. On the very day he established that excellent perfume shop,
eight kārṣāpaṇas would accrue to him on that very same day.
He presented that [money] to his mother as well.
Then, the men who were the shopkeepers of the perfumers gathered together, approached the Great Being, and tried to dissuade him:
"The perfumer's shop was taken over by eunuchs; your father did not establish it in Vaimadyapura."
Having become a goldsmith right there, O virtuous one, he acquired vast amounts of wealth.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having abandoned even that livelihood, established a goldsmith’s shop.
By means of that trade, he surpassed all those goldsmiths in business practice;
on his very first day, he obtained sixteen highly valuable kārṣāpaṇas, and he gave them away.
On the second day, having earned thirty-two kārṣāpaṇas,
he gave even those to his mother for the sake of a distinguished recipient worthy of offerings. GoMk_32 //
Then, a group of men who were goldsmiths gathered and approached him, saying this in order to turn him away from that work:
"Having obtained birth in a family as white as the rays of the autumn moon, how is it that you resort to such a wretched livelihood for the sake of a living? (GoMk 33)
In a fire made terrifying by flames whipped up by a violent wind, with sparks flying about,
it is far more praiseworthy for men to turn back than to proceed toward a fall from their own conduct.

Your father plunged into the treacherous oceans, whose waves were violently churned by the breaths of great serpents, and having reached their roots anchored in the unfathomable netherworld, he acquired wealth for you.
Since you, being clever and desiring wealth, have now resorted to a livelihood that follows the ways of common folk,
how will you not fail to attain the abundant prosperity and the full measure of fortune that belonged to your father, even though he has passed away?
Even the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) could not sustain the burden of false wealth despite the vast expansion of his riches;
how is it that you do not feel shame before him, whose son you are, and whose fame is as pure as that of Mahendra?

Those wise ones who do not count death even in times of calamity, who do not dwell in villages or homes, and who are diligent with hearts free from attachment to kinsmen and sons— they, having crossed oceans of unfathomable waters terrifying with their whirlpools, [attain liberation].
Having obtained their objects, they fill the world with fame as white as the broken tusks of an elephant.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having listened to those words which were likewise appropriate, resolved to descend into the great ocean; approaching his mother, he said:
"Mother, our father was indeed a caravan leader in the past; therefore, grant me your permission so that I too shall descend into the great ocean.

She, whose hope for life had already departed due to the sorrow of her husband's death, now had her heart violently torn asunder by the weapon of grief at the separation from her son—a separation made all the more cruel because it was unexpected.
He said to his own son: "My child, by whom was this told to you—by a causeless enemy?
Whose life is undesirable to you, and who is playing with you?"
"O dear son, by some stroke of fate, you have today been granted one eye to me who am a sharer in suffering; yet now you are being carried away by death."
Before even this single shaft of my suffering has been destroyed by tearing through my grief,
how can a second one be hurled upon me by enemies consisting of evil?
Those whose minds are unshakable by various bitter fatigues and sufferings, and who have renounced life out of a base heart through greed for enjoyments—
they, having renounced [it].
Ignorant people, their faces wet with streams of tears falling from their eyes, go toward destruction by death in the abode of Makara.

Therefore, O best of men, let not that thought arise in you: "How can I make the effort to depart, abandoning this helpless woman who is to be protected, whose life is bound solely by the hope of your survival? GoMk_43.
"O son, having entered a state that risks one's own life, one cannot achieve absolute happiness; since this is how the fortunes of merchants are lost, I therefore dissuade you in this manner."

For her benefit, he cast aside even those flower-like words, though sweet, as if they were mere straw; and with boldness, he replied with something such as this, adorned with the splendor of self-exaltation:
"It would be better indeed if those people who are born were never born at all—those people who are destitute.
If there must be sufferings for one who is born, death is better than life."
Having come to my house with hope, those most wretched and miserable ascetics, seeking wealth from me, a sinner, depart sighing and dejected. // GoMk_46 //
Those embodied beings who lack the power to acquire wealth and such endure hundreds of sufferings;
yet, I cannot bear to look upon this world, which has long been tormented by hundreds of miseries.
Therefore, I disregard these words of yours; I shall go there—cast off your grief!
I will either meet my death right there in the ocean, or I will sever the calamity of this people.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, disregarding his mother, departed from his home and proclaimed himself a caravan leader in the city of Vārāṇasī:
"In this very city, which rivals the city of Indra, there once lived a merchant named Mitra, whose banner of fame was celebrated among gods and men."
"His son will set out for the great ocean on such-and-such a day; let those merchants who have prepared their equipment be ready to depart. GoMk_49 //

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka set forth, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants who had gathered provisions of various requisites, who were auspiciously prepared for their departure on a fortunate day, and for whom the performance of auspicious rites had been offered. Hearing that he was going, his mother said to him:

"O my only son, where will you go?"— uttering this with a most piteous cry, she, devoted solely to her lamentation, struck her chest violently with her two lotus-like hands, which were as languidly beautiful as soft and stainless lotuses, while her noble breasts and thighs shone like magnificent jars fashioned from fine gold;
her throat was choked by the continuous flow of streams of tears.

With her mass of hair darkened by rows of water-laden cloud-banks scattered and agitated by the force of the wind, she approached Maitrakanyaka, the Bodhisattva, with great haste and embraced his feet,
saying, "Do not, my dear son, depart and abandon me!
For men whose intellects are deluded by the grasp of harmful passion do not see what is truly beneficial.
Even the words of those who speak the truth, whose minds are intent on performing deeds for the benefit of the virtuous, do not find a listener.
Maitrakanyaka, with an angry mind, struck his mother— who was overcome by grief and sinking into the surface of the earth— with the thunderbolt of his foot upon her head.
Having repeatedly accumulated sorrow, and being impelled by his past karma,
he became quick-witted and resolved to travel with the merchants.
Then that mother, having risen, said: "My son,
since I have exerted myself to prevent your departure, whatever demerit has been accumulated by me from striking my own head, let it be yours."
May the fruit of this action not be endless suffering; do not transgress the word of your guru even in a dream.

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, wandering through many cities, towns, market-places, villages, and so forth— each more delightful than the last with their various monasteries, dwellings, mountains, groves, thickets, rivers, ponds, and gardens— gradually reached the seashore. There he prepared his vessel for the journey, [and beheld] the vast, pure water, agitated by the force of the wind made restless by the breath exhaled from the mouths of the lords of serpents, its surface colored by the red glow of the mass of rays from rubies as beautiful as the clusters of the morning sun’s beams.

He descended into the ocean, which was terrifying with its fierce waves tossed high by the wind, resembling the submarine fire flickering from the palms of the hands of the lord of the Asuras and Suras; it was a sea where the peaks of the mountains had collapsed out of fear of the fall of the thunderbolt, and where the mass of flames from that bolt struck the mountain ridges.
It seemed to leap into the sky with its surging waves uplifted by a great gale.
It was being seized by the currents of the waters of thousands of rivers, as if by arms that were graceful gestures.
The mass of waters was tossed and turned by the terrifying coils of agitated hooded serpents;
upon their heads were clusters of rays rising from jewels, while the circle of waves was dappled with masses of flames.
He released Śaṅkha, who was terrifying due to the burning of the fierce fire of poison from the words of the serpent-king;
he shattered the mountain with the tip of his fingernails like a thunderbolt, and he struck the schools of fish in the water with the foot of that mountain.
Its shores were raised by lofty waves; swans with soft cries rested upon its banks;
fish were made formidable by the scratches of the swans' claws; and the shoreline trembled as it was tossed about by the leaping fish.
The conch is radiant, covered with jewel-vines, its brilliance increased by the rays of the moon white as a conch;
it is fierce in the great battle against the aged serpent, while the wheel is struck by a terrible great makara.
The thunderbolt in the playful hand of the Lord of Birds struck and split the root-holes of the trees,
while numerous sporting kalpa-trees were crushed by the tips of the tusks of the joyful elephant Airāvata.

Observing that very ocean— a repository of waters possessing manifold wonders and marvels, with its shoreline marked by lines, its interior filled with circles of fish and serpent-hordes whirling within manifest and formidable whirlpools— as the lord of sea-monsters, whose body was as vast as a mountain peak, turned about, [the king beheld] the waves rising up, terrible in form like mountains and fierce with the sounds of their emitted clamor.

Being overwhelmed by massive surges of water, that ship, together with the sailors whose limbs were failing from the terror and despair of death and who were intent solely on piteous wailing and lamentation, suddenly began to sink into the depths of the ocean.
Struck in its center by the surging waves of the ocean— which were as high as mountains, fierce, and possessed of a violent speed like the winds at the end of an eon— that vessel was torn asunder.
In the gaping maw of the fish, terrifying with its fangs, one wretched man perished with piteous cries;
others, their throats choked by the surging water, went to their death, their voices silenced by the lack of breath.
Even after traveling with great rafts and looking toward the shore of the ocean, some—
exhausted by the toil of the long stretch of water and agitated by fear— cried out with loud, piercing shouts.

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, his mind undisturbed by fear, despondency, dejection, or distress despite that great calamity having befallen him, summoned a vast courage and prowess; taking up a plank with haste, he set out.
Thereupon, he was being tossed here and there by the surges of water, which moved with a graceful motion produced by the speed of a steady wind.
With his lotus-like eyes and face withered by lack of food, after many days and nights, he somehow reached the southern shore of that great ocean whose waters were difficult to fathom;
having crossed that unfathomable sea and reached the shore, he cast away the plank.
Remembering his mother’s words, he placed his head upon her hand and spoke this.
Those men who do not listen to the words of their elders— which are beneficial to themselves, conducive to the arising of welfare, and auspicious for their undertakings—
these calamities bring them delusion and prevail over their heads.

By those very wise ones who honor the words of their teachers in this world, the fruit of the tree of birth— which yields manifold misfortunes and is as fragile as the reflection of the moon in water— has been attained.
When shall I reach the end of such fruit—a flower as terrible with the weight of sin—as I, having transgressed the words of my mother who is ever-striving for my welfare? GoMk_65 //

I am a wicked man who, bearing the thunderbolt of my feet upon the head of my preceptor, treats with utter contempt the fierce sky— the thunderbolt of supreme wonder— which is as terrifying as the final traces left by the fire that has consumed all things.
How was it that he did not get stuck in the hole of the chasm when the earth split open?
Those virtuous ones who, with clear intelligence, carry out the words of those who speak for their benefit,
will certainly attain the highest good, just as [the gods did] in the city of the flesh-eaters; whereas those who,
having cast aside speech that is beloved for its great meaning and essence, resort to the opposite.
Having fallen into an ocean of calamities that is difficult to cross, they grieve just as I do.

Then, he gradually reached a dense forest thicket composed of *khadira*, banyan, *sarala*, *nicula*, *bakula*, *tamāla*, *tāla*, and *nālikeśara* trees; a place difficult to traverse due to the tangled masses of various creepers and vines trampled and crushed by the tusks of excellent elephants, boars, yak-cows, *śarabhas*, *śambaras*, and buffaloes;
a region where the feet of forest-dwelling creatures were scattered about in terror at the roar of agitated lions; and a place whose very borders had never been trodden by the feet of human Śabaras.
Following along and stopping at one point, he spoke thus:
"These monkeys, their faces as red as pomegranate flowers, letting out a clamor, have displayed rows of teeth in their laughter; they are devoid of fear."

Having struck with the clapping of their hands the snakes that are terrifying with the fierce flames flashing from their dreadful poison, they flee once more, helpless and terrified by the hissing sounds.
At the base of lovely saffron trees— cool with a thick carpet of shade, covered in soft green turf, and strewn with clusters of clearly blossomed flowers—
he performed the *praccheda* dance to the sweet sounds of flutes and cymbals accompanied by song.
With their minds set on singing together, these delighted kinnaras sing.
Then, having traveled not very far, he beheld a mountain whose form was like that of a preeminent lord of the earth;
in some places, its terrifying cave openings were made fragrant by the exceedingly beautiful luster of fierce jewels,
and in other places, it resounded with the songs of uplifted *kiṃnaras*, while the families of *nāgas* woke up in a state of agitation.
The trees, like dwellings, have their branches swaying with flowers tossed by the restless wind; at their summits, bees are fluttering;
the hollows of the caves are filled with the humming of bees; and within those hollows dwell families of fierce serpents.
The mountain peak was adorned with birds, with perfected beings (siddhas) seated upon the surfaces of its rocky crags;
its lovely groves were frequented by the wives of the perfected ones, and intoxicated birds nested within its bowers.
Delightful with the soft cries of intoxicated peacocks, with lions emerging from the mouths of charming caves,
with elephants agitated by fear at the roar of lions, and with breezes fragrant with the rut-fluid of elephants— GoMk_73.

In one place he saw mountain ridges where peaks were split by thunderbolts from the tusks of massive elephants, and where forests of *śikhāgara* trees grew in full splendor; in another, beautiful slopes were variegated by the outspread plumages of flocks of peacocks cooing in response to the deep resonance of the weight of clouds above;

and in yet another, flowering trees trembled in the wind as bright, fragrant water cascaded down, while the tips of the ridges were scented by the abundance of blossoms—thus he beheld the other [mountain].
He was as if painting the sky with his jagged peaks, casting away the darkness of the oceans with his rays,
bearing the mountain— weighty as a rock— clothed in the garment of the sea, and in some places shedding streams of golden water.
May that mountain, whose peaks and ridges are adorned with groves of trees, which possesses a wish-fulfilling tree as its ornament of pure blossoms,
where pairs of celestial nymphs dwell upon its summits, and which resounds sweetly with flocks of birds, burn away my sins.

In one place, it bore the weight of a crown formed by a multitude of great jewel-buds, made terrifying by the mass of rays shattered by the wind from the wheels of the great chariot of the Sun; in another place, its rocks were washed by the waters of the celestial river, where necklaces of swaying rows of swans were whirled about by the force of the waves as they were churned by the trampling of Indra’s lordly elephant; and in yet another place, it supported the coils of serpents drawn forth from the depths of the ocean when its surface was rent asunder by the thunderbolt-like arms of the great wings raised in the playful display of the king of birds.
In some places, there were great circular moats with waves of blood like lightning, produced by the weapons of the great asuras fallen in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Having seen this, he said:
"These [beings] have gathered upon a spot shaded by sandalwood trees on a mountain peak;
they possess an ear-covering whose splendor is equal to the shadow of the rays of the newly risen sun."
Out of pride, lions gaze upon the elephant as it is being crushed by great force— the elephant whose temples are being licked by bees eager for the flow of rut-fluid.

Thus, having traversed that impassable wilderness while subsisting solely on water and fruit, he wandered about until he beheld a city named Ramaṇaka, which the Lord of the Three Worlds had caused to arise from the mire of saṃsāra— like the world itself veiled by the thick darkness of ignorance— with its lofty, towering,
and fluttering banners resounding with the cries of birds swooping down.
With well-guarded houses shaped like mountains, featuring golden palaces and peaks of jewels and gold; // GoMk_79 //

It is always made into a dwelling by gentle breezes, which are reddened by the pollen of blossoming lotuses and by bees and lotuses that cling to them, and which are delightful with the soft warbling of parrots.

In some places, it was exceedingly captivating with massive trees whose branches were entwined with creepers of gold and jewels, which were like wish-fulfilling trees reaching as high as the temples of elephants, with grasses made of emerald gems and blue as the rays of parrots.
With its golden mansions, white as blooming *navakarnikāra* flowers and variegated with peaks of many jewels,
it bore the entire splendor of the Lord of Mountains, whose broad peaks of precious stones were radiant with their own rays.

In some places it was delightful with the sounds of great drums struck by the fingertips of celestial nymphs; in other places it was crowded with flocks of intoxicated peacocks, gladdened by the sound of cymbals produced by the clouds above.
Then, having regained hope for life upon seeing that [vision], he approached the city of Ramaṇa.

Emerging from that city, four apsarases appeared, their forms as bright as the hue of molten fresh gold; their pair of lotus-eyes possessed the playful beauty of blooming water-lilies, and their slow, graceful gait was weighted by the burden of various beautiful, tinkling jeweled girdles.

Their slender waists were bent by the weight of their full breasts, which resembled golden jars; the sprouts of their lips were radiant like the petals of a lotus awakened from its withered state by the touch of the sun’s rays;

they were adorned with hundreds of various ornaments and possessed a flawless appearance. With both hands joined in the *añjali* gesture like two lotuses upon their heads, they placed their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka and spoke.
A warm welcome to you, whose face is like the moon, who increases the joy of women,
whose mind is refreshed by the nectar of compassion, and who has long held a firm resolve for awakening.
This very day our sufferings have come to rest; this very day the essence of our life and body has been attained;
this very day, auspicious through the excellence of faultless love, our joys stand before us.
These minds of ours, mangled by the goad of suffering and scarred by grief,
have blossomed upon encountering you, like forest glades in the springtime.

The mere sight of you is sufficient as the fruit of those pure deeds, productive of auspicious results, which were accumulated by you in other previous existences; how much more so, then, would it be if you were to remain in my company for a long time?
Do not grieve this very day for the loss of kinsmen and friends; for whom do misfortunes not exist?
We four are your handmaidens, like celestial nymphs; we are but your shadows, incapable of transgressing you.

Jewels, radiant garments, most excellent couches and dwellings, and we ourselves—though our husband has been abandoned, we are worthy of the king of the gods; therefore, O Śakti, enjoy happiness here according to fate.
Moreover,
those who endure for a long time while remaining amidst great suffering that is terrible and without remedy,
being deluded by the onset of the burden of misery, go swiftly to their destruction right there.
While constant separation stands before them in the form of death, they grieve over a separation brought about by fate;
deluded by the onset of passion, they remember it and have fallen victim to the harsh blow of desire.

As he entered that city, which resembled a peak of the Golden Mountain and whose palaces were being pointed out by excellent apsarases with their exquisite anklets and girdles tinkling, many people there bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Furthermore, others wondered:
"Is it the Sun with its blazing rays, or has the Moon with its hidden beams suddenly descended? Or is it the God of Love, Puṣpaketu?
Alas! Is it the Lord of the Gods, who has cast down his supreme thunderbolt upon Hara? Thus was he conjectured.

Others, standing at the lattice-windows of the wind-chambers in rows of spacious mansions, their minds filled with joy, cast down [garlands] with loosened girdles; they were like drawings in the mass of darkness, with eyelashes as dark as a cow’s, wearing necklaces of bright gold and limbs radiant with set jewels.

He entered the abode of those celestial nymphs, a mansion where darkness was dispelled by jewel-lamps, whose floors were radiant with pearls, and where the clouds were pierced by the tips of fluttering banners.
Playing with their graceful movements, playful gaits, smiles, sidelong glances, and sweet chatter,
his mind entirely overwhelmed by passion, he did not perceive the time that passed.
And every day they tried to prevent him from going toward the south;
yet the more he was restrained, the more his mind became intent on traveling in that direction—
wherever a person is prevented by people who intend his welfare.
There, people with perverted minds run about in all directions.
If he were to act upon the beneficial advice of his friends in this world,
he would go to heaven; [otherwise], he will not even reach as far as the pit of the underworld, even in his dreams.

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having fully understood the purpose of those apsarases' visit, set out upon the path toward the southern direction. As he traveled, he beheld a city named Sadāmattaka;
from that city as well, eight apsarases emerged in great haste and led the Great Being inside.
Having enjoyed pleasure there for a short while, and with his departure being forbidden, he proceeded along that same southern path and beheld a city named Nandana.
Therefore, sixteen apsarases approached him, paid him honor, and led him inside.
Having enjoyed his play there for a long time, he departed from that place as well and proceeded to a city named Brahmottara.
There too, having again received hospitality from thirty-two apsarases and experienced the pleasures of the senses, he said to them:
I wish to go there, O ladies;
do not lie in a lake of grief on my account.
For who indeed in this world does not possess sorrows of separation, even when their arrivals are auspicious? (GoMk 99)
Even though I have remained with you for so long, at the time of my end, I shall be separated from you— the very enemies who are like Death itself.
Therefore, leaving you today with your cheeks moistened by the tears from your eyes, I am about to depart.
In this world of living beings, which is as unstable as waves tossed by the wind upon the ocean and is terrifying with its manifold sufferings,
there is no one more utterly deluded in mind than those who find pleasure in the pain of separation.

Then all those apsarases, their hearts withered by the grief of separation from his departure, spoke in agitation; like lotus-pools with the beauty of blooming lotuses and water-lilies, they placed their hands, folded like two lotus-buds, upon their heads and said:
"How could you wish to do us harm when we have offered ourselves to you with devotion and affection?"
Thus, by means of another body, he assumes an age that is perceivable by others.
"O Lord, even though you went to those three cities and have now returned here, you have long enjoyed the riches that are sweet with the pleasures of the senses.
You must not go back; what is the use of saying so much? If you are going, then go."
For when you have fallen into the ocean of calamity and are suffering, you will surely remember our words.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Since the excellence of prosperity for human beings is made stable through the power of habituation,
how indeed could it be prevented, or how indeed could it be turned back?"
Friends should always be urged by their friends toward whatever action is beneficial;
however, those who offer opposition in such matters are enemies by virtue of their enmity.
Having experienced divine happiness in the city of Ramaṇaka,
I was impelled by my own karma and have come here to enjoy the supreme bliss of Sadāmattaka.
Then, through the merit of my own deeds, I reached this desired city of Nandana.
Therefore, you have now been uprooted from the grounds of one who has arrived.
Therefore, ladies, let my departure be permitted;
do not restrain me, for there is no misfortune for us. Thinking, "I shall obtain superior joys from this," I have set out today. (GoMk 107)

Thus, having treated with contempt and disdain the words of those apsarases—which, though beneficial, seemed as if harmful—the Bodhisattva Mitrakanyaka proceeded by that same southern path and beheld [the city]. It was formidable, with four gates whose panels were clearly split open by great bolts; it was encircled by high, vast walls of iron, impenetrable even to the Lord of the Gods; and it was deep and terrifying, resounding with the cries of "da-ma-da-ma" emitted from the circle of wheels revolving within.
He approached the iron city and its gateway;
as soon as he arrived, at that very instant, the door— with its bolts and heavy panels—
burst open like the flank of the Vindhya mountain when its peaks are split apart by a stream of diamond-hard thunderbolts.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka entered there; but as soon as he had entered, at that very moment, the door— its panels and mechanisms secured—
clashed shut in an instant by the great force generated by the winds of his own karma, as if by the tips of mighty arms.

And he heard the utterance of a man whose heart was overwhelmed by intense agony—a most terrifying roar, muffled within the inner walls, which struck terror into all people; and having heard it, the quick-witted one leaped to the gateway. As soon as he had entered, the second door was slammed shut, as if to block him.
Like the gate of the gods, it was as firm as a diamond, pierced only by the force of the winds at the end of time.
Then the Bodhisattva Mitrakanyaka entered.
As soon as he had entered, a third door appeared, secured with a bolted mechanism;
in an instant, that entire city became agitated, and he beheld it all in a state of total turmoil, filled with fear.

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka beheld him— of truly dreadful appearance and magnitude, embraced by a cruel garland of flames, his head being split asunder like a piece of wood by a great, revolving iron wheel that was terrifying to behold with its rows of flickering sparks; his remaining life-breath sustained only by the nourishment of the blood and marrow trickling from his own head.
And having approached him, he asked:
"Are you a nāga, a deva, a chief of the kinnaras, a yakṣa, or a human?
Are you a soldier of the vidyādharas, or are you a daitya, or perhaps a piśāca?"
What extremely terrible karma must you have committed in previous existences, the fruit of which you yourself must now experience as this insurmountable calamity that causes such lamentation?
The man said:
"I am not a nāga, nor a yakṣa, nor a deva, nor a daitya; I am not a gandharva king, nor a rākṣasa, nor even a vidyādhara. Know that our birth is equal to yours. (GoMk 113)
The Bodhisattva said:
"What deed was committed by you, a person of evil mind wandering in the difficult terrain of saṃsāra, such that this iron wheel, blazing with fire, revolves upon your head?"
The man said:
"The Blessed Lady performs various difficult deeds; she reveals the nature of saṃsāra, is intent upon producing the happiness of the highest good therein, and her heart is bound by affection for me."

O virtuous one, I, evil-minded, struck with my foot the head of that mother— who is praised by those of noble intellect in the world as the supreme field for living beings, yet who, under the influence of demonic possession, was intent on committing a grave misdeed.
Therefore, this iron wheel, blazing with fire, revolves upon my head.
Then the Bodhisattva, his heart goaded by that man’s speech as a whip, beholding that contempt for others within himself, said:
“I, of little intelligence, was ignorant enough to reproach myself today;
yet how can I, who am myself submerged in these very multitudes of faults, mark the world with them? (GoMk 116)
I too, a base man, have committed an offense against my mother, who is worthy of offerings;
it is to experience the fruits of that very sin that I have come here, having crossed over the expanse of water.

Thus, immediately after his speech, from the surface of the sky—which was as pure as the petals of a freshly blossomed blue lotus—there arose a deep and majestic sound, resonant like the thundering of a water-laden cloud:
"Does he not see that the karmas of embodied beings are powerful?
Though dwelling beyond the world of light, one is dragged back as if by a noose."
Those who are bound by sense objects in the painful shackles that are fierce due to effortless karma,
and who— having abandoned the words of the Guru and being blind in intellect— resort to evil;
they are liberated by those very karmas which are auspicious and heroic in severing the painful shackles.
Having attained this human state, those of deluded minds who remain intent on ritual actions stay far [from liberation].
Then, immediately after his words, that wheel— terrible with its emission of a mass of sparks from a crackling fire, as if tossed up by the force of the wind of karma—
rose up toward his head and, having split open the head of the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka,
began to spin.
In an instant, his entire body shone as it was bathed by streams of blood flowing from his head,
like the falling body of Airāvaṇa when its frontal globes are split open and its head is severed.
Then that man, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", addressed the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, whose tiny body was being overwhelmed by the intense agony born of the burning:
"There are songs of celestial maidens, enchanting to the mind and bringing about the arising of joy in the heart."
Why have you abandoned those ancient cities and reached this place of endless suffering?
Who indeed, having attained a divine abode and the enjoyment of celestial pleasures through incomparable merits,
would seek out the terrifying pit of ruin with its constantly blazing flames?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Having abandoned forests crowded with the humming of intoxicated bees and with their tops ablaze with flowers, I have come here by that same longing which causes elephants to endure calamity."
Having abandoned kingdoms resplendent with vast wealth and the lotus-faces of women, many lords of men die in battle; it is for the sake of that very desire-tree that I have come.
Just as men meet their destruction in the great ocean— fierce with its surging, lofty waves and filled with the roar of whirling whirlpools— I have come here by that same fickle nature of desire.

I have come here because of that very nature of desire by which people cast aside the vow of the Lords of Sages—the path to the accomplishment of the glory and happiness of gods and men, and the means for achieving a bliss that is faultless and ultimate. (GoMk 126)
How could the dust from the feet of those sages, who are free from all suffering, not be placed upon one's head—
those by whom the precipices of the directions, fierce with potent poison and terrifying with manifold miseries, have been traversed?

What could that suffering be so exceedingly intense, or what calamity—a source of manifold miseries—that would remain far away for one whose mental state is wounded by the poisonous fire of craving? (GoMk 128)
Moreover, O virtuous one,
I am dragged away by my karma even while remaining far off;
for karma drags living beings toward that very place where it yields its fruit.
Moreover,
for how many thousands of years and how many hundreds of years will a blazing iron wheel revolve upon my head?
The man said:
"For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
a blazing iron wheel shall revolve upon your head."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Who else, having cut through this mass blazing with a cluster of flickering flames like the tawny crest of a radiant fire, would go astray? Only another would proceed in such a manner."
The man said:
"Whoever else comes here after having committed an act of harm against his mother, this shall revolve upon his head once more."
He has fallen away from you.

Then the Bodhisattva, although his heart was agitated by the intense suffering born from that burning on his head, addressed that man with a mind of intense compassion aroused for infinite sentient beings:
"Worthy of homage are those yogins who have extinguished the entire darkness of the net of passion and afflictions and who dwell in the expanse of the sky."
Furthermore, let those hosts of immortals, whose bracelets and necklaces quiver and whose crowns blaze, also listen, O virtuous ones! GoMk_133 //

Even if I were to commit an evil deed against my own mother, I would still strive for a long time to bear upon my head this great wheel— tawny with the glow of blazing fire— in order to carry it for tens of thousands of eons, through days equal to those eons, throughout the entire world.
For when I act for the sake of sentient beings, O man, my mind does not feel weary.

Then, immediately after the words of that Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, beloved of all beings, that wheel rose up from his head as if tossed upward; having ascended into the expanse of the sky to the height of seven palm trees, it remained suspended there,
shining brilliantly with clusters of flames flickering as they were struck by the restless wind.
The wheel, revolving repeatedly in the sky with its terrifying sound released,
was like the entire rising orb of the dawn sun shedding its mass of rays;
it hung suspended by means of pure jewels and other gems set within walls of flawless lapis lazuli.
Then the mountains, shaken by the winds that stirred their flowering branches and drenched them with water from cascading torrents,
trembled like those struck down, their long arms of peaks reaching up to touch the sky.
The abodes of the waters, where the waves were stirred up by the agitation of serpents and which resounded with deep roars like the thundering of clouds,
were then overflowed by the waters beyond their shores as they dwelt upon the crests of the jewels.
The orb of the sun-garlanded one, radiant with rays released without exception, shone in the sky;
from every direction, the quarters of the world were seen to possess manifest splendor, their interiors bristling with the sprouts of his rays.
With chests resplendent with garlands of flashing lightning and wrists bound by bracelets of Indra’s bow,
those clouds, shedding a little water, shone in the sky like a canopy.
Variegated garlands fell from the sky, and the inhabitants of heaven, filled with supreme joy, offered their praises;
many who had long been immersed in deep affliction and were tormented by pain became, in an instant, free from ailment.
While the wheel of misfortune blazes, his upper body torn by the edges and all his limbs drenched by streams of flowing blood,
he calms his own mind within the Blessed One, that mass of virtues.
At that very moment, that virtuous man went to heaven as if to his own home.

In the great ford of the water of generosity, perfectly pure through the cleanliness of ethical conduct, fragrant and cool with patience, and possessing a bottomless current of heroic vigor; GoMk_142 //
Standing at that great ford of enlightenment, which is profound and steady through meditative concentration and awakens the lotus of wisdom, one should remain eager for the city of enlightenment.
Washing away his remaining sins, he went joyfully to Tuṣita;
even while staying there, filled with compassion, he took delight after beholding the world.
Why has this been brought forward?

For it is thus that living beings who harm their mother fall here itself into the abyss of calamity; therefore, mothers should be served by virtuous men whose minds are constantly filled with love, faith, and great respect.
Thus ends the Maitrakanyakā-avadāna in the Śrī-Divyāvadāna.

7. Self-made delight in envy obstructs all happiness; there is no strife in the world equal to envy.
Having embarked upon which, men become immersed in a flood of calamities and devoted solely to sighing.
Thus, this being spoken, it is sufficient for the sake of spiritual urgency.
It is heard as follows:
there lived in Śrāvastī a caravan leader named Nanda.
Because he had bestowed gifts upon an excellent recipient in a previous birth, an immeasurable mass of enjoyment manifested from that seed of giving;
yet, due to his habitual practice of stinginess, he was unable to give even the slightest thing to anyone.
That ancient seed of giving, however, had fallen upon an excellent field.
He entered into a vast and flourishing collection of various riches;
yet, because he had not previously cultivated the resolute intention through practice in giving, his mind was then overcome by stinginess, and he was unable to give anything away.

Having attained the diverse splendor of ripening, sweetened by the continuous succession of fruits of renunciation itself, those who delight in misfortune strike at the very roots of prosperity; they are like those who, having abandoned the moonbeams so dear to the summer season, seek instead its spray.
They rush toward the forest fires with their massing, flickering crests for the sake of refreshment.
That miser did not enjoy pleasures himself, nor did he give them to his friends;
with a mind seized by the demon of stinginess, he did nothing but the acquisition of wealth.
Never before had twice-born men entered his house with begging bowls in their hands;
nor did he ever hear from the mouths of wandering mendicants the auspicious words of "May you prosper" accompanied by the gift of sacrificial fees.
Begging mendicants depart from the courtyards of his house with sighs and parched mouths;
even the crows no longer remember to bring him offerings of scattered grains.
Even at times of marriage, the sound of musical instruments did not arise for him;
even on occasions of welcoming guests, the friends in his house were dejected of countenance.
Avoiding his house from afar as if it were a cremation ground, the crowd of supplicants quickly departed by another way;
indeed, even by merely uttering his name at dawn, no one obtained food by the end of the day.
Even upon hearing the discourse on the certainty of giving, the miser trembled; even at the sight of a beggar, he was filled with dread.
He did not conduct his worldly affairs with those who delight in renunciation; indeed, Nanda would laugh upon seeing a donor.
Seeing even the religious gifts of others, he became filled with the impurity of envy;
that man of ignoble deeds never engaged in buying or selling with those whose nature was generosity.

Then once, Nanda—his body overcome by unbearable and harsh pain, his mind filled with fear, despair, grief, and dejection at the thought that he would certainly die—called his son Candana and said: "My dear son Candana, I have indeed acquired and protected this wealth through great exertion.
Therefore, my son, out of regard for what is dear to me, you must not give anything away to anyone."
"Go to the quarters of the outcasts; I shall no longer look upon you with such boldness.
Thus spoke that king, who always acted with deliberation, his eyes quivering with rage.
Having performed those base deeds, that ascetic died; yet even while dead, he first entered into a bond of rebirth within the womb of a Caṇḍāla woman whose eyes were wounded.
The conduct of sentient beings is diverse, and the course of their actions is inconceivable;
alas, the operation of sensual desires is defiled and ultimately terrible.
Blind, old, poor, an outcaste woman, and long afflicted by disease—she has become a source of intense passion; fie on the fruitfulness of those who indulge in such attachments! GoMn_14 //
Then that old Caṇḍālī gradually gave birth to a boy.
This thought occurred to her:
"Surely I have been shown compassion by the deities, since a little son has been born to me."
"Certainly, as this venerable one grows, he will become a staff for me when I am blind.
With her heart overwhelmed by joy, she said to a Caṇḍālī woman who was moving nearby,
"Sister, let it be known at once what kind of boy this is."
Having seen him, she said,
"May no one ever be like this," and asked, "How? How?"
Being questioned on that point, she replied:
"Your son will be like this: his limbs will resemble extinguished coals, he will be hunchbacked with a flat nose, blind, and his body will be shriveled."
Her mental continuum struck by despair, she said, "Alas, alas! I am ruined, I am unfortunate," and thus she fell into extreme distress. And she spoke:
Future objects do not cause such affliction to embodied beings as that which arises when they have been attained and are then subject to destruction.
Then that decrepit Caṇḍālī, her heart transformed by calamity, wept aloud:
"I have fallen into the mire of misfortune, deceived by my own past karma;
why has this dead woman been killed again for me by merciless Fate?"
A calamity, terrible for its lack of remedy, has come upon me;
the course of destiny appears to me to be exceedingly harsh and without cause.
Alas, I alone have been made a target by this wretched fate, which,
like an enraged hunter, uses the arrow of calamity to strike down the helpless and destroy their efforts.
O cruel-hearted Fate! Tell me, what benefit is there in destroying an old woman—her sight failing, her virtuous nature intact, and deprived of food, water, and other comforts? GoMn_20.
Thus, in this and other ways, that ascetic woman wept in many manners.
Then, as if in anger, she cast her young son— who was smeared with the impurities of the womb, whose body was like a wound,
who was struck by pain, and who was crying— upon the hard surface of the earth.
"Having committed deeds that bear the fruit of intense torment, why do you weep now, O wretched one?
Endure various kinds of suffering along with me, my son!"—thus did that ascetic woman lament.
For those established in pleasure, the affection that follows the happiness resulting from false conceptualization increases;
yet for those whose minds are tormented by suffering, these bonds consisting of the conceptualization of "the beloved" become loosened.
Then that ascetic, the outcaste boy— his loathsome body smeared with the moisture of fetal impurities, reeking of a pungent stench,

a veritable landing site for hundreds of worms and flies, his hands, feet, and face moving with painful and indistinct gestures as swarms of ants dragged them away, like a fresh lump of flesh cast upon the ground, even being attacked by crows, and like a denizen of hell whose remaining life was exhausted by his own karma— [remained there].
She endured extreme hardship;
due to his karmic transgression, her mother’s milk was exhausted,
and that unfortunate woman could not obtain even her accustomed alms.
With her body utterly exhausted by the pains of childbirth,
and afflicted by old age and disease, she became terrifying to behold, like a hungry ghost (preta).
He did not obtain even a mere mouthful of water, which even dogs would not have denied him;
this was either due to the karma of his own son, or because of his own actions whose results had turned bitter.

Then, when that *caṇḍāla* boy gradually became capable of walking about through the power of fate, his mother gave him a staff and a broken begging bowl, saying, "Go now and experience the ripening of the fruit of your unfortunate and unwholesome deeds.
Thereupon, the *caṇḍāla* child went to the very house of Candana for the sake of alms.
By that very same prior practice, he went to his own abode;
for action practiced to an extreme degree acts as a guide for embodied beings.
The merchant leader Candana saw that young Caṇḍāla, his hands occupied with a broken staff and a shard of a bowl,
his face drenched with saliva, snoring, and covered by a swarm of descending flies; his body afflicted by both internal and external impurities,
his few remaining hairs on the head roughened by the dust of the streets, and his skin scarred by rolling upon a bed of naturally coarse darbha grass.
He had not undergone the rites of purification or refinement; his face was loathsome, enveloped by fragments of snivel trickling from the cavities of his deformed nostrils.

Having been driven out from the entrance of the street, he was chewing over grains of chaff like a ruminant—a form as hideous as a *pūtana*, exceedingly misshapen, an embodied agitation, like sin personified, a mass of misfortune rolled into one, and an unprecedented creation of a *piśāca*.

He was like the entire fruit of unwholesome karma, a collection of the miseries of saṃsāra, the very mouth of Rāhu for the eyes of the world, the secret chamber of unacceptability, humiliation incarnate, the calamity of the city, the rejection of wrongdoers, the abode of ill-fortune, and the very seat of misfortune.
Seeing him sitting at one part of the house door, warding off crows with a staff, he—his anger seemingly aroused by the awakening of former enmity and resentment—suddenly spoke to the doorkeeper:
"Hey, you wretch! Drive away this inauspicious, luckless, and unsightly lowest of Cāṇḍālas!"
"And rebuke him in such a way that he will not come here again. Having promised "So be it," he [the king] drove away that young Caṇḍāla with a staff, uttering harsh words. (GoMn 28)
"O Kaśmala, if I see you come here again, I shall inflict upon you a punishment even more painful than this. GoMn_29 //
The mental aberration of one who is stained by the habitual practice of cruelty does not undergo contraction even toward the wretched; such is the nature of the wicked.
That wretched boy fell to the ground, his spine wounded by the blow of the staff,
manifesting the very fruit of his own most terrible karma for that hell.

Then that ascetic—his head and skull-fragment shattered, his knees drawn up and bent, his long shanks and arms scarred by fragments of stone, potsherds, and gravel; his body being drenched on all sides by streams of trickling blood; the opening of his mouth choked with dust from the earth and potsherds; his staff cast aside, his alms-bowl crushed, and the remains of his alms scattered upon the ground—was his body struck by intense agony.
Like a fish in the midst of scorching sand, he rolled about.

Then his mother thought: "Has my little son fallen into a precipice? Or has he been devoured by a dog? Or has he been deprived of life by a cow? Or has he been humiliated and tormented by young children? Or has he lost his way? Or [was it] by another?
"He has gone by way of the path;
or perhaps he is not coming? Thinking thus, her heart drawn by affection for her son, she went toward that place crying out, "Son!
Son! And that young boy, recognizing his mother's voice, wailed even more bitterly.
Even when meeting with friends who share one's joys and sorrows,
the sufferings of embodied beings are renewed, even those that have already passed away.
"Mother"—this is an unprecedented refuge of trust upon this earth;
"son"—this alone is the overflowing stream of affection, difficult to transcend.
Embracing him as he uttered piteous cries of "Mother!
with feeble lamentations, she wept with a long, deep, and distressed voice that made the city squares resound.
Whose son was there who felt no compassion for you, a vessel of singular suffering?
And who indeed was so arrogant with fortune, as fickle as the tip of an elephant's ear?
By whom has this manliness been displayed toward you, a wretch?
As one strikes at you, whose hand has not fallen upon the ground?
"By whom, my child, have you been slain by one whose heart is devoid of compassion? You have been struck down by the very bitter ripening of your own past karma."
By whom has this mark of ignobility been displayed upon you?
Who indeed is this one in human form who is being instructed by the rākṣasas?
Whose heart was made of iron? Whose hand was made of diamond? Whose speech was venomous? And who lacked compassion for you? (GoMn 39)
In you, born of a low family, childish, abandoned by friends and kinsmen, blind from birth, and subsisting on the alms of others— what cause for anger is there?
Out of childishness, that wretched and pitiable man, due to his long-practiced stinginess,
grieved over the alms scattered upon the ground, but not over his own body from which blood was flowing.
Then the old Caṇḍālī, slowly stroking the boy’s body with her hand as it was covered in wounds and bruises, said:
"My dear son, by whom has this condition been brought upon you? By what merciless, evil-doing, and lowest of men?
He replied:
"Mother, the noble Candana said to this man, 'Expel this inauspicious, luckless, and unsightly lowest of Caṇḍālas!
It is because of him that I have been so tormented.
Then that old Caṇḍāla woman, sighing long and hot, pressed her five fingers together and spoke these words in a harsh tone of anger:
How can there be nobility in that lowest of men who is short-lived?
This transformation has occurred in you, a fool, who are struck down by calamity.

While that wretched woman, overcome by grief, stood there, a great multitude of people gathered around her. At that moment, the Lord, the foremost of guides, his heart drawn by great compassion and taking up the task of converting those to be trained, entered that city with an unimpaired mind, like a Buddha traversing a bridge of freshly blossomed lotuses.
The citizens bowed from afar to that protector who was approaching like a moving mountain of gold, his form encircled by his own rays,
who had transcended the manifold illusions of worldly existence, with their heads inclined low in humble devotion.
Having gone to the white palace, their movements agitated by confusion like flashes of lightning clinging to the ridges of Mount Sumeru,
the young women worshipped the Noble One— who was like tranquility itself descending in person— with floods of flowers and strings of jewels.

The region of the earth became level, free from stones, potsherds, and pebbles, devoid of depressions and elevations; it was smeared with fresh green grass and covered with a carpet of scattered heaps of flowers.
The sky shone with a canopy of gathered clouds and an archway of risen rainbows;
gentle breezes blew, pleasant to the touch, sweeping away the pollen of the *sirindhrikā* flowers.
Showers of *tāla* leaves and blue lotus petals, with intoxicated bees nestled within them,
fell here and there like fragments of the vault of heaven torn asunder by the peaks of celestial palaces.

Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, the size of a chariot wheel, produced by the power of merit and emitting a fragrance released through the ripening of unfading virtue, the Blessed One, the Supreme Compassionate One, gave instruction to that Candana.
Your father Nanda, who with a body smeared with sweat and a miserly disposition both earned and protected this wealth,
now reaps its bitter fruits born from the poisonous tree of envy.
From this place, moreover, this one of defiled inner self will go to a state of ruin, where there is no refuge from the fear of calamity;
there many wretched and helpless people dwell, their bodies scattered by the blazing fire.
Beholding this state, which causes despair among one's friends and serves as a mere reflection of the darkness of delusion—
what man, wandering on the path of saṃsāra, would not offer even the flesh from his own limbs?

With faces shrouded in the darkness of afflictions and fearsome fangs, like mountain slopes scorched by a forest fire, the hungry ghosts wander in exhaustion, failing to reach water; this is the fruit of the poisonous trees of greed.
Some fools, their mouths parched with thirst, approach and behold a river whose banks are green with young shoots of durva grass,
yet whose interior is strewn with layers of dried mud and which blazes with fire.
The cool rays of the moon burn their bodies like fires, while even the rays of the sun seem to vomit forth embers;
and for them, even the south winds, though they release droplets of rain from the clouds, become as harsh as powdered charcoal.
Trees with pure, dark, and swaying foliage, which were beautiful merely by being gazed upon as if by venomous serpents,
suddenly become trees with parched and withered leaves, as if rebuking those envious men.
The calamities that lead inevitably to rebirth as a hungry ghost manifest among humans as well, in many forms;
thus, the misfortunes of those who hate renunciation—consisting of varieties of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and fear—are to be inferred from what follows.

When even a man of noble birth and virtuous character, his mind smeared with the pride of wealth, speaks weakly and slowly, saying "Give" in syllables rendered feeble by the distress of the five afflictions— that is the baseness of those conquered by greed for power.

Constricted by the fear of frustrated hopes, the wretched man is too miserable even to venture to say "give," though he be poor; that even a poor man observes a vow of silence before wealthy men at an improper time is likewise caused by greed in men.
There is no stain for people equal to greed, nor is there any injury to others equal to stinginess;
there is no friend equal to a beggar, and no other kinsman in the world equal to renunciation.
Just as bees flock to a lotus that has released its fragrance from its core and possesses a full bloom of scent,
so do many virtuous people attend upon a noble being who has cast off both possessiveness and pride.
Elephant lords with their foreheads moistened by rut, their girths bound with straps of fresh gold,
and swift, excellent horses adorned with yak-tail plumes, follow the person whose nature is generosity.
Women who are adorned with discipline, delightful in their conduct, and skilled in the arts of painting and other crafts,
come to the state of servitude for a man when he has previously won them over by wholesome means alone.
The virtuous enter with joy those magnificent palaces, which are as beautiful to behold as the peaks of Mount Meru, created by the very magic of their own irreproachable deeds.
For those who have closed the faults of the doctrine of birth, whose ornaments of conduct have not been stripped away,
and who have abandoned the refuge of turbid envy, rebirth in noble families is not difficult to obtain.

The body of men, possessing the delightful beauty of a cluster of flowers, captivating the bees that are the eyes of men and women, is the fruit of merit; it is steady and far-reaching through the power of their intellect and vigor.

The splendors of those men who have cast off the stains of greed shine with fame that outshines the radiance of a blooming bed of night-lotuses; they are the delightful rays of the moon of renunciation.
That the humble attendants of the king deceive the footstool with the clear, unceasing rays of their crest-jewels is the sweet fruit of that tree of generosity.
What need is there even to speak of those meager enjoyments that are miserable and, moreover, perishable?
Through giving, one obtains a beautiful and eternal fruit that is connected with irreproachable happiness.

Just as the wind disperses the mass of clouds, so do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, shake off the power of their enemies—those who oppose tranquility—and thereby attain the imperishable state; even that [attainment] has its seed in generosity.
Having overcome the hosts of opposing disputants, the Sages, the sole rulers of the world, lead their own teaching toward the ultimate truth; this is the culmination of a succession of renunciations.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the people had formed a resolute intention, possessed unwavering faith in the Three Jewels, and were turned away from dwelling in saṃsāra, delivered a discourse connected solely with the cessation of the suffering of existence:
"These sufferings arise when birth exists; when birth is exhausted, suffering no longer comes again."
Therefore, the wise person who desires not to be struck by hundreds of miseries should strive for the destruction of birth.
This suffering, together with its cause, arises from a source of fear, grief, and despair that has existed in an unbeginning continuum;
it depends upon craving, which deludes one through the conceit of perverted happiness, acting as a rogue in the drama of the three worlds. (GoMn 73)
This very stake consisting of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which burns the mind with the thought "I am this," is indeed habitual for a person;
it causes this beginningless and endless wheel of saṃsāra—devoid of a grasper and lacking peace—to revolve upon the path of birth.
Abiding in stainless morality and attaining mental concentration,
one scrapes away all the darkness dwelling in the mind with the lights of wisdom; thus,
one reaches the secure further shore of the great ocean of existence and its calamities.
With his self completely stilled, that mendicant does not come within the reckoning of either heaven or earth.

Those by whom the fire-sacrifice of the intellect has consumed the target of the connection to the aggregates— that bowstring of craving which aims at the discharge of the arrows of manifold calamities—
they alone are the fortunate ones in this world, they alone are happy, and they alone are blameless.
May it be well with them; they stand facing you, liberated from all fears.
For one whose intellect is overturned by the tasting of the flavors of empty forms and fleeting pleasures, and who pursues even a fraction of that ensnaring and variegated illusion,
bold calamities descend upon the head and roam there.
The fruit of virtuous conduct practiced throughout one's life goes entirely to waste.
Those desiring to attain the wearying splendor of worldly existence and the supreme peace beyond it must accumulate merit;
for a necklace, bright as the full moon, released by skilled men to bring about the king’s death, became instead a serpent.
Moreover,

why should one who hates suffering not avoid the strife of greed in his heart? For even the face of a monk whose mind was once tranquil became, it is said, completely devoid of openings at the time when he was offered alms by a devotee, due to the poison of greed accumulated from previous births.
Therefore, let the virtuous bathe the houses of their minds, soiled by the mud of stinginess, with the waters of giving;
for this wealth, which is fuel for the fire of greed and destined for destruction, must not reach the state of being consumed by the flames of calamity.
Having heard the words of that sole kinsman of the world and beholding that immense calamity of Nanda,
that people dispelled the darkness of envy from their minds and began to spread virtuous conduct, such as giving and other such deeds.
Thus ends the Avadāna of Matsarananda. Megha (based on the edition by Michael Hahn): “The Invitation of the Pratyekabuddhas.”
