8. *Megha*
Bodhisattvas do not reach satiety through merits as those addicted to sensual pleasures do through their perverse practices;
for the steadfast disregard even the pleasures based upon sovereignty.
Those who are treasuries of merit undertake exertion for the sake of merit.
Thus it is heard: the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, was indeed born as a king in the southern region, naturally inclined toward generosity.
Since he gratified the world with the waters of his gifts, just as a cloud pregnant with water nourishes the crops,
that lord of the earth became known as Mahāmegha (The Great Cloud), a title that was truly significant to his nature.
His heart did not become dejected or distracted by the expansion of his royal splendor;
that virtuous man bore those riches which were actually a source of harm, solely for the sake of others, just as a tree bears fruit.
In his presence, the world became as bold in the enjoyment of confidence as it was before a father;
and that lord of the earth, in turn, felt a love bound by affection for his subjects as he did for his own sons.
By nature he was full of reverence toward his teachers, and by his very disposition he was gentle with compassion for the wretched;
even toward those who had committed offenses, he maintained a mind of loving-kindness, while toward his friends he was like Samantabhadra.
The king, whose fame was like that of the lord of the planets,
had no such attachment to his own possessions as the people felt toward his exceedingly abundant riches.
Fearing what is harmful, he won over some by means of generosity; others, with various pleasant words; likewise, some by beneficial conduct; and those who were worthy, by sharing their aims.
This method of practicing for the benefit of others was not his own,
which the Lord of the World of Men did not make his own; rather,
it was some indescribable, radiant power from somewhere that somehow [manifested].
In the worlds, the Blessed One was a friend with whom he had no prior acquaintance.

Once, that lord of the earth, preceded by his assembly of ministers, beheld with a mind filled with supreme wonder the Blessed Pratyekabuddhas descending through the sky toward the north, resembling a mass of flax blossoms;
he then spoke to his ministers.
May you behold it!

These men, their limbs covered in garments as coarse as bark, having plunged into the sky which resembles a heap of *atasī* flowers, approach with movements stilled by tranquility; they are like birch trees whose roots have been uprooted by the winds.
One of the ministers also spoke with agitation:
What has been rightly said by Your Majesty; for why else?
Here come these [monks], fair as heaps of gold, their hems of saffron robes fluttering in the wind;
like ruddy geese with wings spread and not touching one another, they grace the sky as they approach.
Another also said:
These [beings], possessing the hue of clear sapphire, fly up into the sky and descend,
driven by the wind like autumn clouds whose edges are stained by the twilight.
The wind does not chase after these clouds,
nor do they naturally fall toward it;
yet their descent upon the surface of the earth is perceived in the sky.
And the sky, being unattached, is not suitable for the movement of feet.
Just as those lords of ascetics drew near, scattering what seemed like tranquility,
so too did that assembly, filled with wonder and joy, tremble, O King, as if it were ruled by a righteous sovereign.
They remained truly insatiable in beholding those great-souled ones,
yet they eventually passed beyond the range of their vision.
Then that king, his mind captivated by the sight of those great seers, spoke to his ministers.
Having beheld this marvel, my mind is filled with curiosity; therefore, I wish to hear a detailed account of these. (GoMe 15)
Then, among those ministers of the king, a counselor who was most highly esteemed spoke to the king.
Listen, O Great King.
When the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones whose very nature is compassion, do not arise, having cast aside the activity of the passions that has persisted for a long time. (GoMe 16)
When the world is shrouded on all sides by darkness and there is no refuge, then birth occurs for those who go from one birth to another. (GoMe 17)
Their intellects have deeply penetrated the profundity of dependent origination;
they delight in the use of beds and seats, yet they feel compassion for the lowly and the wretched. // GoMe_18 //
Always fearing social contact and devoted to silence, these moving beings wander the world as veritable heaps of merit. (GoMe 19)
Because these [beings] awaken by themselves alone, they are therefore called "Pratyekabuddhas" (Solitary Buddhas), having attained that very measure. (GoMe 20)
Then that king, his heart drawn even more intensely by his virtues, spoke to that minister.
Then [he asked], "Where do these Blessed Ones reside? He replied:
O self-conquered one, these [ascetics], whose latent tendencies toward worldly existence have been incinerated, dwell within the kingdom of King Megha,
amidst the groves of the Snowy Mountains where trees are entwined with the spreading branches of bending *nameru* trees.
The king said, "Is there any means by which these people might come to dwell within my own territory? The minister replied:
"Great King, if Megharāja is requested, then these women, having been so entreated, will surely come and grace your realm with their presence."
Then the Bodhisattva, in order to demonstrate his reverence for meritorious deeds, spoke to his ministers.
Therefore, sirs, make yourselves ready.
"I myself will go and personally inform King Megha of this matter, providing him with a vessel of honor appropriate for it. To this, those men, agitated by the journey, said to the Bodhisattva:
Your Majesty ought not to undergo exhaustion for a matter that can be accomplished by a mere messenger.
Moreover, O Great King:
Sovereignty is the essence of the pleasure of command, yet it is fraught with many calamities and perils;
therefore, it is not fitting for you to go suddenly to a foreign land.
The Bodhisattva said:
What weariness can there be for those who are devoted to their own welfare, whose minds are devoid of compassion, and who wander the path of existence while desiring merit? (GoMe 23)
How could there be weariness for those who, as true kinsmen of the world, have taken up these three realms of existence as their very own self? (GoMe 24)
The successful accomplishment of the task is not more dependent on a messenger than this;
nor is there any other duty for me that is weightier than this.
Nor do I bear the burden of sovereignty out of ignorance or impetuous haste; for we have been made servants here by compassion for the sake of all worlds. (GoMe 26)
The kingdom, which has been brought to fulfillment through many misfortunes,
can be abandoned by that very same king just as one might abandon an enraged serpent.
And having obtained the prosperity, glory, happiness, and wealth of sovereignty solely through dharma, how indeed could a wise man remain indifferent toward that very dharma? (GoMe 28)
Moreover, Venerable Sir.
Without exertion, even the trivial, essence-less, and unstable pleasure based on sensual desires cannot be obtained;
how much less so the state that is the locus of the prosperity of all three worlds, belonging to the incomparable Self-Existent Ones?
Having fixed our minds upon fleeting desires, we have suffered in vain through other births;
now, for the sake of the world's welfare, may these exertions of ours lead to the end of suffering.

How could a wise person not strive toward that [state], when by merely forming a desire for it, one instantly attains the status of a single kinsman even to those with whom one was previously unacquainted? (GoMe 31)
Although that Great-souled One was repeatedly exhorted by his ministers, who feared the calamity of his departure, he did not at all accept their words as authoritative.
Because that king had abandoned all longing, his conduct was everywhere permeated with compassion;
nevertheless, out of affection for their virtues, he remained respectful toward those sages and honored them.
Only those who have arisen through virtues become humble in their practice of worship toward those who have arisen through virtues;
for only those who recognize the excellence of superior jewels exert themselves most intensely toward them.
One whose inner self is afflicted by the desire for a reward examines only the excellence of the recipient;
but the compassionate one, satisfied by the mere fact of the petitioner's need, proceeds toward the essence among those who beg.
How could the wicked, who harbor expectations for rewards, ever find a place in the hearts of the wise, whose very nature— like the birth of trees— is solely the essence of benefiting others?
Then that Great Being, surrounded by a vast force whose devotion was steadfast through its adherence to his virtues, departed from his excellent city.

And as he was departing, the best of the twice-born, their single upraised hands busy with sprouts of dūrvā grass, flowers, and fruits, joyfully hailed him from afar, crying out, "Victory! Victory, O Great King!"

Then that Great Being, demonstrating the non-attainment of worldly auspiciousness and proclaiming the praise of the virtues of the Blessed Buddhas as the true auspiciousness, spoke with a pervasive voice to those brahmins who were attached to what is inauspicious as being auspicious:
For those of weak mind who have been defeated by the enemies that are the afflictions— cunning in bringing about every misfortune— what indeed can be called victory?
He who split apart that which is difficult to break—the darkness dwelling within—with the rays of analytical discernment;
he who burned away the creeper of craving that climbs to the summit of the tree of existence along with its roots;
and he who, having seized the serpent of anger from the depths of the cave of his heart, cast it far away—he is that very one.
Victorious is that Blessed One, whose nature illuminates the world and has shattered the wheel of saṃsāra.
It is tireless, roaming within an exceedingly distant range; it is difficult to restrain, difficult to grasp, and impossible to satisfy;
it is wretched in its craving for sense objects, illusory by nature, and fickle;
it is turned away from the path of absolute purification and oriented toward the side of affliction.
May that sage, who has tamed his mind and whose consciousness is undistracted, be victorious.

He who, casting aside the internal light, has utterly destroyed the long-extended latent impression of darkness— even though it was effortless— and who possesses a cessation that pervades the three periods of time,
whose sphere of activity is the benefit of others in every form, and who is independent of any other cause; [to him I bow].
Victorious is that Blessed One, the Buddha, the bringer of peace to the world, who is pure primordial wisdom.

Gradually passing through his own territory, which was adorned with groves of *tāla*, *hiṃtāla*, *tamāla*, *naktamāla*, *nicula*, and *bakula* trees, he entered a forest dense and difficult to traverse due to thickets of *khadira*, *badara*, *bilva*, *iṅguda*, *śamī*, and *palāśa* trees;
and as that Great Being proceeded with even greater speed, driven by his thirst for merit, [the journey] passed quickly.
The sky, obscured by the dust of the armies— tawny like a swarm of falling locusts— shone like a sandy bank cast up from the ocean;
in some places, it was cooled by the splashing of hands, fragrant with rutting ichor.
With the waters of the lords of serpents and with fresh masses of ground frost.
Having traversed that forest, he arrived in due course at the realm of King Megha. Agitated by his arrival and having learned of his virtues and power, King Megha went out to meet him;
with eyes wide open in great respect, joy, and wonder, he honored him with grand hospitality as he sat upon a costly throne.
He spoke various pleasant words to him.
A hearty welcome to the lord of the earth! Blessed is your arrival;
as this well-spoken word is heard in the world, you shall behold auspicious things throughout your life. (GoMe 41)
Who indeed could fail to honor this meritorious meeting of ours, so tender with the nectar of joy, which is like the union of the Himalaya and the Vindhya mountains?
"You are indeed perceived through your deeds that wander to the ends of the worlds;
yet, that which is the direct sight of you all brings about the arising of auspicious fruit."
Even when a blessing is directly perceived, people for the most part do not believe it, as their hearts are swayed by longing for something far beyond the reach of their desires.
Even as we behold you, the kinsman who brings joy to our eyes, we cannot reach a certainty as to whether this is a dream or an illusion. (GoMe 45)
O King, are you free from physical fatigue? Are you free from illness? Are you confident and unreserved toward me, and open to my affection?
Do your beloveds from the Deccan— the moonlight of the southern region— not cause you longing, their eyes copper-hued at the corners and motionless with deep meditation?
O King, is this association with the virtuous perhaps unfailing and effortless?
And do you take delight here as if in your own country?
Then the Bodhisattva, encouraging that king with words laden with unfading affection, spoke:
O lord of the earth, having seen you who are so worthy of being beheld, I have found rest;
for who would not feel confidence even in one as ignoble as I, when in the presence of someone like you?
When you, a kinsman with whom no bond has been previously formed, stand before me as a relative,
what else could be more dear to me, or a greater cause for my longing?
And I have understood, O Great King, that unions with those dear to me are causes for the exhaustion of striving toward the addiction to the taste of false and trivial pleasures.
Those objects experienced in a dream and those [experienced] upon the cessation of sleep—
no distinction is perceived between them once they have been enjoyed and released.
Therefore, a wise person should not indulge in attachment toward those things that are like dreams and illusions and which change in an instant. GoMe 53.

"‘He is dear to me’— thus do the ancient sages, who have transcended suffering, declare that what is called happiness is actually suffering, which has proceeded from beginningless time, is turbulent, and contains no small measure of latent affliction."
Compassion is directed toward those who are objects of pity, and women are especially objects of pity for the virtuous;
therefore, O King, my mind follows after compassion toward my beloveds, but it is not afflicted by delusion.

Lacking self-nature, functioning dependently, and perpetually afflicted by envy, pride, and passion—how could women not be objects of compassion, like scraps of flesh scattered upon the road? (GoMe 56)
Then that king, his mind gladdened by those flower-like words of the Bodhisattva, bowed to him and said:
Command me, O Great King, as you deem fit;
we stand with bodies bowed in service for the undertakings of those such as yourself.
Perceiving that his mind was serene, the Bodhisattva, wishing to gladden him, spoke as follows:
Only yours is a fruitful birth; you alone live a true life.
Sovereignty rests within your vessel, and prosperity truly belongs to you alone.
Yet you, under the pretext of honoring these Blessed Ones who loathe the enjoyment of existence, spread your fame throughout the world.
Friends are shared with one another through both wives and wealth;
yet sharing in accordance with the Dharma is either difficult to find on earth or does not exist at all.
Therefore, O King, you ought to offer me the hospitality due to a guest according to the Dharma; for among the virtuous, it is never seen that the honoring of a guest results in fruitlessness.
Heaven, liberation, pleasures, wealth, and fame arise from dharma alone;
therefore, by bestowing dharma, one joins oneself with heaven, liberation, happiness, and the like.
One should cultivate a friend who is proficient in the true Dharma, even by force;
this indeed is the most excellent conduct of virtuous friends in the world.
A guest, a friend, and one who seeks assistance—these three are the supreme objects of hospitality; since all three are present in me, therefore grant my request.
A clarity seems to flow from your lotus-like face;
you appear to be pouring forth through your speech a loving-kindness born of the enjoyment of merit.
"O King, permitted by you, let these foremost of those worthy of offerings, whose defilements have been exhausted, dwell in the lands of the southern region."
Then that lord of the earth spoke to the Bodhisattva:
If that merit could be given away when it resides within one's own continuum, I would certainly give it to you, who are so grateful. (GoMe 67)
"We shall grant you the kingdom, or whatever else you deem appropriate;
likewise, you must not understand our sovereignty there to be otherwise."
Whatever merit I have accumulated by honoring these noble ones,
that has indeed been made for me by the untimely moonlight of your arrival.
You are a friend who is exclusively virtuous, a kinsman exceedingly affectionate, endowed with qualities, worthy of offerings, and my unsurpassed protector. (GoMe 70)
What lowly being indeed would transgress your command?
And having beheld a jewel worthy of being seen, one such as you could not fail to be filled with joy. (GoMe 71)
But in this matter, O Great King, I perceive one difficulty,
because my mind shrinks from speaking of these great seers regarding this purpose.
For these great-souled ones, because they delight in the joy of discernment, take pleasure on the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
Behold, O Great King!
For these slopes of the Himalayas, adorned with groves of plantain trees,
were fashioned by the Creator specifically for the seclusion of the virtuous.
Behold the *devadāru* trees, their edges darkened by waterfalls that have lopped away the surrounding grass, rising up like lofty gabled chambers.
The rivers of snow seem to announce the downfall of the worlds by their waves that repeatedly break against the stones on the banks.
These rows of lotus trees, with their glossy foliage and shade,
seem to offer comfort to ascetics whose minds are distressed by the cycle of existence.
This forest breeze, cooled by contact with droplets of frost, dispels the beads of sweat from the weary ascetics.

These foothills of the Snowy Mountain—where the ground is strewn with lotuses, water-lilies, and trumpet-flowers, and where the heat is shielded by *śilīndhra* trees—delight the minds of the wise, for whom the poison of passion has ceased. (GoMe 77)
Beholding the forests of the Himalayas, where the slopes are covered with *sarala* trees,
these wise men attain a state of mind that is refined by the discernment of desire.
The Bodhisattva said:
There, the mountain ridges along the shore— shrouded by dark trees and possessing secluded, expansive caves—
are likewise conducive for those practicing meditation.
There too are rivers lined with palm and hintāla trees and strewn with green stones, their waves stirred by the wings of hārīta birds.
There, the breeze— cool with the spray of the ocean tide— shakes the flower-laden crests of the leafy trees growing near the shore of the surging waves, and thus serves the ascetics.
The sound of the ocean, though amplified by mountain caves, is muffled by the forest whose banks are dark with *sāra* trees, pepper vines, and *śyāmā* creepers;

Fie upon worldly association, which delights in the conceit of slight pleasure at first sight but results in ultimate emptiness; which is accompanied by toil and fear, and becomes distasteful through attachment—
this which is struck down by false conceptualizations and by anger that flares up without cause.
Having cast aside its familiarity even from the vicinity of the head, it goes to destruction in a single step.
Having heard this spoken by him, that first lay follower, interpreting those words differently, reflected thus in his mind: // GoPr_22 //
"Alas! What he has spoken is one thing, yet what I have conceptualized is another.
With his mind despondent from such thoughts and his intentions struck down by shame, he stood there.
And having seen him with his face bowed down in shame, that companion, in order to discern his intention, spoke thus with force: GoPr_24.
O virtuous one, what do you think in this matter, since your face is struck with shame? Speak then before me whatever your intention may be.
Having heard these words of his, that venerable lay follower released all the intentions that were within his mind.
If a person, having inspired their mind for even a moment toward a supreme object of veneration,
attains in the realms of existence a supreme excellence of glory and fortune that is free from duality and delightful;
yet later, they behold the world as mere false lamentation, consisting only of the grasping at conviction—
Having known this, he attains peace; how indeed could he not become a great mass of merit? // GoPr_27 //
Having offered a garland of straw fragments to the Supreme Being, the woman obtained the bliss of peace that extinguishes existence.
Regarding him whose power consists of such inconceivable and extraordinary conduct, to wonder "What is this mass of merit? is the mark of one lacking discernment.

Even by offering a *kośātakī* flower at the stūpa of the Sage, the supremely compassionate one, [the donor] experienced in his own abode the excellence of the bliss of the manifestation of virtues, attaining the prosperity of entering the city of the nectar of women. (GoPr 29)

To him, whose mind was naturally fickle, children once offered a handful of dust; yet having attained that, he reached the state beyond all thought— a fearless station, tranquil and free from the ultimate burning of existence— possessing the vast splendor of a lord of mortals, made beautiful by the laughter of its unfurled white parasol.
How then did that king later obtain [the fruit], and why, O sir, was that great seer not a heap of merit? GoPr_30 //
That very same boar who forcibly left a mud-mark upon the body of the Seer at the shrine— his very form remains there;
such is the true nature of that Dharma, by the sovereignty of which he was liberated from existence.
O friend, how much faith or discernment of virtues can there be in those dull-witted beings who are animals?
But it is indeed the power of that very field by which sentient beings here become fruitful.

Having previously beheld the form of the Blessed Buddha— which was a festival of joy for the eyes of the world, in which all agitation was stilled, and which was encircled by a fathom-wide halo— a peacock,
its throat trembling with rapture and its tail-feathers swaying, uttered a sweet cry.
And because of that, the fire was extinguished, like a flame drenched with a stream of water.
Behold that auspiciousness of the Blessed Buddhas, who possess the greatness of inconceivable yoga, which brings about the accomplishment of all aims and cuts through the sleep of delusion;
for it brings about ultimate peace even for those who have gone to the state of animals.
How much more so for the wise Teacher, who is oriented toward [the welfare of others], an ocean of virtuous qualities.
I believe that the very sight of those virtuous ones has its arising never in vain;
sweet with the assistance rendered in every way, born of previous mental impressions,
it leads even people whose intentions are impaired by hatred to the highest state.
That state is exclusively peaceful and auspicious, due to the disappearance of all afflictions of existence.
In the past, having heard the name of the Tathāgata from seafarers, a sea-monster died with its mouth wide open, having placed a moment of serene faith in the Sugata.
Because of that, it led the lord of rivers— which had been difficult to cross— back across once more, now within measurable bounds.
Having emerged upon the path, he crossed the vast ocean of birth by means of a raft.

Hanging from the depths of the underworld of the miserable realms, the god took refuge in the Lord of Sages and ascended to the highest celestial mansion by means of the successive steps of his own merit.
Out of fear of tigers, a man made an act of homage with his whole being to the Blessed Buddha; and beholding the great merit of the Incomparable One,
he attained a joy that utterly destroys the dense darkness of all misfortunes.
A certain peace, whose domain transcends words, which increases one's profound joy.

Thus, [he sought] that noble Śaṅkara, the source of the eternal glories of the worlds, whose secret conduct is incomparable, extraordinary, and inconceivable— some indescribable Lord, however he may be attained.
I declare that state to be immortal, unassailable, and a mass of merit.
Having heard what he had said, that other lay follower looked at the Venerable One and spoke to him once again in this way: (GoPr 40)
"O virtuous one, you have spoken correctly here;
nevertheless, O friend, hear now my own intention as well."

Even if one should harbor a single instance of malice toward a Sugata who has reached the end of the world— [malice] whose internal fury is washed away by hundreds of jars of the water of uninterrupted loving-kindness— one will,
until the very limit of saṃsāra, have the interior of one's own body filled with the core of a blazing flame of fire.
How could the ignorant plunge into the Avīci hell? How indeed could that Victor not be a lofty mass of merit?
Having cut off Elāpatra’s leaf from the sage out of contempt, that man of negligent nature manifested through his deed an inauspicious course of action like the poison of a *pārthagjanya* snake;
with his head split by the blade of the *elā* plant—
The lord of serpents, whose body is twice as long as his blood-red coils and whose mass of hoods is broad and terrifying, has not yet cast off his slough even today.

Even so slight a lack of respect toward the Blessed One draws upon living beings a continuous stream of misfortune that renders all their sense-bases (āyatana) sapless with affliction; whereas [respect] brings about some indescribable, effortless state that culminates in the highest excellence and ends in greatness.
That heap of demerit belonging to the wicked has attained peace; therefore, he is the supreme among beings.
Having harbored malice in his heart, that wretched man stood at the entrance of the street like an insect consumed by anger, his head severed by the blow of the wheel of the king’s chariot,
as he entered the terrifying maw of the earth— a gaping pit of flames like a mass of blazing garlands.
Therefore, his mass of demerit, having its darkness dispelled, entered that chasm.
Thus, even a slight application of volition directed toward the Blessed Buddha— who has attained the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) that burn away the fuel of deluded rebirth—
was firmly established for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) within their mental continuums.
He is a wanderer whose longing is stuck on tasting a mere fragment of the happiness of existence.
Having understood that [the world] is one's own karma, led by the strings of the sinews of latent tendencies, and deceived by worldly sufferings and by the senses that are wretched for sense-objects—
those people arise who act for the sake of attaining the pacification of calamities for all beings.
Among them, what man is capable of measuring their harms and favors?
Having stolen the garlands from the Blessed One’s relic-receptacles, he immediately became a young boy whose entire body was loathsome, with lumps of raw flesh bursting out with boils;
yet, having performed an act of veneration there, he immediately became free of wounds once again.
Who, indeed, that possesses a discerning heart would not worship this moving ocean of merit?
Therefore, for those with corrupted minds, the Blessed One is a mass of demerit; but for those with serene minds, he is a mass of merit.
By way of explanation, he is one who has transcended all internal afflictions and stains along with their latent tendencies, and who perceives the limit of the sense objects.
Having broken the image of the Ṛṣi while playing with a ball, which she had carelessly dropped from her sprout-like hand,
the woman was overcome by the fever of remorse; yet, having worshipped the Buddha, [she attained peace].
Has Kanakavatī not arrived at the sorrow of having her arms severed?
Just as the rising sun destroys the night-prowlers and dispels the dense darkness of men with his rays so that forms may be perceived,
the fault does not lie with the Sun; rather, it lies with those whose souls are hostile to the Blessed One.
Even the Buddha, though he is the common protector of all, likewise possesses no accumulation of either demerit or merit.
Thus, those two lay disciples, having praised the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities and purified one another’s being, departed.
Knowing this, O Great King, one should joyfully offer honor with faith to the Perfectly Awakened One, the true guru; under no circumstances should one ever do him harm.
For those whose intentions are stained by contempt for the Teacher, the ground yields no immediate fissure;
nor does it produce the various wonders made of jewels for those whose minds are melted with faith in the Buddha.
This must be some extraordinary cessation of other karmas, a marvelous excellence of the power of merit;
for it is through the distinction of the recipient that the karmas of men do not immediately yield their fruit.
This is surely some inconceivable and unique power of that sage, perfected through his extraordinary yoga,
by which those who have committed an offense against him here do not immediately sink into the depths of the underworld.

Therefore, one should cultivate devotion toward the Blessed Jina, who has conquered his internal adversaries; he is a moving tree of merit that yields the fruit of immortality for the worlds. One should cast away all hope that is everywhere entangled in the thicket of sense objects.
As long as this world remains a terrible wilderness devoid of Buddhas.
Buddhas do not arise at all times nor in every place in this world, for they are free from the sleep of false grasping regarding all aspects of reality; rather,
some eon, delightful through the accumulation of merit, eventually gives rise to one.
Wherein the arising of the lords of the worlds occurs for the prosperity of all beings.
Until the rays of the sun of the Perfectly Awakened One illuminate the world, drying up the netted moat of existence that surrounds the city of rebirth— even though it has been brought to peace—
let the virtuous behold the difficult-to-distinguish distinctions between those who have entered upon even and uneven paths.
In the world, clouds of false views flash forth, difficult to ward off, with calamities as their thunderbolts.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and so it is told to you by me;
having understood this, one should indeed practice devotion to the Sage.
Those who always revere the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
free from afflictions and having conquered Māra along with his hosts, they proceed to the abode of the Victors.
And those who hear the true Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth;
having always enjoyed sublime happiness, they go at last to Sukhāvatī.
Those who joyfully honor the Saṅghas do not go to an evil rebirth;
having brought benefit to all sentient beings, they proceed to a pure abode.
Knowing this, O Great King, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
act for the benefit of all sentient beings and practice the conventional truth.
By that, may all that is auspicious for you arise both here and in the hereafter;
and having gradually attained awakening, may you reach final liberation.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, that king joyfully promised,
"So be it," and together with his retinue, he rejoiced.
Those who, with faith and joy, cause this *avadāna* on the heap of merit to be heard, who rejoice in it, and who listen to it with concentrated minds— GoPr_67.
All those great beings, having purified the three spheres and enjoyed the bliss of the qualities of the true Dharma, go to the abode of the Victors.
// Śrī // Thus ends the *Puṇyarāśyavadāna*, number thirteen.

11. Those who are skilled in the cessation of the proliferation of birth declare that the root of the five types of afflictions is birth.
The Tathāgatas are those whose promises are unfailing, and the Bodhisattvas are beings of pure essence.
Thus it is heard: the Bodhisattva, it is said, took birth in a great brahmin family distinguished by qualities esteemed by the world;
he grew together with his own virtues, like the moon of the bright fortnight with its rays.
The virtuous one caused the supreme splendor of his family’s insignia to reach its full renown.
Even while still in his first stage of life, though his mind was intensely attached to the objects of the senses,
he became an object of wonder for the worlds due to his superhuman nature and conduct.

It was a place where evil deeds remained unfulfilled and were rampant; it was characterized by intense exertion that opposed tranquility; its primary focus was the acquisition of wealth, and its activities were dominated by the pursuit of sensual pleasures and worldly affairs, which are essentially hollow;

it was a breeding ground for lack of discipline, quarrels, enmity, and conflict; it served as a dwelling for envy, stinginess, theft, and the like; it abounded in sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental distress, and despair;
it was a dense thicket of deceit, guile, intoxication, and pride; it was presided over by recklessness and arrogance; and it followed the conduct of the ignoble, being the nature of crooked beings.

Having cast aside the state of household life— which is a ground for negligence, beset by various forms of humiliation, accompanied by wretchedness, characterized by unassailed despondency, fraught with the fear of imminent ruin and poverty, an ocean of unbearable calamities, and appearing as a terrifying abyss within a thicket of thorns— he adorned one of the other stages of religious life.

Then, having cast aside the life of a householder— which is full of deceptions, many injustices, numerous calamities, and corrupted by many faults, and which is the root of misfortune— he adorned the peaceful forest of asceticism.

It was adorned with lakes whose waters were variegated by *palāśa* buds, *kuśeśaya* lotuses, and *indīvara* lilies; their shores were darkened by young *kaśeru* grass, where water-fowls and swans slept.
It was closely embraced by the river with its girdle of rows of fish, as if out of affection for a lover;
and it was completely surrounded within by trees green with young sprouts, which, like kinsmen, bestowed flowers and fruits in all seasons.

Having approached that edge of the forest, which was crowded with beasts of prey— like ascetics harsh only in outward appearance— and whose hearts were content with water, grass, and sprouts, that Bodhisattva shone like the Dharma itself incarnate.
Even while existing in the state of a householder, he—

whose mind was steeped in discernment practiced in previous births and whose soul remained unscarred by the defects of domestic life— surpassed those dwelling in the penance groves, who were negligent and relied upon base men.
Those very same forest regions, peaceful and always suited for solitude, cause longing to arise.
For those who have practiced the festival of the bliss of renunciation, dwelling at home is like being in exile;
to them, forests where the branches are curved by the bodies of female deer are better than the finest palaces.

For those who perceive only frustration in possessions, who find contentment alone in their affection for their own wealth, and who regard life in their home as dwelling in a prison, living in the forest is no wonder at all. // GoRp 11 //

He had four companions whose affection, respect, and devotion were unswerving due to the dense impressions formed by the habitual practice of their successive previous births: a crow, a pigeon, a serpent, and a deer.
With minds solely intent on carrying out his commands, they became distinguished in the world for the excellence of their religious practices according to the laws of their own species.
They shone all the more brightly among animals who are generally devoid of refuge, overwhelmed by the impairment of their mental faculties, and abundant in delusion.
Clarified by their passion for the Dharma and beautiful in their practice, they were like rows of lamps on nights of the dark fortnight.

Religious acts performed by those devoid of virtue, though delightful through their skillful execution, cause even greater astonishment—like lotus ponds blooming in forest regions made most difficult to traverse by the heat of summer. // GoR 13 //
Once, while they were engaged in conversation in a state made delightful by the unrestrained intimacy of their affection, this resolution arose among them:
"Sirs, what indeed do you consider to be the greatest suffering? Displaying as it were his own cleverness, the crow spoke first:
In this world, there is no suffering greater than hunger. Why?
Because there are no diseases, nor old age, nor separation from loved ones, nor the misfortunes consisting of union with the undesired;
those various forms of calamity bring such suffering to people as that which causes the torment of exile for one who is hungry.

Having reached the Vaitaraṇī river, which is garlanded with waves of salt water so difficult to cross, the heedless, out of hunger, swallow iron balls; therefore, there is no other calamity equal to hunger. (GoR 15)

Since even an infant, though overwhelmed by pain and having a body repulsive to behold due to the flow of excrement from its refuse-heap of a carcass and the coating of filth, still longs for the breast, the suffering of hunger must therefore be great indeed.

Even when deprived of those dear to him as his own life and fallen under the power of consuming grief, that he nevertheless partakes of morsels mixed with tears—from that [act] the Jina declared that hunger is the supreme fear. (GoR 17)

Moreover, O venerable sirs, born into a great family smeared with the intoxication of pride, he now eats even the leavings of a king out of joy, as if at a time of prosperity when he was tormented by hunger; what could be more miserable than this? (GoRup 18)

Because those dwelling in the borderlands are content with mere grass like ascetics, being ignorant of the calamities of others, the deer become targets for arrows on all sides; here, I perceive hunger as the certain cause of this suffering.

Even when being torn apart by a wind that pierces their vital organs, and with their bodies afflicted by the spasms of hiccups and distortions of the throat and neck, they consume mere fragments of food with a cotton swab; therefore, there is no calamity for living beings equal to hunger.

Moreover, those virtuous beings of the first eon were eaters of food that appeared spontaneously; like gods moving through the vault of the sky, they were radiant, adorned with garlands of flames from their own rays of light.
Obstructed by their attachment to the pursuit of food, they have reached such a state that,
like hungry ghosts (preta), those miserable ones subsist on food obtained with great difficulty.
With minds dejected by the onset of the suffering of hunger, the pitiless eat even dry wood that is damp and teeming with worms, as well as impure things;
some pass their time with harsh armpits moistened by the water of saliva.
Others, lacking self-control and tormented by hunger, devour bones long cast aside.
Placing their feet even upon the heads of the king's inner guards, those birds— having forgotten their fear due to the onset of the suffering of hunger— seize and eat the meat;
they rush with such speed that they pass through walls difficult to traverse because of the dense array of weapons.
Some, wretched with their craving for meat and blood, go to their destruction.
Having previously eaten various foods from vessels of jewels and gold in her own palace,
Satyabhāmā now ate jujubes with the tips of her fingers pierced by sharp thorns.

When Viśvāmitra—whose power was diminished by the bestowal of curses and favors, yet whose fame shone renowned to the ends of the quarters—ate dog-meat out of the suffering of hunger, he thereby experienced the full force of the pains of hunger. // GoR 25 //
A young son, who is the very essence of love, was devoured in the wilderness by a couple;
there is no suffering other than the pain of hunger for those running through the forest of rebirth, which is so cruel in form. (GoRup 26)

Do you think there is any suffering more intense than this: standing at the gates of one's enemies, driven by hunger, speaking without confidence and with a pale face and expression marred by the wretchedness of begging, saying only, "Give"? (GoR 27)
Then, among them, the pigeon said:
"It is true that the suffering of hunger is powerful;
nevertheless, let my intention be heard."
"It is my firm conviction that passion itself is great suffering; for what can hunger do, since it is warded off even by ashes? (GoRūp 28)

Moreover, even sages who subsist on wind, water, withered trees, and fallen leaves— their physical frames emaciated by long fasts— become blind when their power falters due to passion, which arises as something difficult to counteract.

Whether it be during nights when the moonbeams are not yet faded or during days when the gaps in the clouds have opened wide, the base man who is blinded by passion becomes truly blind; therefore, there is no calamity in the world equal to passion.

Passion causes one to close the eyes of modesty, which is the foremost of all virtues; it stains one's reputation, which is of unblemished clarity; and indeed, it brings even the righteous into disrepute, eclipsing their excellences that rival the peaks of Mount Meru. (Goṛp 31)
This [mind] does not weigh the age of men who have passed away, nor does it regard the established order consisting of pure lineage;
even leaping over the thickets of public scandal, the horse of conceptual passion gallops according to its own will.
The breeze, drenched with the spray from clusters of jasmine flowers blooming with radiant blossoms and stinging with droplets of water,
causes the mind of a man who lacks discernment— and whose passion for conceptual constructions remains unappeased— to burn all the more intensely.

Having delved into subtle points and even the depths of complex junctions, and having formed their own convictions regarding various doctrinal systems, do not the wise—though possessed of intelligence—indeed fall into the supreme loss of mindfulness when they are enslaved by the demon of passion? (GoṚp 34)
Even those whose intellects are firmly established on the path of well-practiced yoga, though they have destroyed the burgeoning seeds of the poison of passion,
fall from their asceticism and become equal to beasts upon beholding the faces of women, with their hair-fringe sprouting like young shoots.

Having swept away the power of the defilements that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing, the noble ones— though they remain with only a single thread of the bond of existence left— followed by the piercing of their mental stability, experience a state of ignobility even as a mere trace of shame is consumed by passion.
A man holds his head high among people only so long as he does not serve the whimsical desires of passion;
once embraced by the fever of love, he is brought low and mocked, like a dog trapped in a narrow space.
Moreover, O gentle-faced ones,
he was cooing softly from behind with a voice most faltering due to the obstruction at his throat;
his eyes were reddened by passion as he was repeatedly and timidly rebuked.
Without considering that he has come as a hawk, the pigeon follows his beloved; what deception can there be from afar for a mind defiled by the habit of passion?
Those men who are unable to endure even the pointing of a single finger by their teacher, whose minds are excessively puffed up with pride, and who view the entire world from a lowly perspective—
they are tormented by passion, their fortitude destroyed, and struck down by the feet of women.
These wretched men carry out his commands upon their heads like a never-fading garland.
Even those who, having conquered their enemies, possessed the pride of valor renowned for victory in battle and whose fame spread far and wide throughout the world,
were pierced by the arrows of women’s words, which are inherently fickle.
Furthermore, those who transgress the bounds of propriety cause the world of the living to tremble with infamy.
Even upon hearing the sound of musical instruments practiced during the end of the night,
those women who would suddenly experience trembling terror in their homes— those women, struck by passion, go forth as *abhisārikās* during the nights.
Regions shrouded in dense darkness and terrifying with the howling of jackals.

Those young women, who wander slowly and gracefully upon the secluded palace rooftops amidst heaps of flowers, weary while their lotus-like hands are held by their lovers; being rendered helpless by the onset of passion, they [despise] the difficult, muddy tracks trampled by the hooves of many buffaloes.
They traverse the paths with the impetuous speed of quick steps during the nights of the rainy season.
Trembling when touched by the *kadamba* breezes cooled by fresh spray,

those young women who had taken refuge in lovely palaces spread out through the lattice-windows— now with their flower-arrangements scattered by the falling rain and agitated by the startled deer— [are now wandering in the forest].
With their anklets jingling as they are marked with mud, they travel along the road at night.
The falling of weapons becomes like the touch of blue lotus petals;
the flames of fire become as cool as the embrace of dense autumn moonlight;
and the forms of serpents, flickering like the wind, become like the fulfillment of one's desires.
They attain a state of equality with the garlands of *mālatī* flowers through the humming of bees.
When it was said, "Therefore, passion, which destroys all the sense-bases, is great suffering," the serpent replied:
"Indeed, passion is suffering; it causes the perversions of the mind and leads to misconduct.
But I consider anger to be even more painful, for it is a root that blazes within the heart. Why is this so?"

Since a man pierced by the arrow of anger finds no sleep in a house where the watchtowers are washed by the rays of the moon through scattered clouds, and which is delightful with the sweet singing of women accompanied by the sounds of lutes and flutes;
There is no other suffering whatsoever more painful than anger; therefore, nothing else exists [that is worse].
Even among animals, those whose minds were pacified by the excellence of yoga practice, who subsisted on air, water, and roots, and who had attained a state of trustworthiness,
were mostly consumed by the fires of their anger, like cruel venomous serpents destroying entire settlements.
Because of delusion, there is no other suffering [greater] than that which exists from anger for the sages.

His face was reddened by the flames of the fire from his three eyes, which quivered with fury; it was clouded by the tears of women whose eyes were restless with the particular agitation of fear and exhaustion, and it was made to resound with urgency by children who pressed their faces against the nipples of their breasts.
That Rudra, devoid of compassion, burned down Tripura—that was merely a transformation of his anger.

The trembling wreaths of hair at the roots of their heads, agitated by intense anguish, do not form the cupped hands of supplication; nor do the teardrops of the women, fierce and flickering, serve as the long-lashed glances that shield those whose brows are arched across the surface of their foreheads.
What indeed could be more painful than that, when the minds of kings are as inauspicious as the poison of their wrath? // GoṚp_48 //
Disregarding their mother, who underwent the painful constraints of gestation and is worthy of the highest honor; and their father, whose heart is melted with affection;
and even their friends, who provide security and freedom from harm—those whose hearts are wounded by injury destroy them all.
Those very modes of conduct, though seemingly virtuous, result in a most terrible ripening of anger itself.
Those of supreme intelligence arise for the purification of beings whose intentions are difficult to purify, being defiled by a complete coating of impurities and hidden;
yet even those noble ones are moved solely by the practice of bringing about the welfare and happiness of others.
Overcome by anger, ignoble persons strike those face-to-face with the arrows of their words.
A man seized by anger becomes one whose face has its beauty burnt away; full of the harshness of a circle of flames, the wrathful one goes to the states of woe.
Fallen from those realms, he becomes a source of distress to the eyes of the world.
There is no other enemy like hatred; for there exists no foe equal to anger.
A person acts with affection toward that which he is attached to,
and toward that which he hates, he applies even greater unpleasantries; thus, anger has entered him who possesses little fault and has not yet transcended passion.
Those skilled in the pacification of anger declare that anger is the source of fault.
Like a doe in the forest with her face wide-eyed in terror, her creeper-like brows languid with shame, her upper garment snatched away in the frenzy of the struggle, and the cord of her neck severed—
Duḥśāsana tormented Draupadī, who was like a virtuous woman in great distress.
In that vast assembly, those flickering sparks of anger were as fickle as they pleased.
Dwelling in a solitary forest with a tranquil soul, though having laid aside all violence, he was a friend to the world whose kindness was spontaneous and whose affection brought about their welfare;
yet when the sage Kṣāntivādī was hacked asunder with a sword like a tree being split, [he remained unmoved].
The king sent that gift as a touchstone for the anger of Durjanavallabha.
Consisting of manifold misfortunes and leading to ruin, yet appearing brilliant to the mind—
thus does the enemy that is anger stand at the forefront of all sufferings.
The deer said:
"O Lord of Serpents, I do not understand this violent destruction caused by anger to be so severe;
I do not perceive any suffering greater than the fear of death. Why is that?"
For those who are terrified by the onset of death, even the most desirable bonds of Māra do not delight the mind;
I know of no suffering greater than this.
Beholding the faces of his friends, which are overcast by the stormy waves of thick tears,
he experiences at the time of death a calamity such that I know no other suffering more painful than that.
With their bodies being split as if by saws— winds that are by nature difficult to control—
the wretched ones, fearing the great precipice of the next world, experience intense suffering.
The faces of beloved women— whose cheeks have become deathly pale, whose lips, withered by sighing, have lost their crimson hue, and who are mangled by the teeth of Death— do not evoke compassion.
Her hair matted with the mud of filth, her treatment toward her son free from fear due to his confidence in her,
the mother— seeing death approaching— sinks into the mire of grief, weeping without any refuge.
Hearing the sound of trembling grass, leaves, and shoots in the forest, the deer dwelling there flee without regard for one another, casting even their own offspring aside, terrified of death.
In mountain fastnesses rugged with hard rocks and gravel, where grass, trees, and mountains are scorched by fire, we dwell without any other refuge, terrified by the falling thunderbolt of death.
Even when their bodies are withered by dust and struck by harsh blows from diseases, they endure immense agony; yet, paralyzed by the terror of words, they become oblivious to death.
Like a deer forcibly dragged away from the midst of its kin by a lion,
this world, though its manliness remains unbroken, meets with suffering at the hands of its enemy, Death.
With the channels within our throats completely parched, we reach the banks of the great rivers;
finding no water and terrified by lions, we leap up and flee in every direction.
In every region, seeing the murderous hunter, we, being without refuge,
have utterly abandoned the forests green with the growth of young grass;
now we are helpless in the Vindhya forest, which is as dreadful as the cave of a python.
We go to a state where we are visible only by the claws, mouths, and manes of tigers.
Even upon seeing straw effigies, our minds tremble;
neither by night nor by day do we find happiness, being terrified of death. We see Death like another hunter with his bow drawn.
For those whose limbs are trembling with fear, there is not even the slightest appetite for food.
With lower lips as green as tree shoots and as pale-red as the *pāṭala* flower, and with the lines of hair on their bodies turned grey by the dust of the earth,
the female deer— with eyes naturally flickering— do not delight our minds, which are already afflicted by the thought of death.
Contented in their dwelling on dry land, skilled in relishing fresh water and grass,
they move playfully with their mates, adept at the graceful steps of their gait;
they do not hate the world, nor are they timid, nor do they cause fear.
Even those are slain with effort by Hari, who possesses a fierce mind.
Tell me, what indeed must they perceive to become enemies—even of the deer who roam unobstructed through the forests, subsisting on nothing more than blades of grass and young shoots? GoR 70.
How can cruel enemies of deer strike at the deer, who are upright, whose minds are open, and who subsist on grass and water?
I understand death to be loathsome amidst all suffering and terrifying to all beings; therefore, it is a calamity difficult to overcome. (Goṛpa 72)

Since those great beings were each attached to their own respective doctrines and could not reach a conclusion in their discussion, they approached the Bodhisattva, bowed according to propriety, and spoke this matter:
"Blessed One, among the minor faults, anger, death, and fear—which indeed is suffering?
Or whose well-spoken word do we accept? Then that best of sages said to them:
The well-spoken words of all, and the firm convictions of all—
all these sufferings afflict the three worlds.
Moreover, noble sirs, let my intention also be heard:
"Whatever practice constantly obstructs one's own dharma, I recognize that as a mental affliction for the hermitage, and so I speak. (Goṛpa 74)
Like those vying with one another, these burning impurities associated with birth strike down the worlds themselves, rendering them devoid of light.
What would embodied beings, whose selves are afflicted by the suffering of hunger, not do?
Even a cruel slaughter—a deed that brings about the fruits of the lower realms.
Those who have transgressed the noble boundaries and whose minds are defiled by passion become objects of compassion for those who see reality.
With their distorted eyes rolling due to the tossing of clearly arched brows,
the harsh men appeared in an instant as if they were someone else entirely because of their rage.
For all embodied beings, this death is a long-term exile characterized by separation from everyone else; indeed, it is an absolute terror. (GoR 79)
These and other such varieties of suffering that cause one's hair to stand on end follow birth, just as the compassionate follow the virtuous.
The misconduct of one's mother and father...
what indeed could be more painful than that? (GoRp 81) ...
what indeed could be more painful than that? (GoRp 82)
For one whose breath is utterly stifled like a worm submerged in a mire of filth,
what indeed could be a greater misery than that state of being situated within the womb?
For one whose body is being crushed within the cavity of the mountain torrent of bodily excrement,
what indeed could be more painful than that state while still in the womb?
Therefore, the Jinas—the best of speakers, who have conquered the seeds of doubt—declare that birth is suffering for those who are liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death. GoRp 85.
Furthermore, venerable ones, passion is manifold: it consists of old age, humiliation, the acquisition of enjoyments, their protection,
the calamity of their destruction, great ruin, and the transformation born of association with the wicked.
Since those various disturbances of the mind, which arise easily from the loss of what is desired and the encounter with what is undesired,
occur once one has attained birth in this world, therefore birth itself is suffering here.
To those Blessed Ones whose actions are never sweetened by self-interest but always consist of altruism in every form,
whose births are praiseworthy, and who possess inconceivable greatness through their yoga— to those eyes of the world, [I pay homage].
But for one who is intent on their own self-interest, even a momentary birth leads to ruinous downfall.
Therefore we say:
either apply firm heedfulness for the sake of perfect enlightenment, or strive quickly for the destruction of existence;
for, abandoning these two, people enter unwillingly into the terrifying abysses of the submarine fire-mouths of the lower realms.
If both of these are obtained through effort, then effort is considered by me to be more appropriate for a great result;
for even if one obtains a mere shell as a hole, could that lead to the acquisition of the wish-fulfilling gem? Even labor is better than that.
Therefore, even if it is fruitless with respect to me, the exertion of a virtuous person whose intention is dedicated to the welfare of great beings is better;
for the very undertaking of an effort directed toward a specific object of desire bestows great joy.
Delicate pleasures shared with beloved ones gladden the heart exceedingly;
however, the enduring pleasures that belong exclusively to the great are those which bring about suffering when they arise.
Just as the light of fireflies produces the mere appearance of a body but does not illuminate the worlds—
so too is it for those whose minds are occupied with a mere fragment of knowledge that is defiled by attachment to their own self-interest.
The attainment of wealth that is devoid of discipline does not exist as something equal in value.

Then, having received the command of that best of sages with their heads— his mind being solely intent on the Dharma— they spread his fame, white as an autumn night-lily, in every direction, using words softened by respect and humility.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the Five Sages.
