Endowed with dispassion, well-spoken, and awakening one to the goals of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma; delightful in its absolute solitude for many virtuous people—I shall speak a certain Avadāna; listen now! GoSk_1 //
Thus it shines forth: even great wealth or youth is not sufficient to create an obstacle for those whose roots of merit are fully ripened.
As it is heard in tradition: there was a king named Kṛkī, who was enriched by the glory of virtues such as policy and discipline.

And he had conceived pure faith in the Blessed One, Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. That king had seven daughters who, through the empowerment of the strength of roots of merit planted and increased during the appearance of previous Buddhas, had conceived a sense of revulsion for cyclic existence. With modest conduct and sweet speech, they prostrated before their father and said:
Having observed the instability of the world’s condition, like the reflection of the moon’s orb in water;
having seen sensual desires as resembling the flickering shadow of the coils of an enraged serpent;
and having beheld this entire world set ablaze by the fires of suffering—
"O King, we indeed go to the cemetery with an intention that delights in renunciation."
The king said:
"You are children accustomed to comfort, with your desires for worldly aims unfulfilled; how can I bear to say to you, 'Take refuge in the forest of asceticism'? (GoSk 3)
The maidens said:
"O Lord of the Earth, we know that even toward common people your words are enveloped in a tender essence softened by affection;
how much more so toward us, who have grown up sinless in your own lap and for whom you feel love without cause?"

O King, since even for those like you, who possess faultless and pure dispositions, separation from those dear to you is inevitable, it is our wish that you may attain the state of peace; let there not be this repeated torment of calamity.
Then that king, his heart melting under the power of affection, his pair of steady, copper-hued eyes fixed upon them, gazed repeatedly at those maidens and said:

Having wandered at will within these mansions with their interiors spread with soft and variegated carpets, how will you ladies touch the cremation ground— treacherous as the minds of the wicked, strewn with heaps of white bone fragments for its upper garment?
How could you abandon your father, who is so intent on affection, or your mother, whose face is clouded by the rain of tears of grief, in a single moment?
And how indeed could you delight in asceticism, having forsaken your friends whose minds are filled with unflagging friendship?
Then those maidens, bold through their reliance on unsurpassed fortitude, said to their father:
"Father, mother, friend—these are merely conventional designations for those who suffer the ruin caused by the repeated falling of rebirth.
O King, the world undergoes vain distress, its vision obscured by the impurities of ignorance regarding the true nature of reality. (GoSk 8)
Someone with a taste for misfortune has employed this deceptive stratagem consisting of friends, kinsmen, and relatives;
who here belongs to whom, and how? For this world of living beings is indeed like a dream or a magical illusion.

O Lord of Men, as long as the three worlds remain illuminated by the rays of the words of the True Dharma— emanating from the sun-like Buddha who is garlanded with the radiance of his shimmering fame—
they shall continue to emerge from cyclic existence, whose inner spaces are shrouded by the dense veil of the darkness of calamity.
Therefore, it is right to do so before this most vast and terrible darkness spreads abroad.
Just as those desiring to extinguish a fire do not restrain a man who is emerging from a house licked by rows of flames flickering in the wind,
so too [should they not restrain you] from all of existence, which is seized by the tips of the flames of the great fire of suffering.
The virtuous do not open the door for one who is departing from that which is covered by the net of misfortune.

Then that king, his mind even more overcome by grief and dejection at those words— which were harsh with disregard for friends, kinsmen, and relatives, and which shattered his hope for his own body and life— spoke again.
Austerities undertaken at improper times do not nourish the objects desired by the mind,
just as girls who conceive prematurely fail to develop the beauty of limbs with fully formed internal substance.
Practices of asceticism undertaken at an improper time become fraught with obstacles, like lunar eclipses;
therefore, let this notion of yours regarding these maidens be turned back from here, like a mind wandering upon a wrong path.
Bodies accustomed to comfort and unaccustomed to suffering are not capable of enduring hardships;
they are like mango trees with unanchored roots when struck by the tusks of lordly elephants.
Resounding with the inauspicious howls of jackals containing the sound of fire, its caverns filled with terrifying roars,
and dreadful with the cries of lamentation, the cremation ground would utterly dispel even the fear of fear itself.
Where is your body, as delicate as a young lotus stalk, and where is this mind, as harsh as a saw? Alas!
For one whose heart is devoted to the service of others, how cruel is the Creator’s disregard for me!

O maidens, may these pleasure groves be to your liking— groves where the ground is covered with soft, emerald-green grass like a cloak of beryl, strewn with heaps of various kinds of flowers, and filled with swarms of bees humming with intoxication.

The garden groves of the houses, with flowering trees hanging over their banks; the ponds, whose girdles are rows of shimmering ripples stirred by the breeze; and the sounds of swans resting in the beds of blooming lotuses and water-lilies.
Daughters are a sufficient bond even for Maghavan himself. // GoSk_18 //

O women, find delight right here in this domestic grove, which is fanned by breezes that play upon the waves of water, are fragrant with the scent of *navamālikā* flowers, and are filled with the warbling of cuckoos.

These palaces, from which the wine of flowers is wafted through the openings of their latticed windows, seem like breaths exhaled by Vasava— perfumed with various fragrances— as they rest peacefully upon the curved ridges of their turrets where birds sleep.
May the sounds of singing and musical instruments, along with women, be for your delight.
Then those maidens, unable to endure their father's words, spoke again.

O Lord of the World of Men, there is indeed no other happiness whatsoever, whether in heaven or on earth, that has not been experienced by us hundreds and thousands of times—though we were so unwise regarding our own welfare. (GoSk 21)
Reflecting that there is no satisfaction for the senses— which are voracious through their specific habituation to sense objects— by means of those very objects,
the wise strive for the destruction of the bondage of existence.

Triumphant are the ascetics who have turned away from the desire for rebirth, [having conquered] the six sense-faculties which are fickle, unstable by nature, and as fragile as waves tossed by the wind.
But fools, like pigs in the prison of existence, deceived by the machinations of the Kali-age mind, fall—driven by greed for pleasure—into calamities that are truly endless and terrifying. (GoSk 24)

This people, having fallen into the delusion of "I," pursues sense objects that are like blazing fire-engines; their hopes destroyed, they pursue those causes of intense suffering that extend over a long period of time until their final transformation.
Having understood that this world is impermanent, devoid of independence, and hemmed in by a multitude of venomous serpents that are the sense objects,
those who take delight in worldly existences are but cattle led by human bodies.
Like chowries whose handles are caught in trees, base men meet their end at home—
their paths of intellect obstructed by sense-objects and their minds bound by the false creepers of affection.

Tell me, father, what cause for pleasure exists here in this world of living beings— amidst the incessant intervals of the breaking out of calamities— by which we might find delight even in our own homes, which are full of many deceptions?
O Lord of Men, having exhausted the fortunes acquired in other existences within these palaces,
they become like those who have been robbed, their minds dejected and wretched, destined for the wilderness of cyclic existence.
O King, even men who act with circumspection and are naturally skilled in worldly affairs go to their destruction upon entering the domestic snare, just like fish entering the mouth of a fishing net.
O Protector of the World of Men, mansions and wealth have been acquired by many efforts;
yet, abandoning them all, a man goes forth alone in an instant, following the path ordained by his own past deeds.
For this very reason, the Lord of the World declared: "O King, the world of living beings has its own karma as its property;
when a man faces death, his own karma follows him, just as a suckling calf follows its mother cow. (GoSk 32)

Therefore, enough with those longings for union with beloved kin, which are so cruel in their inevitable transformation; for those whose hearts delight in the company of loved ones certainly reap the sorrow of separation.
Moreover, O hero among men, what lasting affection can there be for the world of the living, whose very nature is impermanent?
For those whose minds are as fragile as the analysis of ultimate truth, the notion that "this is dear" is merely a delusion.
But if you have any affection for us, O Lord of the Earth, then grant us permission;
for it is our desire to enjoy that happiness which is blameless, unassailable, and cherished by the noble.
Then that king, having full faith in the teaching of the Sugata, fearing obstacles to the Dharma, and with his heart overcome by affection,

reflected for a long time in silence, thinking: "These daughters of mine are indeed rememberers of their former births, having understood the purpose through the recollection of their previous lives."
Perceiving their persistence, that bull among men somehow gave his consent for them to go, saying indistinctly, "Go."

Then those maidens, having removed their garlands, ointments, and ornaments, with bodies modest and composed, wearing white, fine, and flowing garments, appeared like rivers garlanded with rows of foam upon waters stirred by the force of the wind; like autumn nights enveloped in the thick moonlight of the full moon; like the stars of the Seven Sages (the Great Bear) with the net of their own rays as upper robes; they proceeded in order toward that place where the middle of a funeral pyre had been prepared, containing a bloated corpse emitting a hissing sound, foul-smelling and loathsome.

They reached a cremation ground that was terrifying on its periphery, overrun by human skeletons whose faces were smeared with the flowing brain-essence emerging from the cavities of skull-pots shattered by the sharp beaks of vultures; it was difficult to traverse due to the harsh surface of the earth strewn with heaps of fragments of decayed, shattered, and discolored bones; it was like the personified site of the undertakings of world-weariness, and had become the abode of death, discontent, sorrow, dejection, and despair.
And there is a verse on this point:
They reached that cremation ground, which was blinded by vultures reeking with the stench of human blood and fat;
it was crowded with the limbs of corpses—moist with entrails and bellies torn open—which were terrifying in their loathsomeness;
and it was filled with skulls, white as yellow jasmine, which, with their crumbling edges, seemed to be constantly laughing.
Terror-inspiring with the various "hūṃ" cries of owls echoing from the hollows of a decayed banyan tree.
In some places, it was terrifying with the clear howls of jackals raised by the flames of funeral fires;
in others, it was difficult to traverse, hemmed in by a network of white skeletons;
and in others, it was filled with swarms of wriggling worms and the moving blue nostrils of corpses.
The foothills were crowded with corpses infested by hundreds of clinging flies.

In some places, it was a terrifying abode where human bodies were pierced by sharpened spears; in others, serpents lay coiled at the bases of withered trees, struck by the fierce winds of the powerful funeral pyres and tossed about as the blazing fires crackled and burst forth amidst fragments of bleached bones.
Like the kitchen of Death, where festivities are constantly in progress.
In some places it was crowded with throngs of piśācas, voracious for the transformations of blood, fat, and liquor flowing from the openings of jars made of human heads;
in other places it was embraced by the crackling fires of funeral pyres.
With intestines like serpents emerging from the bellies of throbbing corpses of hell-beings.
With their hearts bound by a sense of spiritual urgency, those women wandered there,
reflecting upon the fickle and unstable nature of the world of living beings.

Then they beheld the discarded body of a woman, her private parts exposed, foul, and disfigured, with a mass of hair as coarse and reddish-brown as the dust of the earth, and whose eye-sockets were torn open by the claws and beaks of birds.
Beholding that cage of a body with eyes as tremulous from sudden trepidation as the petals of a blue lotus, they uttered many kinds of words.
This is she, who dwells in celestial palaces and mansions glistening with the sprouts of moonbeams,
and who was accustomed to being embraced in the arms of her beloved, now sleeps upon the surface of the earth.
How is this poor woman not afraid— she who sleeps within the cage of her lover’s embrace and is timid even at the thundering of clouds— of the burning heat and of the inauspicious cry of the jackal?
She who moves with the languid gait of one burdened by the weight of her teacher’s hips, and who gazes with playful, graceful smiles—
this very moonlight of her own courtyard is being devoured by birds devoid of all compassion.
"O sister, you have been abandoned here in this cemetery, a courtyard crowded with hundreds of human skeletons;
how could such a heartless lover do this? Alas, fie upon this world of unstable affection!"

How can this poor woman, who used to wander like a bee in the lotus-pool of her own kin, relatives, and friends, and who once moved about in the lap of her beloved, now find delight today in the cremation ground, so terrifying with its night-stalking spirits?
She who formerly gazed upon her beloved with eyes lovely as a cluster of blossoms, reddened by passion and intoxicated, tender, clever, innocent, and sweet— she,
that very same woman, now makes of him a deer caught in the snare of Love for all those filled with passion.
With eyes like those of a startled bird, that woman causes me great distress.

"This excellent woman, with her body-staff hidden within by various impurities, seems to mock those impassioned men whose eyes of intellect are blinded by passion, thinking, 'I have deceived them,' with a face whose lips have been snatched away by birds."
That very same woman who once fell asleep in the embrace of her beloved, her body relaxed within his arms amidst the sweet sounds of lutes and flutes and the soft melodies of falsetto singing—
she now sleeps here, her limbs roughened by the dust of the earth.
In the cremation ground, fierce with the loud and clamorous howling of jackals.
When we examine even a single hair-tip within this foul cavity filled with one's own impurities,
how can these wicked people find delight in this vile body— the abode of disease and subject to death?

Sisters, realizing that this entire world is of such a nature— fickle by its very essence like a dream, a magical illusion, or the moon reflected in water— attain detachment while this [world] still endures.
He approaches the state where only his life-breath remains; he does not meet with destruction from you.

With his vital organs pierced by the thorns of life-threatening calamities, his eyes submerged in water, bitten by the makara of Death, and his head bristling with the white fangs of a mass of grey hair— what wholesome deed could he possibly perform?
The virtuous declare that the desire for merit in one whose body is being pulverized by the fall into the great abyss of the world beyond— a realm of terrifying darkness—
is like the scent of a frog confined within the narrow opening of a venomous snake’s mouth.
"Why do you now observe silence after deceiving the world with words that were fabricated and sweet,
yet so bold in their harsh, slanderous, and baseless talk? Thus,
as if reproaching him impetuously, she bit her lower lip with the tips of her teeth.
But the bird seizes the tongue-flesh with the pincers of its beak.
Having reached the range of the eyes of those fools who are blinded by passion and whose intentions are crooked from the habitual practice of false objects, it shattered their fortitude;
today, we are free from fear regarding that beautiful orb of her hips.
The vultures scratch out a row of nail-marks and footprints upon the noble lady.
By means of those two [eyes], she went, her lotus-like hands placed in the palms of her beloved,
her face turned sideways as she gazed at a painting upon the wall,
slowly, very slowly, across the floor of her own chamber where flowers had been strewn over her upper garment.
This jackal now devours those very feet of the young woman.
In this state, alas, alas, those whose minds are intoxicated by the wine of passion fall into the mire of various natural impurities;
yet you, beholding this inauspicious nature of the body, [should remain steadfast].
Become disenchanted with this world of living beings, which is as transient as a flickering flash of lightning.

He who, having attained the sovereignty over the Dharma as it truly is, brought joy with the water-pitchers of his naturally cooling words of Dharma to those beings who were scorched within by the wounds of the channels of incessantly flowing afflictions.
To that supreme physician of the treatise, let there be homage at all times! // GoSk_60 //
By whom [this] birth is designated— [a state] difficult to discern, deceptive, inauspicious, impelled by afflictions and karma, manifest in every form, entirely unveiled;
wherein the deluded one, lacking self-mastery, wanders like the wheel of a chariot.
The world has its form crushed by the blows of the thunderbolt of intense calamity.
The mother, in her childhood, braided her hair with *pratisaravatī* threads,
upon which her beloved later fastened a jeweled crocodile at the onset of youth;
and that [hair] which had been sprinkled by Brahmins with drops of pacifying water and fragments of beautiful flowers.
Alas! That impudent crow is touching the head of the woman today.

Those locks of hair which were perfumed with fine flowers at the time of marriage, when the mother’s hand performed the auspicious rites of the wedding— now, being shaken by fierce winds, they have become the chowries for the trees of the cremation ground.
Where is that naturally clever glance of hers, looking askance? Where is that graceful gait, languid with intoxication?
And where indeed have gone those smiles of hers, which made her lips dance?
Oh, how well-composed is this wonderful secret illusion of Kali!
Upon that very cheek, tender as the petal of a young lotus and reddened by the reflection of the gems in earrings swinging during laughter, he, joyful and holding her dear as his own life,
carefully placed a sprout as an ornament.
The bird, perching upon his forehead, scratches its face which is stained with red.
In that very lake of a chest, where the rays of pearl necklaces are the foam upon the water, the line of body hair is the moss, and the pair of expansive breasts are the ruddy geese,
the eyes of those in distress find their abode even as her garment slips away under some pretext.
Today, flies and gnats are falling upon that putrid corpse there.
Formerly, that beautiful woman was fanned by maidservants with palm-leaf fans releasing sprays of sandalwood water amidst the jingling of their bracelets;
she rested upon a pillow shaped like a bimba fruit in a palace white with offerings of moonbeams.
But today, the crows fan that very same [body] with the harsh winds of their wings.
Where has that monkey of a mind gone, which previously shook this tree of the body as it wandered among its branches? It has now abandoned this tree.
Where is that rogue of a mind, by which this body— though devoid of action— is perceived as if it possessed action, even though it is not one's own?
Where has that rogue of a consciousness gone— that deceiver of the heretics whom those whose intellects are blinded by ignorance claim to be the inner self?
Where indeed has that magician of the mind’s illusions gone, by whom the world was long deluded and not established in the true principles?
Those whose goal even Kapila and other ascetics do not know—
where is that possessor of the science of the mind, whose sphere of activity is the sky of sense objects?
Where now is that bird of the mind which once moved within this impure, unstable cage of a body with its nine gates?
Possessed by which, the ignorant sink into the ocean of existence— a sea filled with the spreading serpents of the afflictions and brimming with the salt water of intense calamities and misfortunes—
where the waves are tossed by the agitation of the makaras of death.
Having abandoned this body, where indeed has that night-stalker of a mind gone?
Because he is unsubdued, he casts [the sinner], pained and helpless, into the opening of the gate that is tawny with circles of flickering flames;
the Blessed One knows the means for him, whose pride has been removed.
Where has this horse of the mind gone from us—so naturally fickle?
Then, his thick forearms darkened by the luster of his vajra, he approached with humility, his eyes quivering with joy, and said, "Excellent!
Excellent! in a manner charming with conciliation.
Vāsava, whose speech was naturally charming, [addressed] those maidens.
In their youth, these sisters— having become abodes of the god of love—
renounced the pleasures of the glory and fortune of the royal family and undertook that which is difficult even for the ancient seers to achieve.
"I am pleased today by this vow of yours; what do you choose? GoSk_77 //

I consider this sovereignty over the realm of desire, or even the bliss of the Lord of the Thirty-three, to be like the palm of my hand today because of this certainty of yours. Speak quickly, sisters: what shall I do? I am at your command.
It flashes in your minds that I am Śakra, the king of the gods.

Then those maidens, who were free from desire for the pleasures of the senses and possessed of naturally beautiful dispositions, glanced sideways at Śakra and sang this faultless song, their words being full of wonderful meaning:
His nature is as firm as charcoal in the sense that his own roots of virtue have reached full maturity.

O friend of the immortals, we are not led by the continuous thread [of worldly existence] because we are afflicted by the suffering of birth and lusting after mere fragments of the pleasure of becoming; rather, we have undertaken this vow, bound as we are by the mere droplets of the water of tears of grief.
Having cast aside even his kinsmen, whose beauty of countenance was now clouded with distress.

Moreover, having observed the entire world— born after the destruction of the defilements— to be piteous as it is being shattered by the blows of hundreds of thousands of intense calamities pierced by its own wrong conduct;
We are striving to attain the state that is fearless and free from sorrow.
O Śatamanyu, if you are able to grant a boon because of your noble resolve, which is tender with compassion for the world,
then [grant] that noble state— ageless, unassailable, and peaceful like Brahman.
O you who are scorched by the fear of existence, lead us to liberation!
With his body smeared by the moisture of impurities flowing from the streams of bodily excrement, with veins laid bare upon the framework of bones and joints, he falls down, afflicted by fainting;
for without abandoning it, one experiences [this state] emerging from the womb, that dense mire of the mother's impurity.
Suffering and the succession of suffering—cut off that from us, for it is our very birth.
The world is bitten by the demoness of old age, who has turned her face away from all bounds; she possesses the white sprouts of graying hair as her fangs,
and she is the destroyer of men’s vigor, memory, fortitude, intelligence, and fortune.
Therefore, protect us, O Lord of the Gods, if you have the power to do so.
O Lord of the Gods, because his body has not been bitten by that which is called "disease," he possesses a hard belly that heaves with the expulsion of breath, a complexion that is pale and parched,
and he lacks the strength even to enjoy the various and brilliant pleasures that come to him. Thus, he fears that very thing known as disease.
Be our protector from the man who is a messenger of death, if you wish to grant us a boon.
With eyes motionless upon his return, his body paralyzed by the exhaustion and agitation of the pain from the severing of his vital organs, and his limbs numbed by cold,
he beheld his kinsmen whose cheeks and lips were bathed in tears.
By the mere scent of whom one goes to dissolution—protect us from that death!

One whose mind is embraced by that [passion] becomes like a beast, falling into a pitiable state; with a mind too feeble to distinguish between what should and should not be done, he becomes an object of reproach.
Even when embraced by a breeze that releases sprays of tamāla-scented water, such a person finds no joy.
O Giver of Boons, extinguish for us that fire of passion which leads to the states of woe.
Through whose possession the wicked, with eyes throbbing and lips bitten, instantly create sinful, inauspicious hell;
he who has not even been uprooted by sages subsisting on withered leaves and water.
Therefore, O Śakra, drive out the serpent of anger from the hollow of our minds.
By which those of evil intellect, with unguarded eyes and minds smeared with the poison of false views, having abandoned the auspicious path, have resorted to another way; that very thing which they,
whose darkness has been dispelled, proclaim as the cause for the arising of all taints.
O Hara, sever for us that darkness of delusion which dwells within the inner chamber of the mind.
O Śakra, we pray for a boon of this very kind from you;
for the virtuous do not act in a manner that contradicts their pledged word.

Then Śakra, his wonder expanding at those words—which were pure and radiant, showing no regard for the wretchedness of craving for sense-objects—and with the hair on his body bristling with serene joy, said:
"When asked for an impossible object, people indeed fall into the dejection of failure.
Choose a boon, O daughters of the king, whatever it may be that can be granted by me."
Then those maidens, having become agitated and indignant by those words of his which were internally concealed by deceit and sophistry, said to Śakra:
"O Thousand-eyed One, why do you approach us today and thus deceive us?
O you whose intellect is corrupted by the mere pursuit of pleasure, we are not to be approached by such a rogue."
Is it not known to you that this royal lineage has spread its mass of fame throughout the quarters of the world;
for even Kubera, the Giver of Wealth, surely bears a name that does not accord with his reality when compared to the essential wealth of this family?

O Lord of the Gods, it was out of fear of old age, sickness, death, calamity, exhaustion, distress, and poverty— and not out of fear or childish impulsiveness— that we have abandoned him and come to this state.

O Śakra, what purpose do we—who have been tormented by you despite your merit and are now exceedingly distressed—serve you? Live on with your kinsmen, friends, and servants; enjoy your wealth for a long time to come!
If you have become the lord of the gods through the union with the brilliant fortune of well-performed deeds, then what of it?
For the virtuous do not attain prosperity for the sake of inflicting harm upon others, O King of Gods.

Then Mahendra, his wonder nourished by their words which clearly indicated the essence of various and profound meanings, the beauty of his face manifesting through his graciousness, and desiring once more to know their inner state out of a wish to hear further distinctions of meaning, spoke again with these words:
"Wait a moment, sisters!"
O you whose wealth is asceticism, even for the sake of seeing me, people in this world entreat me;
why then, while I am a granter of boons, are you so harsh?
Then those maidens, their anger and resentment having increased even further, spoke with harsh words and indignation to the Lord of the Thirty-three:
"The face of Śacī— with its white-cornered eyes, smiles, and glances— is seen in one way, yet the boon is being granted in quite another."
O Purandara, if you possess the power to grant a boon,
then first slay this wicked female demon of desire for sense-objects.
Alternatively, since sensual desires are difficult to abandon for those greedy with false intentions,
let those very desires be yours eternally, if you possess such power.
O Thousand-eyed One, with your mind so attached to transient desires, tell me: how indeed will you bestow a boon upon another?
How indeed, being yourself carried away by a river of terrifying current,
will you enable others to cross over, when you yourself are dependent on those who are emaciated and dull-witted?
Wearing robes made of discarded rags and with our hair shorn,
when will that time come for us to go from the forest to the village?
Gazing only a yoke’s length ahead, with clay bowls held in our hands,
when shall we wander for alms from family to family with full mindfulness?
When shall we, who delight in the gift of Dharma, purify ourselves from the mire of gain and honor— a mire fraught with the perils of affliction?
When, rising from a heap of straw, clad in robes heavy with frost,
shall we go at will for food and drink, free from desire?
When, sitting at the foot of a tree— dark as a parrot and clad in a garment of soft green grass— shall we attain the festival of happiness in this very life?
When, having abandoned concern for body and life as if they were mere blades of withered grass,
shall we at last attain happiness after long practice?
When, situated in the bower of the river, shall we abandon the rise and fall of the world of living beings with waves that break again and again?
Having uprooted the view of a self-identity, which consists of all forms of the view of a self,
when shall we become free from longing for existence and its enjoyments?
When indeed shall we realize the world, with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as being like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a cloud, or a city of the Gandharvas?
Thus, for those in whose hearts such a longing for the Beloved expands at dawn,
what purpose indeed could there be in wealth that is tainted by sensual desire and unstable?
Moreover, O Lord of the Gods, you whose mind is intent on granting boons: O Lord of the Suras, sensual desires are delightful for only a moment of false conceptualization and are inherently perverse;
they are shunned by the noble-minded and virtuous, like dark and bottomless abysses.
Sensual desires are indeed the cause of all calamities and bringers of humiliation to men;
they are loathsome and terrifying, like black snakes smeared with excrement. (GoSk 114)

Who indeed would resort to those sensual pleasures, which are like executioners, by indulging in which multitudes of beings have gone to their death, are going, and will go— pleasures that have become the cause of misfortune?

Since those who are Śakra and those who are dust-demons possess an identical nature because they both arise from the impulse of unreal conceptualization— who indeed would desire such things even in their mind?
Having abandoned the forests where emerald-green meadows rise like lapis lazuli and where trees burst forth with blossoms,
the lordly elephants— now their frontal globes shattered by the stroke of sharp goads— bear heavy burdens, deceived by the objects of the senses.

Men bitten by the serpent of sensual objects go to their destruction, their bodies impaled on the point of the stake while being fanned by the wind from the wings of flocks of city crows, and watched under the pretext of friendship by the eyes of those very crows.
Having themselves ignited the fire of desire within the houses of their own minds by means of the winds of false conceptualization, these foolish women burn themselves for hundreds of autumns,
just as bamboos are consumed by the fire born of their own friction.

Moreover, O wielder of the thunderbolt, even after dwelling in Vaijayanta—which is beautiful with the radiant manifestation of the splendor of shimmering jewel-rays—those who remain attached to the poisons of sensory objects go once again to the Avīci hell, terrifying with its blazing fires; may there be well-being for that happiness!
Let there be a miserable rebirth at the end of his stay in heaven, or rather,
let him be one whose eyes are tremulous with weakness from the suffering of falling;
for he experiences such misery while still delighting in the world of the gods.
Is it not the case that pleasure experienced by him is what was previously experienced?
If, after having plunged with jeweled boats into the celestial city’s pond— where swans sleep amidst blossoming golden lotuses—
one falls again against one's will into the Vaitaraṇī River due to one's karmas;
In [the river] whose inner waters are agitated by boiling human skeletons.
O Śakra, what longing can there be for those pleasures of the celestial abodes, which are bitter in their ultimate transformation and comparable to dreams and illusions?
The world of living beings is as flickering as the tongue of an enraged serpent.
Having understood all this, we who desire liberation remain steadfast.
"This is happiness" is merely a false conceptualization of the foolish who dwell within the depths of the realms of existence;
the Buddha, the speaker of truth, has declared that existence is suffering.
For from this [body], even in its entirety, all suffering is produced.
In this world of living beings, which is naturally overwhelmed by manifold sufferings,
whatever happiness occurs here is merely accidental;
even that, being overcome by a web of miseries, comes to destruction.
Just as the waters of rivers, upon reaching the ocean, become one with its waters.
For by women, with their bud-like hands— resembling lotus petals, adorned with bracelets, cooled by the embrace of sandalwood paste,
and possessing rounded, copper-hued fingers that are slightly moistened and relaxed through affection— a certain spot was touched.
Having fallen asleep, his offerings of flower garlands were scattered by the breeze from the fans.
Furthermore, with his body heavy with exhaustion, he lies upon a path bristling with the needle-like points of darbha grass,
fanned by winds harsh from contact with ashes;
therefore, one should realize that this world of living beings offers only a fleeting fragment of pleasure and is inherently unstable.

Having abandoned desires that yield only the fruit of calamity, one should devote oneself to the peace of Brahman. Then the Thousand-Eyed One, his body bristling with horripilation at their words, praised their resolve and departed in an instant toward the city of the gods.
Then, having entered the religious life, those maidens— whose eyes of intellect were purified by the discernment of the true meaning of reality—
crossed over the vast and difficult-to-traverse great ocean of the miseries of saṃsāra, which is insipid with pride and surging with waves.
The Sage, whose nature is certain through the discernment of the essence of all things, spoke this Itivṛttaka to all beings—
He who alone possesses eyes everywhere in a world blinded by delusion, for those wounded by the thorns of fear regarding existence.
Thus ends the glorious *Saptakumārikāvadāna*.
The work of the venerable teacher Gopadatta.

13. Like an caravan leader [discarding] withered grass, the virtuous abandon even their bodies without a dejected mind.
Those whose bodies have been washed by the water of compassion act for the sake of extinguishing the fire of the world's calamities.
Thus it is heard: When the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, through his practice of contentment, he was free from any desire for the particular enjoyments of existence;

because he had thoroughly understood the nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), even toward his own body his attachment and its continuity had vanished, owing to his direct knowledge of the defects of craving.

With his mind fixed upon that [goal], he was capable of acquiring wealth even by other means due to his proficiency in various gains practiced over many lifetimes; and because he had accumulated a vast store of merit, he was able to attract wealth and prosperity by mere intention. Thus, although possessed of abundant riches and resources, he remained surrounded by a fleet of merchants traveling under a secret agreement solely for the purpose of rescuing the world from its calamities.
Then, in due course, the merchants approached the great ocean;
they entered that reservoir of waters, which was deep, formidable, and possessed vast rows of caverns,
its white-edged surface streaked with foam shattered by the impact of the coastal mountains.
Whether by their own deeds or through the terrible transformations [of fate], the ocean, by its very nature,
in an instant seized their hearts and became more cruel than the time of universal destruction.
Beholding the ocean, whose swirling eddies were as crimson as the sap of young sprouts severed by the tips of the hoofs of donkeys and sea-monsters,
and which resembled the sky filled with a mass of clouds dyed by the glow of a new dawn, they stood struck with terror.

Beholding on all sides the mass of salt waters— which, like a forest of white water-lilies, was washed by the rays of the moon and made variegated by the arrangement of jagged fragments of white foam— they found no pleasure at that time when their very lives were in peril.
The ocean— its fish terrified by the roar of its bared conch-like teeth, its mass of waves shattered against the tips of the mountains of the serpent-world,
and its vast belly occupied by leaping, deformed crocodiles— pierced the hearts of those men of little strength.

Beholding that ocean— which, with waves as high as mountains driven by the force of the wind, seemed to swallow the sky along with the sun, stars, and moon— all those whose hearts were wretched ascended the swing of uncertainty regarding their very lives.

Gazing upon that abode of the salt-water ocean, whose shores were difficult to behold, which was as terrifying as a garland of venomous fire-breathing serpents with hoods expanded by hissing, they—depressed by the fear of death—fell into a state of supreme delusion. GoSv_8 //

Having plunged into the ocean— which resembled a mass of clouds heavy with water, which seemed to vomit forth darkness through the force of its spray of waves, and which was terrifying due to its lack of refuge— they bowed down to the Bodhisattva, their facial splendor stolen away.
Then, agitated by various terrifying omens never seen before,
they spoke thus with faltering and piteous voices, gazing intently at that Bodhisattva.
This person’s every effort, which was directed toward the hope for all his goals dependent upon you, has now ceased.
Therefore, let whatever must be done here be done quickly; our very lives are now at stake.
While you look on, these people before you, devoid of effort, are sinking into a sea of distress;
it is not appropriate to waste time in this matter, so exert yourself with your own strength. GoSv_12 //
No one who has ever followed at the soles of your feet has ever before been touched by calamities.
Therefore, O hero among men, protect this world as it wanders into the maws of misfortune.
Like a father feeling compassion for his sons, O Supreme Noble Being, deliver us from this fear of being held in the jaws of Death; be our protection against these calamities.
Even those realms of the gods do not move within the scope of your power;
therefore, O you of unfailing might, this is the time to rescue us, who are wretched and without a protector.
We consider that even when merely remembered, you are the supreme protection for all beings from their fears;
how much more so when beheld directly—therefore, O Kinsman of the World, manifest that manly prowess!
These cruel ones, with mouths agape and bristling with fangs like saws, and with bellies wide and vast in their gaping cavities, seek to slay us—
us who are here without protection— from the terrifying *timi* and *makara* fish.
Protect this person from this imminent downfall.

O Noble One, the *timiṅgila* fish, whose rows of waves are severed by their own tails and whose sharp teeth are set within the shells they have caught, will soon rush toward these people who have taken refuge at your feet. (GoSv 18)
O Lord, it is not fitting to delay now; this boat, struck by the waters, is falling apart.
O Hero, these fish are darting about on all sides, their eyes as red as polished guñjā berries.

Then that Great-souled One, his mind tormented by that unbearable calamity of others, disregarded even the loss of his own life; perceiving that terrible destruction of the multitude for which there was no remedy, his heart was overcome with compassion. Despite being in such a state, through his natural fortitude, he remained undisturbed in mind and spoke to comfort those companions with words reflecting his profound meditation on that moment: [The rest of the passage follows: "Friends, do not despair! For this calamity has already occurred; it cannot be turned back. But we must act so as to prevent further harm. Let us therefore quickly assemble all the people who live here and, having gathered them together, let us go to the king and inform him of this disaster. For if the king learns of it, he will surely provide some means to alleviate the suffering of these people. And furthermore, if we remain here, we shall be unable to protect ourselves from the danger of wild beasts and other threats. Therefore, let us depart at once. Thus he exhorted them. They, however, were overwhelmed by grief and could not speak; they merely shed tears and looked toward the face of their leader. Then the Great-souled One, seeing them thus dejected, spoke again to encourage them: "Do not grieve! For even if one is struck down by calamity, one should not lose heart. For the wise man, even when facing death, maintains his composure and strives to benefit others. Therefore, let us go to the king and report this matter. Having said this, he rose up and set out. And those companions, following his lead, departed with him. As they traveled, they saw a great forest on the path, filled with various trees and creepers, where birds of diverse kinds were singing. Seeing it, the Great-souled One, moved by compassion, spoke to his companions: "Friends, let us rest here for a while. For this place is pleasant and free from danger. We can recover our strength here and then proceed to the city. They agreed, and having entered the forest, they sat down upon the ground covered with grass and leaves. There, the Great-souled One, observing the beauty of the forest, began to reflect upon the nature of existence and spoke these verses: [The verses follow. Then, after a short time, a certain hunter who lived nearby came to that spot in search of game. He saw the Great-souled One sitting there, radiant with virtue, like a deity. Approaching him with reverence, he asked: "Noble sir, who are you? Whence have you come? He replied: "I am a merchant's son traveling to another land with these companions. The hunter, hearing this, felt pity for him and said: "If you are weary, stay here; I shall provide you with food and drink. The Great-souled One accepted his offer, and they spent the day there in conversation. When evening came, the hunter prepared a meal of roots and fruits and offered it to them. They ate and rested, and as night fell, they lay down upon the ground. While they slept, a great storm arose, accompanied by lightning and thunder. A massive tree, shaken by the wind, fell upon them. The Great-souled One, waking up, saw the fallen tree crushing his companions. Seeing this, he was seized by a surge of compassion and, though himself in mortal danger, he exerted himself to the utmost to save them. He pushed aside the branches with his hands and freed them from the falling timber. By his efforts, they were all delivered from the tree. Having saved them, he himself lay down exhausted. But the tree, driven by the force of the wind, crushed him, and he passed away. The hunter, waking up and seeing the Great-souled One lying dead, was overcome with grief and lamented: "Alas, how cruel is this world! This noble man, who was full of compassion, has given his life for others. May his merit be a source of peace for me! Having spoken thus, he performed the funeral rites for the Great-souled One and returned home. The merchants' sons, having recovered from their exhaustion, continued their journey and eventually reached the city. There they reported everything that had happened to the king. The king, hearing of the Great-souled One’s sacrifice, was deeply moved and honored his memory with great ceremonies. Thus ends the story of the Great-souled One, who, through his fortitude and compassion, brought relief to many and attained the highest state.
The oceans do not dwell together with the dead; this alone is their eternal renown.
Therefore, relying upon my deceased body, may the virtuous cross the ocean that is so difficult to traverse.

Having entered into this union with me, all of you, casting aside agitation, despair, and dejection, strive to deliver yourselves from the great ocean and me from the mire of supreme suffering. (GoSv 21)

For dear friends who have fallen into calamity and whose hearts are bound by long-standing affection, what other means is there that is so pleasing? Therefore, do not let yourselves fall into this sorrow born of love.
I would ward off even the calamity falling upon an enemy at the cost of my own life,
let alone that which falls upon you, for whom I have long cultivated affection and care.

If even an ant or an insect could become happy through my own bodies, though they be devoid of pleasure, then I would cast off those bodies without distress, as if they were withered blades of grass. (GoSv 24)

What is so wonderful in this that I, whose mind has been purified by the virtues of those who have taken refuge in the intention to protect, abandon my body for their welfare, moved solely by compassion? (GoSv 25)

Those of perfectly pure being, who have made the world of living beings their wife through compassion, undergo weariness while carrying a body that is useless for the service of others—like one bearing a heavy burden in vain. (GoSv 26)

If I do not employ this body for such an influx of merit, which is followed by incomparable happiness, what is the purpose of abandoning this wretched carcass, as fragile as a bubble on the ocean lashed by the wind? (GoSv 27)
If I do not abandon this putrid body at this time of performing the rite for establishing your welfare,
the powerful Lord of Death— intent on the destruction of the world— will forcibly cause me to relinquish it when I am weak.
Shall I abandon you while waiting for fame, or for the dharma that resides in honor?
Or shall I, powerless, cast off this body which is a fetter for those in the Kali age and is already seized by the hands of Death?
Therefore, you should not direct your minds toward grief or impending defeat in this matter;
for this great festival, delightful through its exceptional merit, has come to me in due course.
The wicked, who are led by a continuous succession of many threads of pleasure and pain, cast off their bodies without hesitation as if they were blades of grass;
yet if one gives up a body that is soon to perish for the sake of others—especially if it has been purified by virtuous conduct—is there anything difficult about that?
Then those men, their minds won over by that marvel of his, their hearts even more distressed by the fear of separation from him,

overcome by despondency and wretchedness, embraced at the feet that Great Being— whose deed was beyond the scope of thought, unbearable, and most wonderful— with faces dejected and eyes washed by incessant streams of tears.
And bowing with all their limbs, they spoke thus:
"We would all rather meet our death right here in the great ocean;
we are not able to commit such an ignoble act."
Having seen such calamities befall this most rare and special friend, what purpose is served here by life or wealth? Therefore, O firm-minded one, restrain him from this rashness.
Who will lift us up once we have crossed this flood of water so difficult to traverse, only to sink again into the whirlpool of our own evil conduct?
Surely this ripening of karma alone has now presented itself,
by which this calamity has arrived— terrible and beyond remedy.
Having disregarded this suffering of our friend, which is bound up with evil, by what means shall we again reach the end of our own suffering? (GoSv 36)
One should make even an outcaste’s mental continuum gentle through compassion;
O Noble One, let alone [ordinary] friends, this is the very nature of your past deeds.

Then the Bodhisattva, his intense faith, love, reverence, and compassion further expanded by those words indicating their goodness, and wishing to console those companions, spoke as if sprinkling them with the nectar-water of compassion through outpourings of satisfaction:
"Unasked by you, for my own welfare, I [shall give] that which is called my body."
I am abandoning what is useless; what ignoble thing could there be for you in that?
This moonlight is indeed out of season; it is no calamity for me at all.
For I have found this eternal remedy against all misfortunes.
If you possess any state of mind toward me characterized by friendship, trust, and security,
then you ought not to create an obstacle for the Dharma, which is adorned with fame.
The mind must be directed toward what is beneficial even by force, and the ignoble mind must be separated from what is harmful by the noble ones.
Therefore, you who have tearful faces ought not to obstruct my engagement here in this action practiced by the virtuous.
For him, there is indeed no grasping, nor is there any appropriation for the sake of another;
he awaits me, the wretched body, as those who strike at its vulnerabilities.
"Even though this has been taken up by us, it cannot be accepted;
if it does not serve as an aid for the welfare of sentient beings, what is the use of this which only leads to ruin? (GoSv 43)
If I do not rescue you from this difficult-to-cross [state],
how shall I ferry the world across the ocean of saṃsāra?
Bodhisattvas, whose beings are undiminished, perform these and other deeds;
moving within the sphere of activity for the sake of others, they are permeated by compassion and have no attachment to their own happiness.

This dwelling, with its doors unbarred, shall for a long time become a source of joy for my friends as they arrive to bring me benefit, while it remains a receptacle for the unbearable arrows of the miseries of existence.
Having dedicated my body to this arising of happiness consisting of your protection, I shall certainly attain the unsurpassed,
flawless body of Dharma— which is indivisible, indestructible, unseizable, and imperishable.
If I treat this [body], which is actually an enemy, as a friend and engage in this strife,
my mind will for a long time be consumed by the fire of remorse, with its crest of sighs.

"Free from despondency, sirs, take hold of my body, which is full of life, like a raft; clinging to one another by mutual support, driven by the force of the water, reach dry land by whichever wind or direction it may lead you. There, sustaining yourselves with leaves, roots, fruits, water, and the like, do not let your mutual affection perish, rely upon the fact that one is the master of one's own karma, and contemplate the true nature of the world."
Having set aside disputes, grief, and dejection, await the conclusion of your business.
After experiencing happiness, one experiences suffering;
after attending to prosperity, one attends to adversity.
For those wandering within the prison of *saṃsāra*, this alone is sufficient calamity; yet even more wretched hardships are encountered here, which torment both the ears and the mind.
Indeed, no one who pursues this [worldly life] can be called happy.
For one situated in the midst of a mass of flames agitated by a powerful wind, the suffering of burning is established without even needing to be stated.

For those whose minds are subject to craving, defeat stands face-to-face; all forms of wretchedness lie in their very lap; humiliation is close at hand; fear is established above; and on all sides are the distortions of deception—in short, embracing the entire web of inauspiciousness, craving binds a man.
And you must not allow any room in your heart for the wretchedness of separation from me.
For such is the nature of the world: unions with beloved persons are inevitably followed by the suffering of separation.
Even friendships bound by firm affection through long-term intimacy fall asunder in an instant.
This is the delusion of sentient beings regarding the mind: "This one is dear to me."
In the world of the living, pleasant and unpleasant things are seen to undergo change due to the reversal of various causes.

Therefore, one should not weary oneself by becoming attached to the meeting with loved ones— things that depend on others, whose nature is unestablished, which exist through a diversity of conditions, which are occasions for deception, whose character is fickle due to momentary transformation, and which are times of sorrow and exhaustion.

In that regard, fortitude alone is the support for those who are harsh amidst calamities; it disregards despondency, restrains grief, and thwarts impending misfortune. When joined with wisdom, it brings about one's desired goal. However, the non-cessation of grief needlessly torments the body, obstructs duty, destroys luster, exhausts creative intuition, and afflicts one’s circle of friends who are bound by affection.
It destroys virtue, wealth, fame, and happiness.
Therefore, you who perceive my deed [as such] should cultivate devotion toward meritorious acts;
for merit alone is the unfailing kinsman of living beings in this world and the next, a companion in times of distress, and the provisions for the journey.
It is a lamp that requires no effort to carry through the darkness; a bridge across precipices; protection in places of fear; a blessing established without duality;

an ultimate accomplishment; a master who is easy to serve; a refuge for those fallen into calamity; a source of unchanging happiness; a mine of fame pervading the cardinal and intermediate directions; a treasury of praises; and an unconquered confidence.
Indeed, by the very support of merit, a person easily plunges even into that which is difficult to fathom.
Even in the wilderness of the next world, a place of despair at the time of death, those of meritorious deeds do not despond.
Those strong in merit generally traverse, unharmed, the treacherous passes of birth, however rough they may be with heaps of thorns.

By means of merit alone, they attract the vast abundance of qualities belonging to the Tathāgatas— which, through the activity of their resolute intention for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, is common to all beings and constitutes the great consecration of sovereignty over all realms— let alone the meager pleasures of this world, which offer no room for [higher] bliss, which are fraught with defects, which agitate the minds of the masses, and which are distressing both here and in the hereafter, being defiled by the impact of the infinite arrows of suffering.

"Alas! For the foolish, this entire misfortune—consisting of worldly enjoyments, corrupted by the continuous decay of every moment, harsh with the attachment to various forms of enmity, inauspicious, wicked through its adherence to perverted pleasures, masked by the notion of prosperity, and burning the mind with causeless ruin—is now at hand. Thus he spoke, and having said "Enough," he passed away from that discourse.
"This is my final instruction for the time of action, O gentle-faced ones," having said this, the Bodhisattva remained with one-pointed mind for a moment;
though being restrained by hundreds of friends whose eyes were streaming with tears,
the virtuous one, tormented by the suffering of the world, abandoned his concern for the support of his own body.
As the cries of those whose mental composure was obliterated by despair— cries incessant and indistinct in their syllables—
filled the hollows of the waterfalls, the salt-water ocean was violently agitated.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva also strengthened his vow for the sake of the peace of all sentient beings, [reflecting]:
"Divine prosperity is already by nature fickle and fraught with calamities; how much more so is any other [prosperity], which is a source of limited pleasure and accompanied by misfortune?"
Therefore, I have no need for pleasures that are like dreams and illusions; nor do I seek the bliss of tranquility by abandoning the worlds because of this merit. GoSv_51 //

The world is submerged in the ocean of existence, which has delusion for its whirlpools, death for its crocodiles, pride for its internal rocks, thirst for its waters, passion for its turbidity, and anger for its crawling serpents; it is tossed about by the winds of sorrow.
By this merit, may I deliver the entire world, which is without refuge.
Having thus made this firm vow, his soul as steadfast as the core of a mountain, indifferent even toward his own body which had been acquired through hundreds of virtuous deeds,
he joyfully sliced open his belly with a sword.
With his own heart pained by the affliction of grief, he [acted] for the sake of delivering living beings.
Then there were heard the auspicious words of the gods, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas— words that fell upon him, endowed with his virtues and resting upon a wondrous and captivating subject.

Oh, what skill in acting for the benefit of sentient beings! Oh, the steadfastness of mind! What a marvelous state of being belongs to those of great merit through the excellence of their practice of virtue!
How pure indeed is the conduct of the virtuous, in which attachment to one’s own happiness has vanished! — [the rest of the verse is lost].
Alas! Compassion does not require a support for itself.
Though this world was closed to him, it has been opened up on all sides by the wise man through his fame, which possesses the luster of a night-lotus washed by the moonbeams.
Even as he himself sinks away, the world that was submerged has been raised up by him alone.
Birth is like a cesspool of mud, teeming with the wriggling worms of vast afflictions.
As it was being tossed about horizontally by gentle breezes cool with fresh water, flowers fell incessantly from the trees of the divine grove upon his body;
and rising up from the ocean with their heads formidable with the beauty of the rays of shimmering jewels, they [the gods] approached.
The serpents bowed before him with their heads, soft as blue lotuses, bent at the tips and in the middle.
As if thoroughly anointed by Fortune herself, with a complexion as beautiful as polished gold,
the body of that Lord shone with a serene radiance, as if its vital breath had surged forth once more.
Then, taking his body as their raft, their eyes reddened at the corners by the mingling of tears and water, they crossed the ocean—
where the circles of waves were lashed by the hands of sea-monsters— by relying on the power of his own vow.
Thus, for the welfare of the worlds, that Blessed One— whose stainless resolve was permeated with compassion— performed deeds that were exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
therefore, direct your minds toward him, the kinsman of the world, with faith.
In the Jina, the sole hero in performing deeds that benefit the entire world.
Having pacified your mind toward the Sage, who is a unique jewel-mine of virtuous conduct,
let the words of that speaker of truth be heard— words which are an elixir for the ears; for this world, deprived by not hearing them, wanders about afflicted.
In the path of existence, which is without support and strewn with the thorns of calamity; GoSv_61 //
Thus ends the *Śrīsārthavāhajātaka*.
