14. The virtuous, who give everything and suffer with the suffering of others, do not even regard their own lives.
Thus it is heard: the Bodhisattva ruled over a certain region of the earth inherited through his own family lineage.

For him, [the kingdom] was characterized by rewards that were pleasing to the hearts of those seeking them, which proceeded without partiality, were exceedingly sweet, fulfilled desires at the appropriate time, and possessed a pure splendor through the absence of stinginess regarding the distribution of fruits and vegetables.
As he gratified the worlds with the distribution of his wealth, his name "Sarvamdada" (All-Giver) became celebrated as truly descriptive of his character.
Out of his intense zeal for establishing the welfare of the world, that lord of the earth gradually took up the burden of sovereignty,
which had been brought to him by the power of the irreproachable merit accumulated in previous lives.

The unstable riches that come of their own accord— resembling the *kiṃpāka* fruit, which are auspicious only as long as they are a mere delusion of the mind— did not bind that great-souled one of noble nature.
The exertion of that lord of the earth, whose mind was governed by great compassion, became his dowry;
yet his sovereignty over the worlds remained unimpeded amidst abundant pleasures of power and prosperity.
When even the mental veil of the darkness of stinginess no longer clung to his limbs, then all talk regarding wealth—
which brings unhappiness when acquired and is comparable to a blade of grass as a cause for grief— ceased entirely.

It is said that a certain king, unsatisfied with the splendor of his own kingdom, having abandoned dharma and fame, and cruel in his pursuit of the means to achieve pleasure, set out to displace that Great-Souled One from his realm;

for ignoble men, even after attaining great enjoyments, overstep the path practiced by the noble. Overcome by craving, they vomit forth the poison of anger even toward virtuous men who are compassionate by nature. (GoSd 5)
Even those who, like medicinal trees, occasionally and somehow serve for the welfare of the world—base men, their minds scorched by the fire of anger, burn them down. (GoSd 6)
What noble and conscious man indeed would direct a malicious thought toward those whose fame, as white as the night-lotus, has illuminated the very quarters of the sky? (GoSd 7)

Then that king approached, covering the sky with the dust of the earth— smoky-grey like the throat of a śārikā bird— raised up by the falling hooves of his horses, while his army of rutting elephants crushed the groves of trees in the pleasure gardens that were dark blue as clouds.
Like the ocean at the end of an eon, flooding the world with its tossing waves shattered by the tails of sea-monsters,
that host of the king’s army— its shimmering sunbeams acting as the blades of naked swords— besieged that city.
Fie on the royal splendor and happiness of kings, which, though attained through merits, ends in separation;
it brings about a lack of tranquility, like putrid flesh to a pack of carrion-eaters, and serves as the root of enmity and resentment for men in this world.

Then the Bodhisattva, having long since understood the faults and enmities inherent in the objects of the senses, and regarding sovereignty as being full of such evils as agitation and deception, reflected with a mind untainted by the wretchedness of attachment to his own pleasure and enjoyment:
"Fie upon this ignoble happiness that relies on sense-objects, as flickering as a creeper shaken by the wind!"
There, men whose minds are bound wait upon a state that causes affliction to their kinsmen.

Even with only my two arms as companions, I am capable of destroying the entire enemy force— an army where clouds are struck by the tips of banners fluttering in waves raised by the wind, and which is crowded with fierce lordly elephants whose mace-like tusks are drenched by the flow of rut.
If you have compassion, protect me like a mother in times of distress, so that I may remain unharmed in my conduct.

Or rather, who would desire that prosperity which is attained by one whose soul is consumed by the obsession with killing others— prosperity that is like a garland for a victim, though its flowers are praised by bees?
Even he who has set out upon a path devoted to the pursuit of his own self-interest...
How much more so for this world, which is already afflicted by calamities, that I am striving for its welfare!
Moreover,
if another person in the kingdom shows me affection, that king must indeed be honored by me all the more;
for it is for the sake of others, based upon my sovereignty, that I bear this burden of affliction which is the cause of long-lasting suffering.

Since this lord of men is worthy of honor like a guest, his mind being drawn by the request for the splendors bestowed upon me by me; and since he acts out of a special compassion due to his accumulated merit, as if toward a son—for the sake of discipline—what room is there here for anger?
He who forcibly releases me from this spreading calamity called kingship—
if I were to harbor resentment in my mind against him for this, what other sinner could possibly be equal to me?
Proclaiming the entry into the faults and defects of sovereignty, he destroys fame and happiness;
the lord of men instructs me in truth as I wander in the darkness called "kingship."
For this reason, those who desire their own welfare must renounce the glorious happiness of sovereignty over the earth;
for upon the head of one attached to it, the occurrences of enmity and fear manifest.
Or rather, having abandoned the uninterrupted and entirely auspicious groves of asceticism,
that I should dwell in what is called a "home"— a place of fear— I am not worthy of such calamities.

Therefore, from these vast expanses of sovereignty, splendor, and prosperity— which are as dreadful as they are the abode of manifold deceptions— I shall go to the peaceful forests, which are bound up with the joy born of solitude.
Since it is precisely because of this spiritual friend that the king has today attained the arising of the bliss of renunciation,
may there be only auspiciousness for him, along with his kinsmen and friends, for hundreds of autumns.
Do not give way to pride, thinking "I am a lord of the earth"—abandon this delusion.
Why do you vainly carry out a fragile command that brings imminent suffering?
A kingdom overtaken by calamity must indeed be abandoned; why do you not relinquish it?
I suspect that this king will effortlessly wipe away my wickedness in this manner.
"When will I abandon this home, so unpleasant and crowded with hundreds of misdeeds, and dwell in the forest, which is blessed by the enjoyment of the happiness of tranquility?"—
such were the thoughts that arose and remained persistently bound to my mind for a long time.
By good fortune, having obtained this lord of the earth, they will soon become renowned.

Having thus resolved, the Bodhisattva—whose familiarity with the joy of renunciation cultivated in previous lives had now reached its culmination—experienced a surge of delight like a deer escaping from the enclosure of a snare. With his body made light by the removal of the burden of royal splendor, ornaments, and finery, and his form rendered solitary and secluded, he was unaware by others of his purpose for departing for the penance grove; yet he remained steadfast in his deep-rooted affection, confidence, love, and respect.

And having abandoned his circle of kinsmen and the royal splendor— which, though it had been enjoyed with happiness brought about by the support of his own merit— like a garland whose flowers have become soiled and withered from long use, he adorned another, secluded hermitage.
He was as if being summoned by the leafy trees.

Having approached the peaceful forest edge, which was beautiful with the ornaments of its own flowers upon its branch-like arms, that Bodhisattva attained the deathless state, a bliss of kings never before obtained.

Those very things in the world that consist of sorrow and lamentation for those whose souls are devoted to sensual desires and who have no familiarity with the festival of tranquility— those same things indeed bring forth a blameless joy, characterized by a longing for non-material happiness, for those who are dear to peace.
Fanned by the forest breezes, pure with the lingering fragrance of flowers, he dispelled the fatigue of his body; then,
reflecting upon the sovereignty of men, which is defiled by heedlessness.
The king, however, nurtured only a sense of spiritual urgency within his mind.
Having offered salutations with his whole being to the Tathāgatas, the benefactors of the three worlds, in the ten directions,
[he sat] upon a seat made delightful by the use of unfading green grass mats.
The lord of the earth sat at the foot of the tree, while [the others] sat in the middle.
Wearied by the amorous dalliances of the beauties of the harem, which were conducive to the side of affliction,
that lord of the earth was like one who has found rest upon beholding forest retreats, the source of the bliss of solitary enjoyment.
Beholding the mountain ridges, naturally beautiful and with their dark stone surfaces washed by the streams of water falling from the cascades, he experienced great joy.

Beholding those great trees, dark with their abundant foliage, which were embraced by creepers languid from the weight of flowers as if out of affection for their very lives, that lord of the earth rejoiced.
Beholding the lakes filled with clusters of *pāṭhīna* fish, their lotuses struck by wandering bees, and their stalks of non-coarse *śyāmaka* rice, that king took his delight.
Beholding that forest region, naturally beautiful and conducive to the joy and bliss born of seclusion, the king, whose mental disturbances were completely stilled, attained great delight.
Beholding those forests, delightful with the cries of peacocks whose crests were ruffled by the wind,
that lord of the earth censured royal splendor as being scorched by the poison of manifold afflictions.
Where is that royal fortune of kings, crooked with the attachment to the conceit of false happiness;
and where are the peaceful joys of those dwelling in the forest, which bind the mind to tranquility?
Homage be to that decaying pleasure, defiled by its basis in passion for what is worthless,
by which the wise, having attached the activity of their minds to it, become objects of compassion.
The auspicious rivers, with their green sandbanks sprouting young grass and their currents flowing peacefully, have enjoyed the beauty of their embrace with the reed trees growing upon their banks,
whose tops are bent low. Their waters are stirred by gentle breezes.
Beholding this, the lord of the earth attained a joy that was free from worldly desire.
How can the heart of the wicked, defiled by the habitual practice of anger toward unreal objects, find delight in a peaceful forest?
But that king, through the support of the majesty arising from the excellence of his lineage, [will remain steadfast].
Averse to sense objects, he experienced supreme joy in the solitary forest.

Wealth— fickle by nature, fraught with manifold misfortunes, and incessantly cruel— does not indeed steal away the hearts of those who have reached the forest's edge, their mental agitation having vanished, for the sake of knowledge.
But for the virtuous, the mind becomes refined toward the auspicious through former habituation.
Their borders are trampled by the feet of deer, possessing grassy swards and waterfalls;
their trees are made to sway by breezes variegated with flowers;
and they resound with the diverse songs of flocks of joyful birds.
Whom would the auspicious forest ranges not fill with joy in their hearts?
In the forest— where tranquility is absent, which constantly incites anxiety, where the happiness of the Upaniṣads is destroyed for those tossed about by the winds of sensory objects,
and where there is the pleasure of natural ease free from the agitation and toil of worldly people; [in that forest, one should dwell].
But the mind, though agitated by evil deeds, immediately attains peace.

Now, a certain Brahmin, struck by the suffering of poverty and desiring a remedy for it, though lacking great energy, perceived the Bodhisattva as his sole refuge in distress. Traveling toward the borders of that realm, his mind agitated by losing his way, wandering here and there with a body emaciated by the pain of hunger, his heavy limbs rendered unmanageable and exhausted by the fatigue of the journey.

He reached that hermitage; and seeing him, the Bodhisattva, with a gaze tender with affection— exceeding even the love for a long-absent and dear kinsman— as if drinking him in with his eyes, went out to meet him, greeted him, and after exchanging friendly greetings,
asked the purpose of his visit.
The brahmin said:

"He who is renowned on earth by the name Sarvada, a protector of the world of men whose name is true to its meaning— I have come before him as if summoned by his fame, beholding that refuge for the distressed."
He alone is the protector of those afflicted by calamity; he alone is the singular kinsman of the supplicants.
It is by designating him alone as virtuous that speech elsewhere observes a vow of silence.
Having heard those words of his, the Great Being— whose heart was tender with compassion— trembled, struck by the wind of that man's suffering.
Then that Great Being, sighing long and hot, said to the brahmin:
"O twice-born one, let another means be devised for the pacification of this suffering;
that king, having fallen from his sovereignty, has retired to the forest for asceticism."

Then that brahmin, his mind overcome by the wretchedness of his hope for a desired object being dashed, suddenly fell to the ground and fell into a state of extreme delusion: "The hearts of those attached to worldly things, whose fortitude is overturned by hope, fall into delusion for any reason whatsoever. (GoSd 45)
Then the Bodhisattva, having sprinkled that brahmin with cool water and comforted him once he had regained consciousness, said:
"There is yet another remedy for the fulfillment of your hope;
I am King Sarvadada, so do not grieve here, O twice-born one."
How or when can one be called "Giver of All" if his mind still clings even to his own body?
Now, however, through the joy of your arrival, I shall become one whose name is true to its meaning.
"The king, who is devoted to my kingdom, is indeed searching for me;
therefore, bind me and give me to him, and he will satisfy you."

Trembling from the onset of manifold sufferings, this strife known as the body— having finally found refuge in you after a long time— will today come to serve my purpose for the sake of accomplishing the side of virtue.
O foremost of brahmins, alas, having taken recourse to this body which is indeed a pit for old age, disease, and death, may that long-cherished desire of mine be fulfilled today through your power.
The king will find joy, you will achieve a distinguished goal, and for me there will be the excellence of the perfections;
by relinquishing this single body beset by calamity, behold how a succession of supreme festivals is arriving.
When such a manifestation of affection from a guest has arrived— a source of success for my undertaking—
and while my body is the guest in the maw of the crocodile that is Death, ordained by manifold calamities, what other provision could there be?
Having approached you today, who are the essence, from this essenceless body, I desire to be uplifted;
therefore, O Brahmin, fulfill today my long-cherished aspiration that it may bear fruit.
"So be it," the wicked brahmin replied,
having transgressed the boundaries of noble conduct, his mind overcome by greed.
For those tormented by sense objects that are more terrible even than the venom of a serpent within a hollow tree, what indeed is difficult to do— that is, what sin is impossible for them to commit?
One gave his own body for the sake of another; the other took up the supreme [path] for his own sake.
Oh, how vast is the conduct of men who are devoted to virtues and to faults!
Having bound that Bodhisattva tightly by the back of his arm like a thief, the twice-born man,
naturally audacious, dragged him away even as he was being restrained by the forest deities.

Alas! This great seer, who has descended here like Dharma itself, his transformations of speech, body, and mind utterly stilled, is being led away by that vilest of brahmins, cruel with the arrogance of his lack of discipline.
These trees, with their trembling shoots and faces of noble blossoms shedding tears,
seem to weep as they are being parted from the wise sage by the plaintive sound of the humming bees.
"Beholding him, who brings such delight to the eyes of all embodied beings, is in every way most difficult to obtain"—
thus lamented the forest-dwelling sages, overwhelmed by the agony of their rising grief and consumed by intense sorrow.
Then the brahmin, taking that noble being— who was free from fear and whose mind and conduct were unperturbed—
led him into the city where the king, his rival, resided.
The young women of the city, who had previously beheld with eyes blossoming with affection that lord of men mounted upon the neck of an elephant like a god,
now saw him in the power of another, clad in bark garments.
With faces whose eyes had eyelashes heavy and motionless from the exhaustion of grief; // GoSd_62 //
Him who had the gait of an elephant in rut, white as gold,
tall like Mount Sumeru variegated with the jewels of the [major] marks,
clad in bark garments, and bearing a mass of matted hair long and tangled—
Seeing him, the king, his enemy, trembled out of lack of fortitude.
Beholding him in such a state, her mind agitated by trepidation,
she reflected: "Who indeed is this, with a chest as beautiful as a slab of gold,
a slender waist, and arms hanging down like the coils of a serpent?"
Though he was young, he was steadfast in his practice of discipline; he approached me as if reproaching me for being so preoccupied with evil deeds.
Whence comes this man, who is like the Dharma descended in embodied form, wearing bark garments yet beautiful to the eye;
though bound, he is not subject to wretchedness or despair?
And this treasury of splendor seems to emit tranquility itself. // GoSd_65 //
Then that lowest of brahmins said to the king:
"Victory, victory to the Great King! By good fortune you prosper.
That enemy king of yours, having entered the forest for some purpose and donned the garb of an ascetic, has begun some act of wickedness."
"Desiring to do what was pleasing to you, I have brought him here by force, struggling like a fish once caught; therefore, in this matter, Your Majesty is the authority.
Then the king, unable to believe that such a deed could be committed by that evildoer, said to him: "Wait a moment, sir!"
This best among the powerful, who has only his two arms as companions, is capable of conquering the earth girdled by the oceans— he whose tree-like arms hang down like the trunks of elephants.
O friend, how can you possibly overcome this broad-chested man?
Tell me that, [by which] deer do not overcome the lion with his quivering mane.
He disclosed the truth to that king;
and being rebuked with the words "Shame on you! by the king, who looked upon him with eyes clouded by anger, he was overcome with extreme shame.
Then the monarch himself released his bonds, seated the royal sage comfortably upon a costly throne, and, with his body bowed low in great respect, spoke to him.
O King, out of devotion to your virtues, the foremost among gods and asuras proclaim this superhuman and most excellent account of your deeds with their heads bowed low, softened by great respect.

O King, if the title "King" is established for one who is capable of pleasing the subjects, then you alone, O treasury of the jewels of virtue, are the true king; one devoid of virtue is unable to please the world.
Instruct us as you did before regarding your own city; we are ever intent on obeying the commands of those such as yourself.
Out of discipline, please forgive our transgressions; for one whose vision is clouded by grief stumbles even upon level ground.
Then, perceiving that the king had conceived faith and had become a worthy vessel for his virtuous conduct,
that Bodhisattva— whose voice was like the thundering of a dark rain cloud— spoke to him who was bowed down by the weight of reverence, as if he were a disciplined disciple.

The lifespan of men perishes in a short time, like a drop of water cast upon the surface of a heated stone; attachments with loved ones always end in the bitterness of separation, and prosperities are unbearable due to the poison of their inevitable transformation.
Sensual pleasures are delightful only for a fleeting moment through false attachment; their enjoyment is like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree.
Sovereignty is not exclusively pleasant, being bitter with obstacles, fraught with fear and enmity, and serving as the cause for heedlessness, slaughter, and imprisonment.
Therefore, always perform deeds that are sweet in their ripening and which bind the minds of virtuous people;
but abandon those deeds by the time of whose ripening men have faces distressed by tears of grief.
I have no further need for the pleasures of sovereignty— pleasures that are unstable, empty, and unreliable,
which serve as gateways to enmity, exertion, despondency, wretchedness, and strife, and which depend upon others; rather,
the mountains with their clinging clouds arouse longing within me.
The auspicious regions have their borders darkened by groves of *kadamba* trees from which flowers are hanging down.
With its soft grass-robes grazed away by herds of deer and strewn with fallen white flowers, the ground at the edge of the forest appears like the sky with its stars;
it forcibly carries away my mind, which has ceased all longing for the pursuit of sovereignty.
Then, having learned of that pure being’s resolve to go to the forest, the king—
his heart captivated by those very virtues— stood as if turned toward the forest himself.
And once his mind had been understood by that king, who was bowed with discipline, the Bodhisattva—
though his longing for sense-objects had ceased— turned his heart back from going to the forest.
Even in their dwellings, Bodhisattvas are like those in a forest, unafflicted by the calamity of sensual pleasures;
like sages inclined toward dwelling in the depths of the woods, they abide solely in the flavor of tranquility.
Like in a monastery, even in the forest those holy ones apply themselves solely to the means for the welfare of the world;
they sacrifice even their own bodies for the sake of others, yet they do not fail the requests of those who seek their favor.

Therefore, in this world, both the palace and the forest are equal for those whose mental resolve is dedicated to the ultimate task of benefiting the world without exception, through the vast expansion of their abundant resources that sustain all beings.
Having accepted what was given by him, that King, the charioteer of the world,
bestowed upon the brahmin wealth exceeding his desires and gave back his own kingdom.
Having heard that wonderful and sublime discourse on the Dharma uttered by the Brahmin,
he abandoned the poison called anger— which is more unbearable than any transformation of enmity— and,
as if placing it upon his head like a crown, [he remained] with his mind uplifted.
The king himself instantly fashioned a crown of garlands that was devoted to her lotus-like feet.

When he had departed for his own city, having submitted with humility, the king of noble merit, having obtained a kingdom free from enemies, ruled the earth according to Dharma— a land as beautiful as a silken garment on the shore, adorned by the foam-crests of the ocean of fame made white by righteousness.
The life-story of the Lords, whose splendor transcends all comparison, cannot indeed be followed by anyone;
nevertheless, this act of extreme audacity was performed by me, of narrow mind, for my own benefit.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me today through composing this account of the deeds of those whose nature is compassion,
may it swiftly lead to peace for the world, and from that, may the teaching of the Tathāgata blaze forth.
Thus ends the *Sarvadadajātaka*.
(Śvan = GoŚv, ed. Michael Hahn)

The virtuous, distressed by the suffering of others, hold even the sovereignty of the gods in contempt.
Thus it is heard: when the Blessed One was still a bodhisattva, he exercised sovereignty over the city of the immortals, which had been brought to him by the particular ripening of his own merit.

With a heart free from distress, he manifested the unfailing fruit of his merits alone through a majesty that surpassed all the worlds, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the inhabitants of the city of the immortals.
Having seen the world struck by the falling thunderbolt of endless calamities,
the Blessed One took no delight even in heaven, though it was naturally beautiful;
for then that wisdom, free from attachment, incessantly pierced his heart.
Inclined toward the welfare of others, supremely compassionate, and devoid of attachment to worldly pleasures.
For those whose minds are miserly and who have not performed virtuous deeds, the cause of their own state is that which the mind holds in high regard.
The mind of one who brings benefit to the world, having attained sovereignty through his own conduct, is not attached even to great sensual pleasures; it is well-guarded.
Once, while surveying Jambudvīpa,

he saw the world thus overwhelmed by the suffering of diseases that are impossible to remedy; its medical skill rendered futile by the harshness of the malady, it was dragged toward death, paralyzed by its resolve, and— as if chewing the cud— experienced the sufferings of hell right here, having forgotten the purpose of affection, kin, friends, and the practice of purity.

Then that transformation produced by disease— a great calamity, terrifying because its remedy was impossible— proceeded like the execution of the work of Death (Kṛtānta), resembling a minor kalpa-ending dissolution.
Overcome by the consciousness of hunger and thirst, wailing with persistent cries, their limbs scattered about, their hair disheveled and covered in the dust of the earth,
they remember again and again the jasmine creepers that shed drops of water— [what else could they do?]
The paths were filled with swarms of bees, hovering nearby.
With nostrils split wide by bellies swollen and hardened by labored breathing, their mouths terrifying with parched and tasteless phlegm clinging to the corners of their lips;
they are supported only by a frame of skin and sinews, matted and tangled with networks of coarse, thick veins.
Some reviled the impure karma they had previously committed, which was firmly rooted in their intention.

Some, with their bodies filthy and disfigured, vomited streams of pus from the cavities of their boiled flesh; so hideous were they that they could hardly be looked upon, yet even with their arms, bellies, thighs, ears, eyes, and noses mostly devoured by swarms of worms, they still implored for Time.
With the cavities of their lips, throats, and palates completely parched by the burning fire of thirst, their mouth-cavities dry, emaciated, and gaping, they are as exhausted as hungry ghosts;
[they gaze upon] the trickling waters concealed by groves of blue lotuses agitated by swarms of intoxicated bees.
Beholding the waters of the lakes, some entered the abode of Death.
With the corners of their eyes obstructed by films of rheum, foul-smelling and with bodies smeared with thick filth,
others— whose frames were weakened by exhaustion— became the abode of persistent maladies.
Some, lying wretchedly on the roads with their long beards matted and soaked by a profusion of flowing saliva, their bodies exhausted,
are beset by circles of fierce-crying crows swooping down upon them.
Having turned away from this calamity, those who were helpless underwent intense suffering.
Beholding that great and most terrible calamity of the world, compassion arose within him.

Then that Great Being, his mind distressed by that affliction of living beings and shaken even more intensely by his burgeoning pity, fell into reflection like a father unable to bear the misfortune of an only son.
For those who have gone thus, what means could there be for the happiness of eradicating the afflictions of living beings?
May I, therefore, become free from debt even to the Tathāgatas, the kinsmen of the three worlds.
May my vow indeed be fulfilled for the sake of accomplishing the practice of the welfare of all the world;
may those who endure the suffering of human birth attain liberation from calamities.
May I not falsely assume the designation of "Bodhisattva," while upholding the command of those who know all things, who are beyond reproach, and who are compassionate toward the signless.

May I alone be the supreme refuge for all beings— wounded by the arrows of the suffering of existence— who, like a mother and like a father, shall become a shoreless embankment against the flood of the ocean of worldly misery.
As long as people, overcome by suffering, do not enter the mouth-cave of the black serpent of Time— terrible with its fangs of disease and formidable in its enjoyment of devouring the entire world—
so long should one cast aside attachment to dualities and the delightful pleasures of the glory of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
I offer my devotion even unto the sacrifice of life, which brings the joy of love, for the service of all beings.
Having understood this resolve of him whose deeds are most wonderful,
the immortals, pained by the fear of separation from him, then cried out in lamentation.
O Compassionate One, where will you go, abandoning us who are suffering,
like a loving father leaving behind his young children when they are in danger?
O you of lovely appearance, do not depart, leaving us who are innocent, like one who neglects trees that he has been nurturing with the abundant waters of the True Dharma.
O Master, do not abandon us, who have been carried away by the horses of the senses— restless in their craving for sense-objects— and who are wandering toward the edge of a precipice.

Then the Lord of the Maruts, consoling the immortals whose eyes were flooded with tears—men whose heads were bowed low in the act of prostration and who were distressed by the onset of intense grief—spoke thus: GoŚv_19 //
It is not that my mind is not tender with affection for you, nor is this lack of regard for my own welfare; rather, this is my firm resolve:
to protect the world standing on the brink of blossoming calamities.
Therefore, let heedfulness be practiced; that alone will surely become your certain refuge in times of distress.
For reunions with loved ones are indeed deceptive: delightful at the moment of meeting, yet terrible in their ultimate consequence.
Even after remaining for an incomparable time in the abode of the Thirty-three, enjoying the extensive pleasures of various sensory delights,
the gods fall down due to the exhaustion of their karma, like the wish-fulfilling trees struck by the winds of universal destruction as they remember [their former state].
Moreover, even if the wicked plunge into the Mandākinī, whose banks are strewn with blooming golden lotuses along with the Apsarases,
they must again resort to the Vaitaraṇī, which has salt water and banks of blazing darbha-grass embers.

What wise person indeed would fix their mind upon those pleasures produced by the enjoyments of heaven— which are comparable to the petals of a flower tossed aside— and which end with an immersion into the submarine fire-mouth of the lower realms?

Having experienced pleasures together with their beloveds upon stone slabs that serve as couches, illuminated by many jewels in groves of wish-fulfilling trees, they once again find themselves in the midst of forests of sharp sword-leaves.

The pleasures derived from the enjoyment of sense objects by the intellect are as flickering as the eyes of a startled young deer and are driven by the wandering hand of the transformation of time; therefore, O gods, exert yourselves in the accumulation of merit.
Just as fires are extinguished by fuel, the fires of desire are not quenched by sense objects which are like the drinking of poison;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying your calamities, adopt the path of the Tathāgata, which delights in blameless happiness.

For the sake of pacifying those beings who are destitute, whose minds are exhausted by wretchedness, who are bitten by the multitude of venomous snakes of suffering, and whose bodies are as if carved away by axes—
even we shall imitate the behavior of animals.
We shall do so, having abandoned our attachment to the enjoyments of the celestial abodes.

Having seen the accomplishment of the ripening of my own good conduct— consisting of an unwavering commitment and a long-standing attachment to the aspiration for the benefit of the world— [I shall act].
Indeed, the virtuous ought not to create obstacles to what is wholesome.
Setting aside even his wondrous superhuman majesty, that Great-Souled One, drawn by compassion,
established himself in the state of animals, though it brings suffering, for he was supremely noble.

The arising of virtuous people for the benefit of the world is like the emergence of wish-fulfilling trees; they possess intentions tender with the nectar of compassion, and their minds are free from attachment to their own happiness. (GoŚv 31)
The prostrations of the hosts of gods, streaked with the rays from the crest-jewels of those whose crowns were the various gems of the Vinaya,
were unable to turn back him who was of firm resolve as he approached, bringing happiness to the human race.
Gazing piteously at him with eyes distressed by the agony of separation from their beloveds and with corners clouded by waves of tears, they were unable to turn back that being of pure essence.
His mind was not compassionate toward his own kin, nor was he by nature even upright;
nevertheless, having understood that superior disposition, that virtuous dog acted accordingly.
That benefactor of those afflicted by disease, as heavy as the Himavat and Meru mountains, a teacher to all creatures, that preeminent personage,
on account of the excellence of his virtues, surely rose up to a very great distance.

Out of compassion, he has renounced like a blade of grass that sovereign power of Indra— which those who subsist on water, fruits, roots, and air strive to attain through long austerities, heavy with the refinements of *yama* and *niyama*.
He attained the state of commonality with animals for the sake of benefiting the world.
Through the very practice of the auspicious, having exhausted the causal conditions for misdeeds,
the Tathāgata attained mastery over the projection of states of existence; thus,
he who is skilled in accomplishing the welfare of others acts according to his will and wherever he desires.
For thus was he born, solely for the sake of pacifying the calamities of birth for all worlds.
Great beings, bound by compassion, cannot endure seeing people afflicted by calamity—like a flame of fire clinging to the edge of a garment—though that prosperity follows their own will. (GoŚv 38)
At the very moment of his birth, a sound resonated through the world, beneficial to the ears:
"O Kurus, whoever reaches this place, worship him; by consuming his flesh and blood, attain auspiciousness. (GoŚv 39)
Then, hearing that superhuman sound, the men quickly approached that place in a body;
beholding that saintly and patient one whose form was as massive as a mountain, they drew near with trepidation.

Seeing those hosts of gods rushing forward with speed, their hands clutching swords that were whirling and splintering, the throngs of deities cried out loudly and piteously, "Alas! Alas!", as their crowns fell away and grew loose.

Upon seeing me with my body so massive, vast, and long, or upon hearing the lamentations of the inhabitants of the celestial city, no one remained with an unshaken mind; for a moment, everyone was moved by the thought, "This is merely a mass of fat, blood, and marrow. (GoŚv 42)

Beholding those citizens as if they were his own friends, the joy that expanded in the mind of that wise one— He, whose intellect was as firm as the essence of the mountains, considered that very joy to be the sufficient fruit of his exceedingly difficult task.
Considering his own body, though its flesh had grown full, to be a vessel for providing desired assistance to the worlds,
that virtuous one conceived a deep attachment even to *saṃsāra*, which is the target for falling into absolute calamity.
Those bodies of his, which were destroyed in the continuity of existence— lacking the capacity to provide for the welfare of others and fragile as they were to momentary dissolution—
the Great-souled One, having reckoned them as being as high as mountains, assumed his own body out of pure purification alone.
Perceiving him to be thus possessed of extensive transformations, they, out of fortitude, cut him down with sharp axes as if he were a tree;
with minds free from hesitation, devoid of compassion, and turned toward cruelty, even he became like a tree, his anger having been removed.
Others, like enemies, scattered him with swords, their forearms crimson from the blood of those they had severed;
yet he, whose actions were pure, remained as if his heart were blossoming with joy at the successful accomplishment of his desired task.
Then, from the cuts made by the edge of his sword, blood flowed from him— red as the petals of a blooming karavīra flower—
like water from mineral-rich torrents on the variegated peaks of the Vindhya mountain when the rainy season has arrived.

From the cavernous openings of his wounds, as if from the fissures of a body wounded by caustic acid, there flowed rivers with vast white waves, obstructed by masses of foam due to their great volume; thus they say.
O noble-hearted one, because he somehow fulfilled the hopes of those who relied upon the power of his vows,
he experienced incomparable joy even when, upon reaching the city of Āmrapura, his body was about to perish.
As his body cavities were pierced by the sharp edge of the axe,
blood flowed forth like molten gold from the groves of Mount Sumeru, whose peaks are licked by the flames of a bordering fire.
When his tender body was fearlessly shattered on all sides by those fierce weapons,
the despondency vanished from the heart of him whose pure intellect remained steadfast amidst the destruction— a heart moist with love.

As his body was being cut away—having become like a moat for the sky—the channels of blood, following the paths formed by habitual practice, acted as broad torrents from mountain rivers; yet there was neither despondency nor exhaustion in his mind.

In his expansive caves, whose floors were mud from the abundant flesh, blood, and fat, the hosts of predatory beasts roamed about free from fear and suspicion; yet neither despondency nor exhaustion arose in his mind.

If the flesh taken from his body by ignoble beings were somehow gathered together in its entirety, that mass of flesh would surpass even Mount Sumeru; yet there was neither malice nor weariness in his mind.
The weapons recoiled upon their own bodies against that virtuous one, whose disposition was naturally gentle and whose resolve remained unbroken;
and in his mind—which was tranquil, enjoying the delight of being intent upon the welfare of others—neither despondency nor weariness arose.
Those whose limbs were smeared with his blood shone, freed from disease and dejection;
and those who drank his blood, though previously diseased, flourished, freed from all ailments, as did all the worlds.
As he gazed upon the people free from disease, a deep-seated joy arose in the mind of the Friend of the World;
yet, as he beheld again the useless flesh [of his own body], his fickle heart once more began to swing with restlessness.
With the layers of skin flayed away, his raw flesh exposed and copper-red, and with blood streaming from his wounds leaving him an exceptionally deep crimson,
that transformed body of the resolute one shone like a heap of hibiscus flowers reaching toward the clouds.
Beholding that suffering as being centered in a single locus while his body was being cut by very sharp weapons,
he dispelled that suffering with ease, having attained a state of mental unification between himself and the other person.
The course of the latent impression of self-attachment is indeed harsh in its transformation;
by it, people of defiled intellect stumble even toward the virtuous who are like fathers.
Whoever consumed the flesh of this compassionate one was cured of their disease;
in due course, he thus delivered the entire world from the ocean of calamity and suffering.
Then the entire world, freed from all diseases and calamities, having conceived love, reverence, and great respect for that Great Being, bowed down to the Bodhisattva dog and said:

Oh, what excellence of goodness resulting from the practice of compassion! Oh, what devotion, free from all stain, toward virtuous qualities! Oh, noble one, this deed of yours, performed for the sake of others, is exquisite and transcends the human! GoŚv_63 //
Oh, the moistness of the great compassion for the world, the supreme among all beings! Oh, the lack of desire for one's own happiness and worldly exertions!
Oh, how the minds of the wise—who follow the path to enlightenment—are steadfastly fixed upon what is auspicious! GoŚv 64.
Oh, how inconceivable is your skill in means! Oh, how sublime is your delight in the welfare of others!
Homage be to you, the sole kinsman of the world, who acts for the sake of the virtuous through such an inconceivable excellence of conduct.
You are our father, if you are indeed a father; you alone are the teacher who desires our welfare, if you are indeed the spiritual preceptor of the Dharma;
you alone are the deity, if that is not merely a worldly convention; for you alone are the supreme refuge for the world in its distress.
Therefore, you ought to purify this world, which has been defiled by a mind intent on your own exertion, through the consecration of your command.
Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his mind was filled with serene faith, spoke to him.
One should not constantly think, "This suffering is mine," while wandering through the cycle of rebirths for the sake of sentient beings alone;
rather, having beheld you overwhelmed by calamity, my mind now finds its health and happiness in the thought, "Suffering has come upon me."
There is no task more weighty for me than the welfare of others; this alone is what binds one to the prison of saṃsāra.
Therefore, transcending conduct that is defiled by evil deeds, always perform what is beneficial to yourselves for my sake.

Knowing these worlds to be the fields for enjoying one's own performed actions, and that they rest in the palm of Death— who is harsh even without occasion— you must strive to avoid sinful deeds, which result in the arising of unbearable torment, even at the cost of your life.

Accumulate merits—which have a good end, which bestow fruits that are not to be despised, and which are like provisions for the path through the dense forest of birth—with the thought of repaying me; for the word of a spiritual friend must not be transgressed. GoŚv_71 //
Having thus instructed those living beings, the Great-souled One— his body worn out and shattered by the edge of the sharpened axe,
his task completed, and having cast off that body of most hideous form— ascended straight to heaven.

Thus, these oceans of supreme glory, which are the livelihood of the world and were once struck down by the falling thunderbolts of calamity, now—through the conjunction of prosperity—extend as far as the limits of the sky when free from the clouds and darkness; like the rays of the moon, they rescue the world.
Thus ends the forty-third Jātaka, the Śvajātaka, in the glorious Jātakamālā.
